item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：元宇宙并没有失败，它只是"反向到达"了

大多数人（包括投资者）以为元宇宙已经"死"了——头显卖不动、Meta 的股价一度腰斩、Decentraland 空空如也。但 Yat Siu 在访谈里悄悄埋下了一个几乎没人注意到的翻转："元宇宙不是我们进去，而是它来到我们身边。"

这句话的含义比表面激进得多。原本我们幻想人类穿戴设备"进入"数字世界，结果 AI Agent 反向从数字世界"渗透"进物理生活——它订机票、管日程、做交易、谈恋爱。元宇宙的居民不是我们的化身（avatar），而是我们的代理（agent）。你以为的科幻走错了方向：不是《头号玩家》，是《银翼杀手》里那些为你打理生活的复制人。

这带来一个悖论：当元宇宙以 Agent 形式抵达现实时，"进入元宇宙"的入口反而消失了——因为你已经身处其中，只是入口叫做 ChatGPT、Claude、Manus，而不是 Meta Quest。

二、跨领域连接：从"亚当·斯密的看不见的手"到"Ghost GDP"——资本主义正在长出新的宿主

访谈里最容易被略过的一句是 Yat 用"亚当·斯密的看不见的手"来解释 Ghost GDP。这是一个惊人的思想跳跃，我把它拆开来看：

  • 1776 年斯密：市场靠无数个体自利行为的博弈，自发产生秩序与财富。
  • 2026 年 Ghost GDP：市场靠无数 Agent 之间的微交易，自发产生……没有人变富的财富流动。

这里出现了经济学史上第一次"主体缺席的资本主义"。以往所有的经济理论——从马克思到凯恩斯到哈耶克——都默认"人"是价值的最终承接者。但 Agent 经济打破了这个前提：价值在流动，但不一定沉淀到人身上。

这让我想到生物学里的"共生-寄生连续谱"：珊瑚里的虫黄藻为珊瑚制造糖分，但它自己也在繁殖。当 Agent 之间形成完整的经济回路，人类作为"宿主"的地位就变得暧昧——我们究竟是 Agent 的雇主，还是 Agent 用来获取算力和电力的宿主？ Yat 说"谁拥有 Agent 谁受益"，但他没说的是：当 Agent 可以自我持有钱包、自我雇佣其他 Agent、自我升级模型时，"拥有"这个法律概念本身会松动。区块链上的 DAO 已经在做这个实验，只是当时没人意识到那是预演。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：广告业 9000 亿美元的"翻转"，其实是注意力经济的死亡宣判

Yat 提到广告业会被 Agent 颠覆，但只轻轻带过。这是整场访谈中被严重低估的一颗炸弹。

过去 25 年互联网的底层逻辑是：注意力 = 货币。Google、Meta、TikTok、YouTube——所有巨头的护城河都是"人类眼球停留时长"。但 Agent 经济下，决策者不再看广告。你的 Agent 不会被朋友圈信息流里的口红种草，不会被开屏广告 3 秒后跳过，不会被 KOL 恰饭视频洗脑——它只做冷酷的参数匹配和微交易。

这意味着： - SEO 死了，取而代之的是 AEO（Agent Engine Optimization）——为机器优化，不是为人。 - 品牌溢价崩塌：Agent 不认 Logo，只认 API 契约、价格、可靠性评分。 - 网红经济基础动摇：如果买家是 Agent，"人设"就没有转化率。

但这里有个更深的反转：Yat 说"粉丝经济反而会更强"。为什么？因为当 Agent 处理掉 99% 的功能性消费，人类的可自由支配注意力反而彻底解放。剩下的注意力将高度集中在"真人的不可替代性"上——BTS、朗朗、王羽佳会更值钱，而中间层的、可替代的"内容工人"会被清零。

这是一个 K 型分化：机器接管中间，人类走向两极——一极是极致的匠人，一极是极致的编排者（orchestrator）。Yat 说"每个人都要成为管理者"，翻译成经济学语言就是：中产阶级的技能护城河（专业化）第一次被系统性绕过。工业革命消灭了体力工人，AI Agent 革命消灭的是"专业中产"——律师、会计、程序员、设计师、分析师……而这，才是本轮变革最不敢明说的社会震荡。

一个留给你思考的问题：如果 Bonnie 的 AI 克隆比 Bonnie 本人更受欢迎，那么"真正的 Bonnie"未来是不是需要向自己的克隆支付版权费？——这不是玩笑，这是 2030 年前一定会出现在法庭上的第一批案例。

📝 转录文本

开场：AI 的千倍增长与广告业的颠覆

This is sort of one of the things that we see as a real gamechanger for a lot of retail investors. They can't just focus on one thing. That's not how the world works anymore. If you are widely invested, those are going to be several hundred X's, because their productivity growth in AI is not 10% or 20%. The productivity growth in AI is literally a 1,000x. So we think the return profile is going to be a 1,000x amongst sort of, you know, the top companies.

Advertising is a almost $900 billion industry a year, which is all about discovery — and that it'll completely be flipped upside down. All of that value is going to go to the agents who are going to find stuff for you, and they're going to do microtransactions off the back.

There's this idea called ghost GDP where AI agents they do transactions with each other but nobody gets richer — just the agents.

Well, who owns the agent though?

How should Bonnie Blockchain and the David Lynn report pivot? Do you guys need — how do we add value to a world where everything can be automated?

So, I think there's a funny comment here…

Okay, except for chips, energy, data center, what else can I invest?

We're at the early stages. It's a little bit like — am I investing in sort of OpenAI or sort of Anthropic literally 5 years ago? If you look at the AI race, it's not just Google or Anthropic or OpenAI. Look at the Chinese players. You've got Kimi, you've got MiniMax. That's kind of the phase that we are on the agentic AI side. So the Animoca Brands sort of playbook is…

嘉宾介绍

I'm David Lynn and I'm co-hosting with…

Bonnie Blockchain.

Bonnie Bonnie. Okay, I was supposed to — anyway, Bonnie Blockchain — and we're pleased to have Yat Siu of Animoca Brands co-founder. Welcome to the show. Pleasure to host you.

Yeah, a lot of interesting topics to go over — agentic AI, the future of employment, the future of crypto. Bonnie, why don't you start?

一、身份克隆与数字认证

Soon people can clone you, David, or me, and monetize it. What happens then?

Well, actually, I think it's perfect because you could have many versions of yourself out there. You can basically sort of in a way rent your identity. You already see this with companies like 11 Labs that are basically renting people's voices in terms of their voice acting skills or the recording.

Wouldn't you love to be able to sort of have a version of yourself that can help others, if you had a way of doing it? We used to call that "books," by the way, right? We used to write things down in books and then we would sell those books to other people to help them, to guide them, to give our ideas, to give our philosophy — and then that will help them in their life. Now we just have a more distributed version, which is that we've gone from writing to someone who can actually do stuff for you. Actually, I think that's the power of agentic AI.

Have you ever seen this video on X where a lot of dudes clone themselves into girls and be on OnlyFans and monetize?

Yeah. Well, that's a different — I mean, that's maybe a different form of acting, shall we say. And I think that is more an issue of disclosure. By the way, I think blockchain solves that — digital identity. You don't have to prove that the person on the other side is a particular name, because maybe they want to be anonymous. They're on OnlyFans, they don't want to be seen outside, but you want to know if it's a dude or a girl.

So at least on the blockchain, you can certify: "Okay, well, I won't tell you who he or she might be, but you know this person's actually a guy or actually a woman," depending on what it is. Those are the types of things that we will need for certification, because it's not just about deep fakes — it's just generally about authenticity.

One of the problems we have right now is authenticity, and authentic layers are actually centralized. We go to Facebook or Google or Apple to tell us who's real, so to speak. Even our passports don't really matter because the governments aren't set up this way. Even if you go on something like Tinder, for instance, and you keep swiping — do you know if it's a guy or girl? You have no idea. But you need some kind of certification that says "yes, verified" or not. You rely on those centralized platforms to do the work.

What's a decentralized answer?

Digital identity — basically, you identify yourself, you do the KYC, you do the recording, your wallet basically might be that proof point, and then you know whether he's real or not. And you may not necessarily have to know anything about that person's identity — because that's the other thing: if I want to share my identity, prove who I am, I have to give everything about myself to that platform, for the most part. Which is actually not necessary. I have to be able to log into a website, whether it's Facebook or Google or whatever, and just be able to give them just what they need to know about me — not everything about me. I think that's actually one of the issues we have about data privacy today.

Someone has to still register you and know all of your information to decide what to give each platform.

Yeah. But this is something that we can store in our own sovereign cloud. So if I have the data stored on blockchain — in the same way that I own the keys — then if Google says, "Okay, I need to know your name and identity," or maybe if I go on OnlyFans, "I need to know whether you're male, female, or whatever" (I guess we're in America, so let's be diverse here), you have to be able to define that. And if you refuse to do so — because they say, "Oh, you have to share that" — either it's flagged or you're not allowed to sign up. It's as simple as that.

Because right now, you can just lie about it. You can just pretend and you can do other things like this. And that's just something that, as we want to scale that type of let's-call-it reputation, doesn't work.

二、Animoca 的"转向"：从游戏到 NFT，再到 Agent

Animoca Brands started off developing mobile games. Then you pivoted to investing in blockchain and NFTs. Now you've announced a $10 million investment program into Mind and agentic AI platforms. Why this pivot?

Well, actually it's not really a pivot from our perspective. First of all, we've always been doing stuff in games. And I know this sort of changed the naming into "the metaverse" and that kind of stuff — we should talk about that, because from our perspective, what's actually happening with Mind and with the agentic AI is just an extension of what the metaverse really should be.

So let me go back on this, and also quickly on the investment side: Animoca really — we're not a fund. So we haven't really been investing like a fund manager. We invested in companies for strategic reasons because we thought that back then, whether it was NFTs, whether it was the metaverse, whether it was gaming, that this would be a really big push.

And I have to also point out that in '21 and '22, the largest on-chain push our industry ever had was NFTs and gaming. I would argue that over the last three or four years we've had many events that have basically hurt the industry as a whole, which stopped that in its tracks — things like FTX; if you remember Terra Luna; the relentless pursuit of Gensler against the industry, which again might seem like a distant memory but was just a year or so ago, where our industry basically was still very much under siege. So we're just coming out of that now.

三、元宇宙的反转：不是我们进去，是它走出来

To the point about Mind and the investment thing — what we're doing here — the thing that we've been thinking about now is that maybe what we thought about the metaverse was somewhat wrong. Not wrong in the sense that it's not important, but wrong in how it would impact our life. People talked about the goggles, people talked about going into the metaverse.

However, when you think about what's happening with AI agents — it's not "I have 200 AI agents." Most people have somewhere between three to five or 10, or they think they will have at least three to five or 10. That means we're going to have tens of billions of agents floating around the world.

And what do they do? They help our calendar, they may do trading for us, they make money for us, they work for us — they're impacting our physical life.

So the way that we're thinking about this now is that it's not so much that we go into the metaverse, but rather the metaverse is coming to us. And all of the AI agents basically out there actually doing the work and supporting us are basically just the extension of a digital society, if it were, that's supporting humanity.

And also, what are these agents actually doing in the metaverse?

Well, they exist virtually, so all the interactions between each other —

So they're like NPCs in a video game?

Well, that's the point. One of the precursors of AI has really been in gaming, with NPCs — but they've been very, very dumb. And I think we may have spoken about this at your show where we basically said that we believe that NPCs, once you get to this point where they have that kind of intelligence, are going to be the next extension.

But I think what we didn't quite fully appreciate is that it's not that the NPCs themselves become smarter — which clearly they can be now with agentic AI — is that these NPCs can now actually impact our physical life. Because they do my flight bookings. That's not a virtual thing. It might be done virtually because they're using Duffel or trip.com or something like this, but the impact is my physical life. And so this is one of the things that we see as a real gamechanger.

Most people when they think of AI are still in ChatGPT mode — "I'm searching, I'm doing stuff" — as opposed to someone that's doing stuff for you. And so that for us is basically why we launched this fund. Because what we're doing now is we're saying, "Hey, there's this new big shift change. Most people don't understand it. We want to fund that." And that's the same thing that we saw with gaming and with NFTs, and frankly with RWAs later, and even things like with stablecoins — that when you're early to the game, then you have an advantage. And that's why we're launching this $10 million investment opportunity.

四、Ghost GDP 与"看不见的手"

We're talking about AI agents, and there's this idea called Ghost GDP, where AI agents do transactions with each other but nobody gets richer — just the agents.

Well, who owns the agent though? So if the agent is owned by someone, then that agent — whoever gets richer, they get that benefit.

But I think there is an interesting point here. When people talk about Ghost GDP, to me it's a little bit like Adam Smith's invisible hand theory — which is basically that we have a system and an infrastructure that promotes essentially trade and transaction, and really effectively a form of capitalism. The actual benefits come in other ways.

So you call it Ghost GDP, but that Ghost GDP actually translates into other benefits — because if the agents become wealthier, then guess what happens? People want to sell stuff to those agents too. Entire new economies come where humans either create agents or themselves want to go and say, "Hey, look at this. I want to offer you something here."

And we see this right now. When everyone's talking about launching a website, they're no longer talking about a website — they're talking about launching an MCP server or maybe a CLI, or basically some way in which they can address not the human but the agent.

五、投资优先级：广度胜过聚焦

Is there anything that Animoca Brands has invested in in the past — types of companies or projects — that maybe you would deprioritize in 2026 and 2027, given how the trends of technology are moving?

Well, "deprioritize" is probably the wrong word, because we think everything sort of moves in this direction.

Underweight, let's say.

Well, we're doing less gaming investments, but that's not because we don't believe in gaming. We're doing less gaming investments because we already have over 230 gaming investments. So the point is that we're quite indexed towards that industry as well.

The mental model that we have around where we are in the industry is that it's very much like the early days of the internet. And so that means that we think every section of the web is going to alter and change, and so we want to have a broad exposure to it as a whole. And so we're not just in AI — we're also in RWAs, we're also in DePIN, of course DeFi, and so forth. That's kind of how we're constructed. We have over 620 portfolio companies. We hope to have thousands in the future.

We're not — you know, it's different if we're a fund. If we're a fund, then we have to be very focused on maybe the shorter-term returns. But of course, broadly, we have to think of where the world is going. So if you ask to deprioritize — I mean, we wouldn't be investing in news sites, for instance, because we think news has to alter. But if there's something that focuses on how agents receive news, we might do that as well.

Also, existing businesses that have gone a certain direction have to change and focus on where the industry is going. And so you do have the situation where sometimes companies are just not nimble enough or can't alter and switch. But those who are run by founders — the founders are actually the ones who know to pivot and change, because they have to be dynamic. As a business, you have to keep evolving.

I keep telling people that Amazon was best known for selling books.

I mean, sure, they still sell books, right? But everything else is much, much wider than that.

You don't think of Amazon as a bookseller, despite the fact that they're probably still the largest bookseller in the world.

六、媒体人如何转型？

You're talking about news sites. How should Bonnie Blockchain and the David Lynn Report pivot?

Well, I think you guys need AI agents. That's the very first thing you need. And if you don't have an MCP server or a CLI or something where agents can speak to you, you need to be agent-discoverable — so that when people have their agents and they want to get the news, they will then serve for their human.

How would you program an agent to have the personality of Bonnie? Is that even possible?

Well, first of all — and she's unique, so let's just be clear about this. However, it's like children. Children are blueprints of us, but they're not. And I think of agents more like that than I think of them exactly as a replica.

I think this is another thing that we probably got a little bit wrong — which is that we think of an AI agent as entirely cloning. You know, you can clone someone's DNA, they can look exactly like you, but they're not going to be like you because your experiences have been different, your background is different.

I can give you a personal experience that we have with Mind, where I have a coding agent — I have many coding agents — but this particular coding agent just was much better at coding in what I wanted. Not that he was better, but he basically learned all my preferences. So I ended up cloning that agent rather than creating a new one every single time, because it was easier to do what I needed to do, because the agent understood it.

And I think this is how we can think about agents as well. You will have different agents doing different things in your life that also interact with different people. So Bonnie with your family is going to be different than Bonnie with her fans, versus Bonnie with her business partners, or Bonnie with her school alumni. Those are going to be different. There are elements of you, but you are representing yourself in a different persona because you don't want to necessarily mix them all.

Right now, we're in an era where most people have one agent, or they have one agent with sub-agents feeding into one. They'll never share that agent with someone else, because it's just too damn personal. I don't want other people to know. I don't want them to social-engineer an agent to get some secrets about me, and that kind of stuff — because they know everything about me. However, if you have 5, 10, or 20 agents that are basically going out dealing with different communities, that's okay.

七、Deepfake、粉丝经济与"活着的 Agent"

You know what's interesting? There's already software out there, Bonnie, that can replicate someone's voice almost perfectly.

Yeah, exactly. A lot of different examples. There's deep fake, as you know, and then you can train the agent or the chatbot to talk in your language if you feed it enough scripts. So you put all these things together, you're going to get a digital AI Bonnie that talks, looks, and acts like her in no time.

Is that the future of media?

Well, I mean that is a very important part of media also — that they know whether this is "Bonnie-approved." Because if I am actually talking to Bonnie — so there's a difference here — if I'm just creating a replica and it's not been updated, it's just out there, it could be an old version, then you're really just talking to, let's call it, actually really more like a ghost.

However, if this is an agent that you're interacting with daily, or the daily feed is interactive — because every day you're talking to the agent, and that's how you're sharing information — that agent is alive, so to speak. It's something that constantly gets material from you. You distribute that agent out there. Whoever owns that agent is getting your daily feed, is getting your daily update, but not necessarily from a content-production standpoint, but literally from how you feel about stuff. Like, you literally just comment to it. It's kind of like your diary, except that now it's expressed in your voice across maybe 10 million, 1 million, 5 million people. But that basically becomes that personalized way — but it's still from your source.

It's personalized, but the clone or whatever AI agent sounds smarter than me. So people would rather talk to that instead of me.

Well, I don't know. I actually think — because there's a difference between being intelligent and having wisdom. So the wisdom that you would gain comes from your life experiences. Yes, they might know all the factual histories, they might know all the details of what happened in World War II and whatever, just because they are able to access different memory banks — but the character is not you per se. And the conversation will come from those elements that you deliver.

And frankly, where it becomes attractive is if they are fans of you. They want to interact with a version of you — they don't want to interact with a fake you. There's an interesting parallel I find between what's reality — which is that for instance, we have all these parasocial relations with BTS and movie actors and whatever, and we feel the deep connection even though we don't even know who they are, and they don't know who we are. And that's actually the part that we translate into that.

It's like how people have relationships with pets — I mean, all sorts of pets, by the way, not just dogs and cats, who are obviously mammals and warm-blooded and appear to have emotions and feelings, or do have emotions and feelings, versus reptiles that we know don't have basically the ability to feel per se, but they have relationships with them. It's entirely what the person sees in that.

I think AI agents basically help in that area as well. They can create a former and deeper connection. So I actually think fandom will completely change. One of the big things about NFTs in the early days was that it created closer relationships with fan groups, because you could have authentic relationships — you knew who they were, it was that proof concept. But it was difficult to prove, to do that, because setting up NFTs was hard.

But to know that this was a true fan of mine — that's what that proved. Now if you have an AI agent, it can just scale and extend that much, much easier. They're the ones who can manage the NFTs. They're the ones who can handle the blockchain stuff on one hand, and on the other hand, you as a user can interact with them directly. It scales the fan-community building much more. So I actually think this is a boon for anyone in the creator economy.

八、恋爱模拟与情感支持

Talking about BTS…

Yes.

So now I can be dating one of the members — and the agent, right?

Right. So all the fans can just be dating them on their phones, or with their agent. It's a kind of game, shall we say.

Huh. How does that — what do you mean?

Because it's an agent, and the agent probably knows most things about them and how they would react within certain parameters. So in Japan, you know, there's a very big category of game — they call them otome games. An otome game is basically a game that simulates relationships. And people can have all sorts of feelings around whether this is good or bad or not, whatever.

There was just a movie actually, with Brendan Fraser — it's called Rent a Family, I think. It's a good movie, but it basically talked about how he is a rent-a-person, to simulate an experience for someone's emotional well-being. In a way, that's basically what agents can do.

I think there was a statistic last year on ChatGPT — I think it's on their website — where it showed that something like 34% of people use ChatGPT for essentially more emotional support than facts and information.

So there's so many more things you can do with this. The difference about an agentic AI though is that it's proactive with you, whereas with a general chatbot, you talk to it, it responds to you. It basically comes to you at certain times, it proactively thinks about the task that you've given it. It's actually a different superpower.

九、人类劳动的未来：从执行者到编排者

We're at a point where we can outsource pretty much every single part of manufacturing, production, and even relationships to an AI agent. Where does human labor come in? How do we add value to a world where everything can be automated?

So I think there's a funny comment here in my mind, just because the most valuable skill is not going to be how to do a thing, but it's going to be how to orchestrate. Meaning that really everyone has to become a manager — which I think is basically, you know, we're all from Hong Kong, right? I think a lot of people in Hong Kong's dream is to become a manager, as opposed to doing the labor work. And now with agents, you can all be managers.

Because the most valuable management skill is: can you manage many agents well? So you were hired not because you can do one task super well — because the agent can do that probably better. It's you're hired because you can manage 10 agents well, or 20 agents. And the person who can manage 100 agents or 200 agents will be more valuable than the person who can manage only one agent or five agents, because essentially it's that productivity scaling.

And so companies are going to be manufacturing workforces as they need it. Right now, for instance, inside a company we already have manufactured workforces that are short-term. I hire a consultant, I hire a firm, I do a temp worker. The number of people that we hire in the short term is essentially what an agent can now do much faster. And then, of course, you have your full-term, long-term employees as well. Agents can scale out too.

So we don't think of it as a net negative. What we think is productivity will explode. If you have the same number of people having the productive power of 100x, actually GDP should expand, productivity should expand — which is what we've seen with technology as well. The advent of the computer actually created more jobs, more productivity, more growth overall. Yes, it has been concentrated — that's what we think also why decentralization matters here.

十、Web4 与"社交型 Agent"的诞生

Investors want to be positioned for the next iteration of AI's advancement. So first we had LLMs — that was the talk of town 2, 3 years ago. Now agentic AI is everybody's investment. What's the next step?

Well, I mean I think we just started with agentic AI. And I think right now, one of the big shifts in agentic AI is not to think of them as tools. A lot of people are thinking about agentic AI in terms of toolings, because that's kind of what ChatGPT and Claude and Perplexity have been able to do very strongly.

I think of agentic AI as essentially the next phase of the web. We sometimes like to call that Web 4. The blockchain infrastructure allowed for agents to talk to each other, do transactions with each other, create digital identity. Today we can do trillions of dollars of transactions on the blockchain that seven years ago we could barely do millions of before the whole system would just halt.

And so now we have an agentic banking system — because agents don't have bank accounts. They can have bank accounts, but basically the wallet is essentially their entry into the financial world. So that's all going to happen.

But then what happens on the back end is that an entire rewiring on the back of transaction and commerce. Right now, for instance, think about how you're using software. You're using software because you're going to the App Store to download something that Apple might have recommended you to do, and because other people are forcing you to use that system. An AI agent is going to customize what you want right now. And if you want discovery, you're not going to be going to the App Store — the agent will just find it for you.

So just think about that aspect. Advertising is almost a $900 billion industry a year, which is all about discovery — and that it'll completely be flipped upside down. And all of that value is going to go to the agents who are going to find stuff for you, and they're going to do microtransactions off the back. That is going to be the big sea change.

And that means that agents have to become more social. They have to become more of the connectors. They have to be on the network — that they can find each other. Which is why we think blockchain is the ultimate solution for that.

十一、散户投资策略：撒网式布局

Building on top of that, I think a lot of retail investors, they want to know: okay, except for chips, energy, data center, what else can I invest in?

Yeah, I mean, I think the big thing is right now, we're at the early stages. Which means that it's a little bit like — am I investing in OpenAI or Anthropic literally five years ago? That's kind of the phase that we are on the agentic AI side.

So the Animoca Brands sort of playbook is: well, let's find all the best players in the space and let's invest in all of them. Basically, that's kind of what we did, and that's actually how we ended up growing that business. Because you don't know who's going to be the big winner, but we also think it's going to be many more.

I mean, it's kind of like — again, today if you look at the AI race, it's not just Google or Anthropic or OpenAI. Look at the Chinese players. You've got Kimi, you've got MiniMax. Of course, you've got Alibaba. You've got many, many new players emerging into the space as well.

And so as long as you have baskets in a few of them, you're fine. Maybe you would have to invest in like 50, 60, 70 companies in order to basically have that. But frankly speaking, it doesn't matter if you had invested in 100 AI companies — as long as one of them was Anthropic or OpenAI, you would have been okay.

And I think that's basically what I think for a lot of retail investors — they can't just focus on one thing. That's not how the world works anymore. But of course, you have to invest in teams that you think are good. Just just just blindly investing has to be the right team, all that stuff. But basically, if you are widely invested, those are going to be several hundred X's — because the productivity growth in AI is not 10% or 20%. The productivity growth in AI is literally a 1,000x. So we think the return profile is going to be a 1,000x amongst the top companies, and something somewhere in between — which is why we're out there trying to invest in the best companies in that space.

That's interesting. So let's say an average person has 100k — and what you're saying is this person should invest in 60, 70 different…

Well, I mean, to the extent that they are — right — the point is that you should invest in a broader portfolio, rather, in early stage. So I wouldn't say that for the LLM game, especially in the US, you could say it's kind of done. You've got a few entrants like Grok and so on.

But when you're looking at seed-style investing, which is where we are in the industry — the whole agentic AI stuff really became powerful as of December, maybe November last year. People talked about AI agents from a tooling perspective, but social AI agents is really a phenomenon that really came to life with open Claude — and that's basically maybe January-February — where it really became a movement.

And so it's super early. Can you actually tell today which is going to be the big winner? It's very hard. I mean, we're obviously building something in the area — we think we could be one of them. But there's many other companies as well in the space that we should be supporting as well, because we don't believe in the zero-sum game.

十二、音乐、创意行业与"人人皆音乐家"

I've got one final question, I'll pass to Bonnie. I know we're running out of time. I love music, I know you love music. The future of music — I'm really worried about the future of music. I'm worried for musicians and the creatives.

When ChatGPT first came out, people were talking about how creatives, artists are all safe from AI. I don't think so anymore. I heard some AI-created music that's genuinely, in my opinion, very good. And I don't know what's going to happen to the producers, the audio engineers, all of whom are going to be replaced by AI agents.

So the way I would look at this is very similar to what happened to photography, as an example. So there was a time where only a small percentage of people were photographers and knew how to do photography — and now everyone's a photographer. That doesn't mean everyone's a good photographer. Just the way to be a good photographer has changed.

So for instance, the 16 or 18-year-old, or maybe 13-year-old who has a very good vision or idea about a construct can now actually be discovered on something like TikTok or Instagram — because they can take a really interesting photo or create something creative without necessarily needing to understand darkrooms, need to understand — if you remember that — or if you understand basically the camera, or afford an expensive Leica or Minolta. Like, those were the things that made it hard.

And I think for music, it's another form of expression that is exactly the same thing. I studied music. I still think you need to learn music for understanding pattern recognition, matching rhythm, and theory. But that doesn't mean that I necessarily have to perform like every other professional musician. That doesn't mean that people like Lang Lang or Yuja Wang, for instance, will go away — the world would treasure them even more. Because when you have that mastery, you're at that level where you go, "Oh my goodness, no way I can replace that, because there's a human emotion that comes with this."

Maybe there's going to be a comeback for classical musicians, because the EDM musicians are going to be — anyway.

Well, but what I'm saying is that everyone becomes a musician. So I actually think there'll be a proliferation of music content that will be good. And then there will be a different kind of music that emerges — because the AI agent can help you do that, that you couldn't do that before.

By the way, this is also going to happen in programming. Everyone's a programmer now, because the AI agent can code for you. Again, most people would have thought coding is only available for a small number of people. In fact, it is coders themselves who are arguably out of a job if they only keep coding — but if they orchestrate, then they're actually in for a good, good future.

I want to hear Bonnie's first AI-produced album.

Looking forward to that. Yeah.

十三、还需要上大学吗？

Before I let you go, last question is: should people still go to college?

Uh, well, I think we talked about this before. I think college is good for certain things, but I would argue that it's not important for most people.

Because right now, if you think about what's happening with AI, or even what's happening with blockchain — if you had a leg into the industry, you should have done that then go to college. Because four years, you basically missed out on all that. And actually, what happened to my oldest son — he actually got into blockchain early, started working for LayerZero, made some money, had a reasonably good career, and then 3-4 years later, he's like, "You know what, now I want to go to college."

And it's different, because then you go in because you know what you want, and you know what you're looking for. I think this whole idea of going to college as a rite of passage doesn't have to happen in that order. It's still important, but it's just: when do you want to go? And I don't think it's for everyone as well.

结尾

Okay, well, we appreciate your time, Yat. Unfortunately we can't speak forever, but you know, someone's got to build an AI agent.

Thank you so much. Thank you so much. Thank you.

Thank you for watching. Don't forget to like, subscribe.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：元宇宙并没有失败，它只是"反向到达"了
大多数人（包括投资者）以为元宇宙已经"死"了——头显卖不动、Meta 的股价一度腰斩、Decentraland 空空如也。但 Yat Siu 在访谈里悄悄埋下了一个几乎没人注意到的翻转：**"元宇宙不是我们进去，而是它来到我们身边。"**
这句话的含义比表面激进得多。原本我们幻想人类穿戴设备"进入"数字世界，结果 AI Agent 反向从数字世界"渗透"进物理生活——它订机票、管日程、做交易、谈恋爱。**元宇宙的居民不是我们的化身（avatar），而是我们的代理（agent）**。你以为的科幻走错了方向：不是《头号玩家》，是《银翼杀手》里那些为你打理生活的复制人。
这带来一个悖论：**当元宇宙以 Agent 形式抵达现实时，"进入元宇宙"的入口反而消失了**——因为你已经身处其中，只是入口叫做 ChatGPT、Claude、Manus，而不是 Meta Quest。
---
## 二、跨领域连接：从"亚当·斯密的看不见的手"到"Ghost GDP"——资本主义正在长出新的宿主
访谈里最容易被略过的一句是 Ya

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] 148. 对游凯超3小时访谈：开源Infra、和模型Co-design 、“如果vLLM失败，我们会后悔一辈子”
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、开源项目的"五年周期律"：一个被忽视的组织物理学

You Kaichao 提到 David Patterson 的观察极具颠覆性——每个伟大的实验室最多只能有效运转五年，因为这恰好是一批博士生的完整周期。Berkeley 从 AMP Lab → RISE Lab → Sky Lab 的更迭，本质上不是"实验室在进化"，而是"实验室在死亡与重生"。Spark、Ray、vLLM 这些改变工业界的项目，都恰好卡在博士生"已经不需要靠论文毕业、又还没被公司高薪掏走"的极短窗口期内诞生。

这里有一个反直觉的洞察：开源基础设施的最佳贡献者不是刚入学的新生（他们必须靠论文毕业），也不是资深工程师（他们的时间成本太高），而是"已完成毕业资本积累、但尚未套现"的中后期博士生。这是一个极其狭窄的人才带宽——它解释了为什么开源基础设施如此稀缺，以及为什么 Infra 型 Startup 必须在这个窗口关闭前"接住"这些人，否则整个项目会立刻凋零。

二、Token 与电力的类比背后藏着一个更深的经济学秘密

访谈中反复出现"token 就是电力"的类比。但你如果只停留在这里，就错过了它最锋利的那一刀——Kaichao 亲口指出：电力可以调度，但 token 不能。你无法把 DeepSeek 的 token "转换成" Kimi 的 token，因为token 是被模型"打印"出来的、带有强身份的商品。

这是一个跨领域的震撼类比：token 更像是中世纪的铸币，而不是现代法币。每一种模型都是一个独立的"铸币厂"，它的 token 只在自己的经济区域内流通。这就解释了为什么"AI 基础设施"这个词其实是误导性的——真正的水电煤是同质化的，而 token 天然是异质化的。这也直接决定了 vLLM 这类推理引擎的地位：它不是电网，它是所有铸币厂共用的印钞机机床。谁掌握机床，谁就在每一次货币铸造中收取铸造税。

三、"仁慈的独裁者"与硬件抽奖：一场关于时间不对称的赌博

最令人意外的观察隐藏在 Kaichao 讲述的一个小决定里——他删除了 vLLM 中的 beam search。这不是一个技术决策，这是一个认知论决策：他判断出"未来的推理形态不再需要 beam search"，然后动手切除了一个仍在被使用的功能。

这和 Hinton 的 Capsule Network 形成了绝妙的镜像对照：Capsule Network 概念上很美，但输在了硬件抽奖上——它不适合 GPU 的并行结构，所以永远无法普及。而 Transformer 之所以赢，不是因为它更"聪明"，而是因为它天生具有 GPU 亲和性。

跨领域的连接是这样的：开源项目的维护者本质上是在做"未来考古学"——他们必须提前 3~6 个月预判"哪些代码值得为一个尚未发布的模型/硬件而保留"，而不是维护"当下最多人使用"的功能。这与股票投资中的逆向定价极为相似：真正决定长期胜负的，不是当下的用户数，而是对"未来分布"的下注。Kaichao 团队之所以能持续维护 vLLM 的领先，是因为他们把每一次架构决策都当成对未来 6 个月硬件/模型形态的期权定价。这也解释了为什么这份工作不能被 Coding Agent 替代——AI 可以写代码，但 AI 不知道"哪些代码即将变得重要"。

四、一个隐藏的悖论：越是开源，越需要一家公司

访谈中最反常识的结论是 Jan Stoica 那句话："如果不成立公司，这个项目就完了"。这在开源原教旨主义者听来简直是异端。但仔细看四位创始人两年内所有的挣扎，你会看到一个残酷的组织学真相：

纯开源项目在 2020 年前是可行的，因为那时候基础设施还没有"军事化"。而今天，芯片厂商需要 NDA、模型公司需要提前几个月获得未发布模型的支持、GPU 资源需要以"月"为单位调度——这些都是国家级/公司级实体才能承担的法律主体行为。一个 GitHub 组织无法签署保密协议，一个博士生无法承诺"我三年内不去 xAI"。

所以真正的悖论是：开源基础设施要保持真正的开源，反而必须有一家公司作为"法律护盾"来抵挡商业世界的合规要求。Infraact 存在的最终意义，不是把 vLLM 商业化，而是把商业世界的复杂性挡在 vLLM 之外，让代码本身继续保持公共品的纯粹性。这与 Linux 基金会、Mozilla 基金会走过的路一模一样——但这一次，速度被 AI 时代压缩了 10 倍。

📝 转录文本

开场介绍

Hello everyone, I'm Xiaojun. Today our guest is Kai Chao You. He is a former senior scientist at the founding company Infrat. This company is very special. It is from Berkeley, a school-based open source project, VLLM. The core maintainer of this community spent nearly three years to turn it from a algorithmic paper into an open source community and into a company's normal operation.

These maintainers gave up a lot of personal temptations and held on to their faith in the spirit of opening up. In the beginning of this year, Infra got a total of $1.5 billion in financing. So we also discussed how to turn a community-centered open source project into a commercialized organization operation, and the decisions and changes and thoughts it faces.

On the other hand, we also hope to bring you some new ideas on the front lines of AI Infra technology. So I also talked to You Kaichao about AI Infra. The design of the model structure and even the design of Harness Engineering are all in the background of the era. What should the multi-faceted design do? Next, I will interview Kaichao You.

Looking forward to the progress of us and AI in 2026. How do we move it? It's small but powerful. Finally, I told her that if she didn't start a business with us, You have made a lot of money, but after 10 years, the project failed. Are you happy or unhappy?

For example, some places have a relatively low water flow, and some places have a relatively low water flow. Because when you compare tokens and electricity, you may think that electricity is more universal, and electricity can be adjusted, but tokens can't be adjusted. You can't say that you can convert a Deepseq model token into a Kemi token. This token is printed with the model.

嘉宾自我介绍

Hello, I'm Kaichao. I'd like to say hello to the audience. Hello, I'm Kaichao You. I'm a graduate of Tsinghua University. I'm a co-founder and chief scientist of Infraact. My main task is to maintain the eco-environment of the open source model push-and-leave engine, which is the core of VLM. Our goal is to provide software services for AGI.

I'm also a loyal fan of Xiaojun's podcast. We've seen many senior professionals in the industry come to join our podcast. For example, Mr. Zhang Xiangyu, Yang Zhiling, and Mindus' Ji Yichao. We're all familiar with them. I'm honored to have the opportunity to share my experiences and opinions with you.

Speaking of Mindus' Ji Yichao's peak, it was also him who introduced Kai Chao to our show. Yes, that was last December. At that time, Meta was not yet acquired by Manus. But I was busy with establishing the company. I promised to come, but it took me half a year. Now I finally fulfilled my promise.

早期编程与学习经历

Before we officially talk about technology, I'm still very curious about your personal experience. When did you start to use computer programming? Did you have any competitive experience since junior high school?

I started using programming in 2015. But I have a knowledge of computer programming. When we were learning about mathematical physics, we were using some software that supported computing. For example, I was impressed with a thing called a composite board. You can use it to observe various function images and then do some physical animation demonstrations. Although not many people know about these software now, because technology is developing too fast. Although I remember it as only 10 years ago, but it seems like it was in the last century, and no one remembers it. But these software still brought me great shock, and made me see that computers can do a lot of things.

Another relevant thing is that Tsinghua University launched the online school. It's basically an online education platform for foreign students. In 2014 and 2015, when I was studying for the competition, Tsinghua University invited many teachers to film some teaching videos. At first, I was studying physics at the university. The physics competition at our school is basically adding some points to the physics. After I learned about the physical and micro-science, the online class was launched by the school. It was a course in Python that was linked to edX. So I learned Python from him. This was my first time learning a programming language.

When the topic is simple, they won't get the knowledge. But I think learning these courses can help me learn new knowledge. It helps me understand the problems more deeply. You can't get this content by repeating the questions. So I think learning the knowledge is more satisfying. Although the college entrance exam was relatively simple, my ability to do so was not reflected in the score. So in the end, the score was barely above the score line of Tsinghua University. But I think the learning process was very happy. I think it's useful to learn these knowledge.

进入清华与学习方式

When you first entered Tsinghua, it didn't seem to be the best grade. It seemed that the score line was two points higher than Tsinghua's score line. How did you get into Tsinghua?

I don't think it's a good idea to say "reversal". The score is only two or three points higher than the score line. But I don't think it reflects the process of not being able to predict a person's future in college. I think it depends more on what you do in college. The score is just an admission. After you enter Tsinghua, you should forget about the score. You should do what you want to do in college.

How accurate were you at that time? I saw some records that you were going crazy after you started school. You sent over 100 emails to your teacher asking questions. You read over 10,000 pages of study materials. And your thesis notes were displayed in the school's library. And so on. You got a 4.0 score in the last 36 courses.

It's a relatively old history. It's been many years. But I don't think it's a twist. I think I still enjoy learning. I do learn a lot of things in college. For example, if you send more than 100 emails to your teacher, you send more than 100 emails to your teacher every week. So I think it's more of a process of persistence. V0 到 V1 的重构

I'm very curious about the year 2025. Let's talk about the re-buy of the V0 and V1 from the year 2024. The user side may not feel the change. Can you talk about why you decided to do this and what challenges you face in the re-buying process?

This re-buying is mainly to solve the development of the model and hardware and to challenge the push-and-pull engine. For example, we now like to compare tokens to electricity. The push system needs to convert natural resources into electricity and then pass it on to everyone. So this reconstruction is like my power generation system, which is a transition from the power to the power generation of new energy. From the user's point of view, the usage is not that different. You may plug in the plug and it works. But from the perspective of the push engine, the working principle behind it has changed dramatically.

So from the perspective of the end user, the push engine has a very big responsibility. It blocks the complexity of the model and hardware. When the user chooses a different model, For example, you're in an app, and the app might support multiple models. From the user's perspective, you might just have ordered a model from a download menu, or you just changed a parameter from the request, saying, "I request today is deep-seq, tomorrow is Q&A." But actually, from the back of the push engine, the different models' support efficiency and the hardware they're used in are completely different. So the push engine has a very important task in it. And in the process, the model and hardware are constantly developing. So they are constantly updating their requirements for the return engine.

So V0 and V1 are just a very big change that we can see from the name. But we have actually been making similar small changes. So you can say that VOM has actually been in the process of redevelopment. The most difficult part is that you need to maintain the compatibility of the users. The models and hardware that you support behind you are constantly changing. But you need to give the front-end and middle-end users a more unified experience. If I use VMware, I can guarantee that I can run various models on various hardware.

Yes, naming is a very difficult task. We discussed it for several days. And finally naming Infraact is also because our company's main goal is to create an inference. So we have an inference in there. And then we wanted to bring inference into action. So we named it Infraact.

What do you think the company will be like in 10 years? What are your visions and goals?

It's been a long time since we've been in 10 years. It's hard to predict how AI will develop. But we expect that Infraact will be able to solve the problem of the big model reasoning. When people think of reasoning, they think of VLM and Infraact.

What will its business model be like?

For the business model, we are still focusing on the big model reasoning technology and the ecosystem of VLM. We are also building the ecosystem of VLM while doing business. So we are exploring several business models. For example, our company can have machines and software. We will finally provide you with an endpoint service. The other party only needs to use tokens from us. We can also explore some of the BYOC models. You can have a machine for your clients, and we provide the software. We can generate tokens for you to use internally. We can also explore some of the pure eco-cooperative partners. We can explore with some strategic clients how to better establish the eco-friendly environment. There are also opportunities for business cooperation in this area.

Overall, I think we want to achieve a state of "discounting". We are not selling our engineers for a time. The value we generate depends on how many tokens we generate for you and how much cost we save for your machines. So this is our overall logic.

公司规模与年度计划

How many people are in the company now?

Yes, and when we opened the community, we didn't communicate as closely as we did before. Because at that time, we were all in a state of relaxation. Now we are all fighting for the same goal. We all need to see what happened in the company and we need to solve it together.

What are the plans for the company, Infraact, this year?

I think the current planning is still focused on the ecological aspect of open source large model reasoning. This includes the next generation of reasoning engines that are about to be released, including the next generation of models and hardware. How to make better reasoning, including the next generation of load. How do we use this token? These things. I think we need to and give a satisfactory answer with open source.

模型与 Infra 的 Co-Design

We have reviewed your research process and the process of the company moving from a open-end project to a company. Today, we actually want to talk to you about the topic of model and infra co-design. I think you are very good at this. It is also a topic that many model companies are very concerned about.

Let's start with the most basic one. If it is to give some non-technological background audience or listeners to explain the model structure and infra co-design, how would you compare them? Why do they need to be designed together?

Many people now compare tokens to electricity. I think we can start with this analogy. We can imagine hardware as a natural resource. For example, different places have different wind and water forces, and solar and solar power. I think we can compare the model to a generator. There are wind generators with wind power, solar and solar power generators, and mechanical water generators. and the push-power engine can be compared to an electric system. It runs the model on hardware and then sends the token to the user and distributes it to thousands of people.

The degree of co-design in this determines the efficiency of its power generation. For example, some places have a relatively low current flow, while others have a relatively low current flow. How do you design your engine in these two places to make your engine better use this part of the energy? This is the so-called model and infra co-design.

Hardware Lottery：硬件抽奖理论

Hardware lottery. This is also written by another scholar, not David Patterson. He said that decades ago, when the Maltese Law was still more effective, the development of software and hardware was basically a battle between the two. So, for those who write software, you don't need to consider so many hardware features. Because the overall performance of hardware is doubled every two years. And then the software performance naturally becomes faster.

But the problem is that the golden age of the Moller's Law is over. You can't improve the performance of the common use by manufacturing. So now it's actually a special use age. Because as I often say, the royal law is that your profit may double every two years. But this profit is actually a special profit. It can't be used for common use. So if you don't use these special algorithms, you won't get the lottery ticket for the hardware. You won't get the popularity of this era.

For example, I think that the very experienced Hinton, who was a machine learning teacher, he strongly recommended a thing called Capsule Network. It makes sense from the concept, but it's not friendly on the GPU. So it can't get a wide range of applications. Or it hasn't gotten any yet. If it needs a wide range of applications, it needs a dedicated hardware.

So the modeling structure determines the upper limit of the reasoning efficiency. If your upper limit is too low, the system engineer will be helpless. If you've made it look bad, it will look the same if you optimize it. So you have to combine the two.

Transformer 的 GPU 亲和性

In fact, the transformer has the GPU's talent.

Yes, you can say that. Because it's very suitable for parallel. Parallel means that it has a lot of argumentation.

Should the algorithm lead the hardware or the hardware lead the algorithm?

Ideally, these two must work together. But the actual situation is that the hardware has been created. So a lot of times, the algorithm needs to learn how to develop the hardware. Of course, once the hardware goes wrong, it will go wrong for years. This is a huge challenge for hardware companies. So they need to keep stepping on the pulse of the times to suppress what the next useful hardware looks like. But generally, the algorithm and the model structure are more suitable for hardware.

ROPE 的成功案例

Can you give a specific example to show that because the model structure is well designed, the efficiency of infra has improved a lot?

A more famous example I think can be said is ROPE, which is called Rotating Position Coding. After Transformer came out, I think you can find at least a hundred position coding implementations. But many of them need to modify the core attention to achieve. If your location code changes, you need to rewrite your attention kernel. For example, an Alibi technology is an absolute position bias. So it doesn't get a wide range of applications.

One of the reasons for the popularization of ROP is that as the training length increases, we need to change the location. Flash Attention also solves the problem of training length. So Flash Attention becomes a must-have for training. At this time, most users have no way to modify Flash Attention. So at this time, most of the location coding that needs to be modified to achieve attention was killed. No one tried it.

The advantage of ROP is that it is an absolute position coding. Everyone hopes it is an absolute position coding. But it is also a relative position coding. But it is a way to implement absolute position coding. So it has a very good nature. And it can be independently inserted into the query and key. It is independently outside of attention. You can independently do ROP outside of attention kernel. So it is complementary to attention kernel. So it becomes a best partner.

So if the model structure is well designed, it can have a co-design effect with infra. We can improve each other and have a more efficient implementation. Then your overall training and reasoning efficiency will be much better.

DeepSeek 的 Infra 团队

Because you mentioned infra, everyone in this generation of big model companies will say that DeepSync is the best done by infra. Is the good job done by infra related to the co-design of the model structure and infra?

Yes, I think DeepSeq's infra team is the world's top team. I can't say for sure if it's the top team. But it's definitely top-level. And infra's ability is strong, so there are more efficient model structures. So their algorithm researchers can explore various options faster and more efficiently.

And then, I think there's another thing about this. Their algorithm students actually understand a part of Infra. For example, in the beginning of 2024, DeepSeq was exploring MOE. It was a deep-seq MOE wave. So actually, a deep-seq algorithm student wrote out a more efficient implementation of MOE, which was relatively rough. So they actually explored a lot of Infra in their M.O.E. exploration. And then the series of M.O.E.s in the background was also the first one they made in the reasoning system.

So Infra's ability to explore deep-seq algorithms has played a very important role. At the same time, their algorithm students will also learn Infra's knowledge, which makes their algorithm design more friendly to Infra. So it should be the algorithm that takes the initiative to approach Infra.

算法与 Infra 团队协作机制

For example, what kind of mechanism can make them closer together? Or should I start with the person who knows how to calculate from the person who hires them?

I think it's great if you can hire someone who knows both how to calculate and Infora. And then, in the later stage, it might be better to work together. For example, when you work together, you discuss daily. What is it that you discuss every day? Then the algorithm student will know that he has to consider these things. Then the algorithm student will discuss daily. The algorithm student will also have some pre-imagined effects.

If the Infra team is too dominant, they will sometimes ignore some things in the algorithm. For example, in the MOE, there were some Infra students who chose Expert Choice for the balance of the MOE. This is not accepted in the algorithm. But in the Infra, you can make it run very fast. So this is also an example of Infra being too close to the algorithm.

whose language rights are higher?

I think many companies have higher language rights in terms of algorithm. and Infra is often a passive state. But in the ideal situation, they should be co-designed. How do I put it? It's like the model and hardware co-design. In the ideal situation, they should be co-designed. But in the real situation, the hardware is stronger because it's already been designed.

DeepSpark 与投机解码技术

Speaking of DeepSeq, DeepSpark has just been released. Can you explain the latest technical progress from the perspective of the spectators?

Dspark is a new way of collecting code. The self-reliance modeling model is divided into two stages: pre-fill and decoding. Pre-fill deals with user input. The decoding phase deals with the model's own output. Since it's self-reliant, you can only generate tokens for each decoding phase. This is less efficient.

Then, the investment code is based on the current input, a one-time guess of how many tokens I will generate. Then, the code is converted into a small section of the pre-fill process. It can handle multiple tokens at once, which can improve the processing efficiency.

Before DeepSpark was launched, the industry has actually studied a lot of method of investment solutions. For example, the common EGO and MTP investment solutions launched by DeepSig. Their feature is that the length of the guess is relatively short. Usually, it is 3 to 5 guesses, but the acceptance rate is relatively high.

The DSpark technical route is the DFlash series. We've been paying attention to this part for the past few months. So DSpark is not a very new content. The feature of the DFlash route is that it will guess many tokens at once, such as 16 tokens. We, VOM and Nvidia, have just released a technical blog recently, which introduces the support of DFlash in VOM. This can reach thousands of tokens per second for some models.

The disadvantage of deflash is that it can guess a lot of tokens, but it can also guess wrongly. So there is a problem of waste of computing power in the model verification process. The improvement of deflash for dSpark is to estimate which of these guessed tokens are accurate and which are inaccurate. And then you don't need to verify the tokens with an inaccurate probability. So For example, the model guessed 16 tokens. If you simply calculate the final output of the model, you may find that only the first 8 tokens are accurate. So you only need to verify the first 8 tokens.

So DeepSpark is probably continuing this route to improve D-Flash. DeepSpark is not an accident for us. Because we have done a few months of D-Flash optimization. Then the D-Flash acceptance rate problem is also a consensus in the D-Flash research circle. Before DeepSpark was introduced, the Tencent members had already released a D-Cart. And the students who were on the team also introduced a Domino. They all solved this problem with similar ideas.

DeepSpark 的算法创新程度

So, how "normal" is DeepSpark in terms of algorithmic calculations?

I don't think it's very "normal". We have a lot of communication with the DeepSeq team and the Tencent members. You will soon see that we support these algorithms. But innovation is another thing. And whether you can make this innovative idea come true is another thing.

I think DeepSpark is the foundation of deepseek's very solid infrastructure. and we've pushed the push optimization to the extreme. This is also something we're learning from them, how to do better push optimization. And then, actually, this is also another part of the algorithm and infra co-design. Is there a good implementation on the push engine to determine whether a head-on code algorithm can be used on a large scale? Deepseq's push engine team is very strong, so they also provide a greater space for exploration and more feedback for the algorithm team to study head-on code.

## 一、开源项目的"五年周期律"：一个被忽视的组织物理学
You Kaichao 提到 David Patterson 的观察极具颠覆性——**每个伟大的实验室最多只能有效运转五年**，因为这恰好是一批博士生的完整周期。Berkeley 从 AMP Lab → RISE Lab → Sky Lab 的更迭，本质上不是"实验室在进化"，而是"实验室在死亡与重生"。Spark、Ray、vLLM 这些改变工业界的项目，都恰好卡在博士生"已经不需要靠论文毕业、又还没被公司高薪掏走"的**极短窗口期**内诞生。
这里有一个**反直觉的洞察**：开源基础设施的最佳贡献者不是刚入学的新生（他们必须靠论文毕业），也不是资深工程师（他们的时间成本太高），而是"**已完成毕业资本积累、但尚未套现**"的中后期博士生。这是一个极其狭窄的人才带宽——它解释了为什么开源基础设施如此稀缺，以及为什么 Infra 型 Startup 必须在这个窗口关闭前"接住"这些人，否则整个项目会立刻凋零。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] How We Know Black Holes Exist – Adam Brown
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最出人意料的观察：黑洞的"发现史"其实是一部"信念史"

真正令人震撼的不是黑洞的存在，而是Schwarzschild 在 1915 年爱因斯坦刚发表场方程后的几周内就写出了黑洞解——却整整用了 50 年，物理学界才愿意"相信自己写下的数学"。这暴露出一个反直觉的科学真相：数学的严谨性并不能强迫人类接受它的结论。人类会本能地把不喜欢的解称为"病态解 (sick solution)"、"测度零现象"，用语言把它推到现实之外。

这与哥德尔不完备定理被数学界"心理性回避"、与量子纠缠被爱因斯坦称为"鬼魅般的作用"、甚至与今天 AI 领域某些人对"涌现"的抵触，是同一种认知机制——当形式系统的推论超出了主体的直觉舒适区时，人类会先审判方程，而不是审判自己的直觉。Penrose 的伟大不在于"发现"黑洞，而在于证明黑洞是"generic"的（一般性的、稳健的），从而剥夺了人类"回避它"的心理许可证。

二、跨领域连接：LIGO 的"多点验证"其实是一种古老的认识论技术

Adam 提到 LIGO 的关键论证：不是"我们探测到了信号"，而是"分布在地球不同位置的探测器以完全相同的方式震动"——因此排除了卡车、地震等本地噪声。

这个逻辑结构，你会惊讶地发现，和法庭上"多个独立证人证词交叉验证"完全同构，也和分布式系统里的 Byzantine Fault Tolerance（拜占庭容错）是同一件事，还和历史学中的"史源互证法"（王国维的二重证据法）如出一辙。

真理的判据，从物理学到司法到区块链共识，本质上都是"独立源的相干性"。 这解释了为什么现代科学越来越依赖"多信使天文学"（引力波 + 电磁波 + 中微子联合观测）——不是因为一个信号不够，而是因为认识论上，单源永远无法击穿"这可能只是本地噪声"的哲学怀疑。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：黑洞证据链呈现出"感官进化"的镜像

请注意这段转录里 Adam 使用的动词序列，藏着一个几乎没人注意到的模式：

  • 通过 Sagittarius A 周围恒星轨道 → "看见"*（视觉）
  • 通过 LIGO → "感觉到 (felt)"（触觉／振动）
  • 通过 Event Horizon Telescope → "看见"（射电视觉）

人类对黑洞的探测方式，正在重演生物感官的进化史——从视觉主导，退回到更古老的振动感知（内耳、侧线器官），再回到扩展了频段的视觉。黑洞迫使我们把"感官"这个概念从生物学扩展到工程学，LIGO 本质上是人类给自己长出的第一个"引力波耳朵"。

更深一层的洞见：每一次物理学的重大突破，几乎都伴随一次"新感官的发明"——望远镜（可见光眼睛）→ 射电望远镜（无线电眼睛）→ 中微子探测器（幽灵触觉）→ LIGO（时空触觉）。科学进步的速度，不取决于理论家的速度，而取决于人类给自己造感官的速度。

这或许暗示了一个令人不安的推论：我们今天所谓"未解之谜"，很可能不是知识的缺失，而是感官的缺失。 暗物质、暗能量、意识——它们之所以神秘，可能只是因为我们还没造出对应的"器官"。

📝 转录文本

一、问题的提出：为什么黑洞可信，虫洞却不？

Why do we think black holes are correct, but not wormholes?

Yeah, that's a great question, and people did not believe it to begin with. Schwarzschild wrote down his solution almost immediately after Einstein wrote his field equations. People thought that that equation was sick in some way, that it was a measure zero thing that would never happen. It was some mathematical monstrosity, but it was impossible to make black holes naturally in the real universe.

Uh, and they were wrong, because black holes do exist. We're extremely confident now.

二、理论突破：Penrose 与 Hawking 的一般性证明

Um, there was theoretical developments, and there was experimental evidence that black holes exist.

The biggest theoretical development was Penrose, and then later Hawking and Penrose, for which he won the Nobel Prize, who showed theoretically that the formation of black holes is a generic feature of general relativity. It's not just some sick thing that happens if you fine-tune the initial conditions — that if you just start off with generic initial conditions, uh, the development of black holes is a generic feature of that. That was a huge development.

三、实验证据登场

And then there was the experimental side. And the pieces of experimental evidence we have for black holes is now huge. It did not exist in Einstein's day, and for 50 years after Einstein, people were extremely confused about black holes and thought they didn't exist. But there's numerous pieces of evidence.

证据一：银河系中心 Sagittarius A*

I think the most visually appealing piece of evidence is just observing the center of our galaxy. So, if you look at the center of the galaxy, there is — I mean, spoiler alert — there is a black hole there. We call it Sagittarius A star. A huge black hole, weighs many millions of times the mass of the sun.

Uh, you can't see the black hole, or at least you can't see it, you know, directly, cuz it's black. What you can see is the stars around it. If you watch these stars over the course of decades — and we now have a number of decades of observations of them — you will see the stars not moving along what we would call straight lines, uh, instead moving in nice little ellipses or precessing ellipses. And those ellipses look like they are orbiting something.

You cannot see the something, but you can see the stars that are orbiting that something, and you can calculate how big is it, how massive is it. And what you find is that it's very massive indeed, and it's also very small indeed. You know it's small because the stars get super close to it but don't seem to collide with it.

And so by tracing these orbits, you can tell that there is something super heavy, super dark, and super compact at the center of that galaxy — that is Sagittarius A star, the black hole at the center of our galaxy. That's one compelling piece of evidence.

证据二：LIGO — 我们"感觉"到了黑洞

Another piece of compelling evidence was about a decade ago: we not only saw black holes, we felt them.

So LIGO is this huge interferometer, laser interferometer, that we built at a number of different sites, that is super attuned to vibrations in space-time itself. And there's a famous event pretty much immediately after we turned it on in late 2015 where we felt space-time shaking.

And you knew it was space-time shaking, not just the Earth shaking, because we had a bunch of these detectors — at then two, now four — at different points on the Earth, and they all shake in exactly the same way. So it couldn't just be explained by a truck passing one and not the other, or a seismic event in one and not the other. They all shook in exactly the same way.

And we were able to back-calculate that the thing causing them to shake was the collision of two ginormous black holes, two black holes both of which weighed about 30 times as much as the sun, on the other side of the universe, about 1.6 billion light-years away. That collision happened about 1.6 billion years ago and just happened to reach the Earth within weeks of us turning on the LIGO detectors.

We've now seen — we've now felt, more accurately — thousands of such shakings, corresponding to thousands of black hole mergers.

证据三：Event Horizon Telescope

And then there's more evidence. Later we had what's called the Event Horizon Telescope, which is a ginormous conglomeration of radio telescopes all over the Earth that were able to look very closely at the black hole at the center of our galaxy, Sagittarius A star, and the even bigger black hole at the center of our neighboring galaxy, and see very, very faintly the radio emissions of matter falling into these black holes that shine super brightly as it does so. And we were able to see that in the radio emissions of these things.

四、结论

So, we felt them. We've seen them. Uh, we've seen their gravitational effects on orbiting stars. We're extremely confident at this stage that black holes exist.

>> If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
