EVIV is the most, you know, longest running, ubiquitous, widely adopted standard for this type of product. We have many other families of indices that are live today and coming soon. And essentially we've built the Bitcoin volatility index standard for the digital assets/crypto market.

BVIV 指数的运作机制

So I think to kind of summarize what you said: people look at your indices and then they try to understand what level of volatility traders are expecting over certain durations. I know that you have different timelines. It's not necessarily an indicator of which direction the market's going to go, but it does give you a sense of how widely they expect the market to move over a certain period of time. Is that correct?

Essentially, BVIV is a measure of implied volatility for Bitcoin, meaning the forward-looking moves, the forward-looking risk in the digital assets/Bitcoin market. And so largely it's associated with negative shocks to the market. When the market is fearful, BVIV tends to always spike. It's very persistently negatively correlated in times of fear, but can also go up in times of greed. And so it's a very versatile product which provides this robust and mission-critical measure of the market's expectation for volatility.

Yeah, it's kind of funny. I mean, I used to — back when I was at Forbes — I think I did a story on Deribit implied volatility products and was kind of looking for some of those correlations between traditional market moves, like not only in crypto but then also as it relates to the S&P etc.

I mean, I'm sure you're familiar with the term "short the VIX," and anyone in TradFi listening here knows what that means. And I was curious to see what types of correlations there were there. And at the time, this was a few years ago, I didn't actually see a lot of it, but I guess today things are much more mature. I mean, this may have even been before ETFs had been approved. Things are a lot more correlated. So I'm interested to kind of see that. And it's all based on the price of the options to kind of hedge that — that's where the "implied" aspect of the name comes from.

宏观背景:Clarity、油价、FOMC

So let's dive into what you're actually seeing in the market, because a lot of people are wondering: how do I try to position for the upside if Clarity does pass, but protect my downside? And there's a lot happening as we roll into these next couple of crucial weeks.

Bitcoin, ETH, SOL — I mean, they have all bounced off of recent lows and have had a couple of good weeks. But again, now we're running into a lot of different factors. I mean, there's Clarity. There's price of oil going back again above $100 a barrel. The ECB decided to keep rates the same today, but the FOMC is meeting next week and, while the Fed's being tight-lipped, it's hard to anticipate what the Fed's going to do — and futures traders are pricing in, I think, one or even two rate hikes this year.

Essentially, we've noticed a slightly elevated volatility index for the 14-day in the term structure, and this could be due to the Clarity Act being either imminent or different developments coming. There was also some call-buying activity last week in the options market for a two-to-four-week-out calls, and so there seems to be some ramping expectations for the Clarity Act in the coming weeks.

I mean, obviously we both hope that that happens. That would be a tremendously positive advancement for the industry. But yeah, there's a slight elevation in the BVIV 14-day index, or between the 7 and 14 day. And we're looking forward to the Clarity Act hopefully coming to market. I know there's been a lot of folks on the Hill putting in a lot of work related to this, and that will create a lot of clarity and reduce the nebulous nature of some of the things that are maybe holding back tokens and the industry broadly.

当前 BVIV 读数与期限结构中的"扭曲"

Yeah. Maybe, if we could, let's dive a little bit more into the indices that you mentioned — and, even if you need a moment to just kind of pull them up on your screen, I'd love to kind of get a sense of where they're at, and where the current levels of volatility fit within the historical timeline.

Is this a period of time where we're seeing a lot of expected vol? I would imagine it's not going to rise up to like pure fear and panic when FTX collapsed or something like that, but what's the historical context for where maybe your Bitcoin and where your ETH indices are sitting?

Yeah. So essentially the BVIV index is currently at 41. It's actually come up and sort of seen a rise in the index value in terms of points and percentage gain in the last couple of weeks. And so on a relative basis, we show this metric called BVIV rank / BVIV percentile. BVIV rank is basically where it's at in terms of 52-week high and low. And in the last couple of days, Bitcoin has seen a rise and there's been some positive correlation between the BVIV index and the Bitcoin price rising.

As mentioned, typically you see a very negative, persistent correlation where markets are fearful. On February 6, Bitcoin went from 68k to 60k, and BVIV went from 40 to over 80 at its peak. You can also observe this different behavior in times of bullishness in the crypto market, where Bitcoin goes up and BVIV also goes up with it. So that's kind of what you saw in the last couple days. All right. So, we were just talking about your BVIV index, but one thing I find really interesting is that you have one specifically related to options on IBIT — which should have very little delta vis-à-vis Bitcoin itself, but by the nature of financial products, it does. I'm just curious, before we get into a couple of other assets: is there any interesting divergence between your IBIT product and BVIV, and if so, what might that mean?

So we have the BVIV index, as you mentioned, and the BVIV US index. The BVIV index tracks the global spot options market — Deribit, OKX; it looks at these type of venues and kind of aggregates this single number that looks at the entire global options market.

About six months ago — so BVIV is about four years old now — about six months ago, we rolled out the BVIV US index on the back of the success for the IBIT options. And IBIT options launched at the end of 2024, in November, and have quickly become the dominant form factor for Bitcoin options in the US market. The regulated ETF options market and the offshore market are roughly the same size. They're both about 25 billion on any given day recently.

And basically, you can observe that the BVIV index is a couple points below the BVIV US index. This is largely attributed to a small premium for really like transparency and the clearing house setup of the equity options exchanges in the US market. So you'll think BVIV US is at 42 and BVIV's at 39, something like this. And so there is a small premium on the sort of IBIT index. But largely the performance of the indices is very, very similar, and it's something that we pay close attention to. We've published a lot of research on the growth of the IBIT options market and something we're tracking closely. It's very interesting to juxtapose the two markets and two indices.

ETH、SOL 与 Clarity Act 的关系

Okay. And we spent a lot of time talking about Bitcoin, but as you mentioned in some of your earlier remarks, every token has something at stake with the Clarity negotiations. But I guess one could probably argue Bitcoin has the least, given that it's pretty settled as a commodity and, just sort of by design, its rigid nature — there's less onion activity you can do with Bitcoin beyond just sending it back and forth.

I want to kind of get your sense of what's happening with ETH, SOL, some of the other major alt L1s where — I mean, aside from just perhaps getting a little bit of clarity on which regulator has privacy — there's a lot at stake, in particular for DeFi and some of the sort of activities that you can do on top of these multi-purpose blockchains.

So, are traders positioning themselves differently for these tokens related to Bitcoin? What does your platform tell you?

In general, I think that Bitcoin is bonafide-ed and clearly under the CFTC's remit, based on previous administrations and the sort of regulatory seats and things that they've said. And so Bitcoin is very clearly a commodity. I think ETH is also very similar in that regard. But a lot of the things that are built on top of Ethereum and Salana stand to benefit — and maybe things like Hyperliquid and Lighter and others stand to benefit from the Clarity Act and the increased clarity in the ecosystem.

I think that it's nebulous how certain things are regulated — what is a security, what is a broker — and the Clarity Act brings transparency and clarity to those areas. And so I do think that Ethereum and Salana ecosystems, Hyperliquid, have a lot to gain from this act, the statute going through, and it's very interesting to see how the market will react to that.

I mean, you've seen in recent days that on a 7-day time frame, Ethereum is up almost a percent and Bitcoin is roughly up half a percent. And so this might be indicative of the fact that Ethereum and other smart contract platforms, as well as other decentralized applications and exchanges, have a lot to gain from the Clarity Act going through. So you might see this in the EVIV index if I look real quick. The EVIV index is up around the same amount of percentage points as BVIV, but you can definitely see this in the Ethereum price and the SOL price and the HYPE price. And so it's going to be interesting to see how the broader market reacts to Clarity going through, and the prospect of it going through.

年末展望:期限结构里的信号（或缺席）

What is the longest term duration of contracts that your index tracks?

It is 180 days. We should roll out at 360. That would be cool.

Okay. All right. So, that pretty much gets us to the end of the year, which is where I kind of wanted to take this next. I was looking a little bit at oil futures before we went on. And again, it's — I say this, I feel like I say this a lot on the show, but there's many different ways to look at the world.

I mean, for one, rates are hiking across two years, 10 years. Bonds are suffering there. Bonds are suffering. Traders are anticipating rate hikes across the world over fears that the Iran conflict, which has now moved from the Strait of Hormuz into also the Red Sea, and what all that means. People are bracing for a rough couple of months. But oil futures — timed toward the end of the year — are actually relatively muted and not too far up from where they sit today.

And I'm wondering what crypto is telling you when — at the end of the year. Do we see a big run up into 100k? And I know you don't look at particular price, but are your models predicting a lot of volatility between now and the end of the year? I would anticipate, given that we've been in a crypto winter and hopefully it's bottomed out, that if there is a lot of volatility that would mean volatility to the upside, not the downside.

When I look at the term structure for BVIV, I don't observe anything that jumps out to me as elevation in the term structure — as you might see with the Clarity in the next couple of weeks. Although definitely I think that by end of the year, crypto could look a lot different.

Like I mentioned, there's a strong institutional appetite for tokenization, blockchain as infrastructure, stablecoins right now — and then that could translate back into the liquid majors: Salana, Ethereum, Bitcoin. And so I think it's a very interesting regime we're in right now, very institutional regime, and I think that the market could look a lot different by end of the year. There's definitely a lot of appetite for institutional pilots and everything right now.

Nothing jumps out in the actual term structure for the BVIV index, but — gut feeling — I think that the market could shape up a lot.

Poly Market 合作与预测市场

Okay. All right. Before we wrap, I want to talk a little bit about prediction markets. So, you have a partnership with Poly Market. Could you just kind of walk me through the terms of that, please?

Essentially, Volmex and Poly Market have a collaboration — our indices are available to trade on Poly Market. There's a monthly tenor, a yearly tenor, and essentially we're a partner of Poly Market that makes a robust, mission-critical volatility index tradable in the prediction market format.

And so it's been live for the last couple of months. Traders that would like to express a view on volatility increasing or decreasing can use these contracts to easily hedge or speculate or other different strategies that are more sophisticated. But essentially, Volmex indices are available to trade on polymarket.com, and we're a big fan of the Poly Market platform and think they're doing important work making derivatives more accessible and intuitive for retail, pro-tail and even institutional investors.

So, very excited about that. Right now there's a BVIV and EVIV contract expiring in the next 8 days, and so something to pay attention to as the expiration is kind of a forcing function for price discovery.

Yeah. And I'm really curious to — I mean, if you're seeing anything kind of noteworthy on how those contracts are trading — we always... I've long looked at the CME Fed Watch tool, and now it seems like Poly Market's markets for pricing sort of the next Fed rate moves are sort of quoted side by side with CME. So I'd love to kind of hear how people are using that product.

And in particular, I wonder too, like — how just the rise of different things that you can bet on in relation to Poly Market — how that changes the way people use your product, or how you might try to develop it in the future. I mean, I was just looking on Poly Market now, and you could bet on things like an Iran coup attempt, you could bet on things like a ceasefire, you can bet on prices that change minute by minute. There are a lot of different ways — I mean, you could bet on Clarity — there's lots of different ways to express views on things that are related to just price volatility.

So, how does that impact the way people are using your product? And I'm really curious, too, just further out: how does that impact the way that you might try to build your company and the types of products that you launch, given that there's so much demand for different flavors of expressing expectations for different price movements?

Yeah, thanks Steve. I think Poly Market and prediction markets broadly are a very intuitive form factor for a lot of different investors and traders. It's really distilling markets down to a green button and a red button — buy and sell — and give you some implied probability of something happening, and you can take a stance on a pure event, something happening in the markets, in culture, in geopolitics, in political markets.

And so essentially I think that this makes it really easy for investors and traders to take a stance on a particular issue without dealing with the cumbersome and arduous process of trading options — which obviously we love options, and our product is predicated on options, but it's quite complicated for a lot of investors and traders. And so Poly Market really distills that down into a very simple user experience.

I think this has been a very successful collaboration so far, where our indices are tradable in the very simple format of a prediction market. And typically, if you're a retail investor in the US and you want to trade the VIX, you might need to trade the VIX options — and so that's much more complicated product. It really simplifies things to have a volatility index in a prediction market wrapper.

And so I think that this unlocks just a lot of new product offerings for us, specifically making BVIV tradable on different tenors. We have one month and one year that are currently available on Poly Market, but I think that there could be surface area to have shorter duration contracts that are expiring in a matter of days.

I think that as we create new indices, this is a really great medium for trading them and commercializing them. And so I think that we think a lot about prediction markets, and it's a really great product. I liken it to the innovation of perpetuals, right? I mean, perpetuals have really changed the landscape for crypto derivatives, and I believe that prediction markets is another generation of that — with making it really easy to trade all sorts of assets.

And so Poly Market's doing great work, there's a number of other exchanges doing great work in the space, and it seems like every day more and more incumbents kind of enter the prediction market space and have some plans to get involved there. And so, I think it's a — we think a lot about perpetual futures and regulated mediums for trading our indices, but also prediction markets is becoming a pillar of sort of the go-to-market strategy. So, it's something we're really excited about, and I think it's a great development.

收尾:14 天视野、BitMart 停运与嘉宾寄语

All right. Great. Well, we'll have to kind of stay tuned and keep watching it, because I think — right, then — there's a lot of exciting opportunities for someone like you and the products that you offer. So we'll have to keep watching there.

And you mentioned perps. I think I'd be remiss not to at least acknowledge BitMart in the news that it was shutting down today. I mean, they essentially — I wouldn't necessarily say they created perps, but they definitely brought them to crypto, and nowadays perps dominate crypto derivatives. So, it's a sad day for them, but they can clearly hold their heads high based on what they were able to create.

We're going to have to leave it there. Uh, lots to cover, lots to continue watching. I'm going to pay particular attention to your 14-day time horizon, given how closely it lines up with the August recess for the Senate. Clarity still seems like it could go either way. I know Poly Market and some of the other prediction platforms have it at, I think, somewhere 30 to 40%. That'll change eight times by the time someone listens to this on Apple Podcast or Spotify. But a lot of work to do. Hopefully, we're going to see some positive movement, because I think it would be beneficial to everyone in the community.

Cole, thank you for joining. Are there any last thoughts that you'd like to share with the audience?

Thanks, Steve. It's been great to be here. Thanks as always. And I would say check out our indices — charts.volmex.finance, or Volmex Finance, or on Trading View, Bloomberg, Refinitiv. And let's see how Clarity, the August recess, evolves — and there might be some interesting moves in the market in Bitcoin and ETH and Salana and different tokens. So it's an exciting time and look forward to next time.

Yeah, absolutely. Thank you to everybody for watching and listening today. That wraps up this week's episode of Bits and Bips: the Interview, but come back again same time next week where we'll have another exciting guest. Have a good day.

Hey, hey hey. Hey, hey hey.

item.description:
## 一、期限结构里的"政治日历"——立法程序被证券化的瞬间
Cole 提到 BVIV 在 **7-14 天** 这段出现一个"扭曲"(kink)，而访谈时点恰好距离参议院 August recess 约两周。这看似技术细节，但真正令人震撼的是：**期权做市商正在把国会议事日程编码进 sigma 里**。
换句话说，Clarity Act 从"政治事件"被翻译成了"波动率曲面上的凸起"——立法者的每一次拖延、每一次委员会日程调整，都会通过期权定价流回市场。华尔街不再"等待"华盛顿的消息，而是把华盛顿的**议事流程本身作为可对冲的现金流**在实时报价。这跟企业财报季形成 IV bump 是同构现象，只不过对象从盈利变成了法案。
## 二、比特币与 BVIV 同涨——一个被忽视的"贪婪波动率"信号
访谈里一带而过的一个观察其实极其反常：**BTC 从 62k 涨到 66k，BVIV 也同步上行**。传统认知里，VIX 是"恐惧指数"、与标的负相关；BVIV 大部分时间也确实如此（2 月 6 日 BTC 从 68k 砸到 60k 时，BVIV 从 40 飙到 80）。
但这种"标的

item.title: [All-In Podcast] The Fight Over Open Source AI, Anthropic's $1.5B Payout, NYC Socialists: Evictions = Violence?
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、表面之下：这不是"开源之争"，而是一场关于"知识经济时代终结"的葬礼预演

大多数评论把这集当作"美中AI博弈"或"Anthropic的监管俘获"来看，但真正令人不寒而栗的洞察藏在 Friedberg 最后那段几乎被忽略的独白里——中国的开源战略并不是为了赢得AI，而是为了让AI这一整个赛道"贬值归零"。

想想这个反直觉的结构： - 美国过去50年积累的财富，本质是"把一个比特转换成另一个比特"的知识经济溢价 - 中国用20倍的制造产能、8倍的电力产能，长期押注的是"分子转换经济" - 如果开源让"智能"变成像自来水一样的公共品，那么美国最擅长的那一层价值就会像2000年前后的电信带宽一样瞬间坍缩

这里有一个让人不适的类比：Anthropic 和 OpenAI 现在的处境，像极了1990年代末的 Encyclopedia Britannica——不是被更好的百科全书打败，而是被"百科全书这件事本身不再值钱"打败。他们向政府求救的动作，本质是在为一个正在消失的商业形态申请"临终关怀"。

二、跨领域连接：Anthropic 的"IP盗窃"话术，是一次法律上的自杀式袭击

这一集最精彩的隐藏逻辑，是 Sacks 指出的那个几乎所有人都没想到的悖论——Anthropic 为了打击中国竞争者所使用的"蒸馏=IP盗窃"话术，正在同步引爆自己脚下的地雷。

跨界看这个结构：这跟1980年代烟草公司为了打击电子烟前身产品，主动强化"尼古丁成瘾性"的科学论述，结果反而给自己后来的集体诉讼递上了证据链——是同一种"策略性话术反噬"模式。

  • Anthropic 主张"用他人输出训练模型 = IP 盗窃"（对中国）
  • 但 Anthropic 自己的整个商业模式建立在"用全世界作者的输出训练模型属于合理使用"上（对纽约时报）
  • 一旦"蒸馏即盗窃"的框架被政策制定者接受，纽约时报、Reddit、YouTube、音乐产业的律师会立刻把这句话钉进法庭陈述
  • 他们不是在为自己筑墙，而是在为整个内容产业锻造攻击自己的利剑

更精妙的是 Cursor 的 Composer 和 Mira Murati 的 Thinking Machines 都是基于 Kimi K2.5 蒸馏而来——这意味着如果这个话术站住脚，美国自己最有希望的下一代开源生态会被自己的旗手 Anthropic 一并团灭。这是一场"堂吉诃德式的自我毁灭"。

三、最出人意料的观察：Mamdani 的"驱逐即暴力"与 Anthropic 的"蒸馏即盗窃"，是同一种病

如果你只把这集当成几个不相关议题的拼盘，你就错过了它的深层几何结构。这集里 AI 议题和纽约社会主义议题共享同一个思维病灶——"通过语义重构来剥夺他人的处置权"。

  • Mamdani 的团队说"eviction is violence"（驱逐是暴力）→ 一旦你承认这个语义，房东就丧失了对自有财产的处置权
  • Anthropic 说"distillation is IP theft"（蒸馏是盗窃）→ 一旦你承认这个语义，开发者就丧失了对公共领域产出的使用权
  • 两者的操作手法一模一样：先给一个中性行为贴上道德化的暴力标签，然后以"防止暴力"的名义调用国家强制力

这就是为什么 Friedberg 引用 John Quincy Adams 关于财产权的话在这一集里显得如此关键——财产权的本质，不是"东西归谁"，而是"由谁来定义边界"。Mamdani 在重新定义物理财产的边界，Anthropic 在重新定义知识财产的边界。两者共享同一个哲学根源：把"边界的话语权"从产权人手中转移到国家或大公司手中。

四、一个几乎没人注意的暗线：token经济的"暗物质"

Jason 提到的那个数据点值得被单独放大——Open Router 显示超过 50% 的 token 消耗是"暗 token"（dark tokens），也就是运行在私有服务器上、不进入任何营收报表的模型调用。

这意味着我们现在讨论的 Anthropic/OpenAI 的营收曲线，可能已经系统性地漏掉了半个市场。这跟天文学家发现宇宙中 85% 是暗物质是同构的——你能观测到的部分，其实只是冰山浮出水面的那 15%。当"能看到的经济"和"看不到的经济"比例失衡到这种程度时，任何基于可见数据做出的估值判断都是在盲人摸象。

这是为什么 Chamath 的判断比 Sacks 的乐观数据更可怕：当一个市场的暗物质比例超过临界点，可见的"增长"其实是在被吞噬。

📝 转录文本

开场

All right, everybody, welcome back. Episode 282 of the world's greatest podcast. It's your podcasters favorite podcast. It's your mom's favorite podcast. It's the all in podcast with me again, David Sachs from up here, David Freberg. It was a big week, was a big week.

一、Kimi K3 与白宫围绕"封杀中国开源模型"的博弈

The continuing number one story in the world is Kimi K3. It sparked a debate about banning Chinese open source models here in the United States, and it's gone all the way to the White House.

Last Friday, we talked about it here — China's Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 open source model, obviously performance on par — not six months behind, not 12 months behind, but now on par with models like Opus 4.8 and GPT 5.6, which in and of itself is extraordinary, but about 50% cheaper. And this has created a bit of a panic, similar to the DeepSeek moment that we had here back in early 2025.

The White House, David Sachs, has gotten involved. Michael Kratsios, friend of the show, said, quote: "We have information that Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic's Fable for the development of its K3 model."

Here's how the Trump administration has reacted so far: - Monday: Axios reported the White House was considering banning Chinese open source models. A couple of weeks ago, David — I think it was three weeks ago — I gave that to you as a hypothetical. And here we are. - Wednesday: Wired reported that Howard Lutnick from our Commerce Department, friend of the show, does not want to ban Chinese models. So apparently, palace intrigue — there might be different opinions inside Trump's White House. And instead they want to incentivize more US frontier labs to develop better open source models. - Polymarket says 45% chance US government bans an open source model in 2026. That was a brand new market — it was at 22% a couple days ago.

Sacks 的"胜利 fap"

Sax, you called it two months ago — our first victory fap of the episode.

I think where it's all leading to is an effort to ban open source models. There's a lot of breadcrumbs leading here. You look at a lot of the rhetoric around how models need to have guardrails, and that with open source models the guardrails can be removed and therefore they're dangerous. You see this rhetoric already in Anthropic's blog posts — any threat that they describe, they kind of go out of their way to take that shot at open source models. I think, again, they're trying to create ideas or put predicate facts in the public record to justify an action later on. I think it's just a matter of time before they feel like they're at a position where maybe they can push for that type of ban directly.

All right, there it is, Sacks. What's going on at the White House? What is the administration's position here? Why are we getting multiple — is the White House testing and probing to figure out what their position is here? Or is it just this is a super dynamic situation? What's going on?

Sacks: Well, look, I mean, I have it on good authority that there is no decision by the White House to ban open source models, and I think they want that known. I think there's an ongoing conversation happening around what to do about Chinese distillation, and we should talk about that. But no decision has been made, and the president listens to a chorus of voices. He wants to get advice from as many people as possible, and I'm confident that if everybody weighs in, that the president will make the right decision as he always has with these tech issues. I think his instincts have been absolutely impeccable on this, and he's always supported a, let's say, lighter regulation, more open approach, and that's why I think the US is winning the AI race. I think that's where things stand.

Sacks 的核心立场：不能因蒸馏惩罚美国开发者

Where do you stand, Sacks? That's what everybody wants to know.

Sacks: Yeah, I think it's important for me to make my opinion known in the spirit of, again, contributing my voice so the president hears all perspectives and then can make the best decision. Look, I think it would be a tragic mistake if the government were to take action against the open source ecosystem. That would do nothing but hurt America's position in this AI race. It would backfire badly. And I think that the key point here is that regardless of what you think about distillation, you cannot punish American developers for it.

So, you know, you can't say that American companies and American developers can't use Chinese contributions to the public domain. That's just cutting off our nose to spite our face. American companies have to be able to use everything that's in the public domain because the rest of the world will be using those things.

对 Anthropic 的"监管俘获"批评

And let me just say, I've said for a while that Anthropic is guilty of regulatory capture — of attempts to seek government protection. This is a company that is the fastest growing tech company at scale in history. They started the year at 10 billion of ARR. They're now over 70 billion of ARR. This is not a company that needs government protection. This is not a company that is under threat from competitors, whether they're Chinese or otherwise. And yet they have been very successful at trying to panic everybody into thinking that they need some sort of government protection.

And the tell on this — the way that you know that this whole distillation thing is fake — is because if stopping distillation was their primary objective, Anthropic would push to ban Chinese access to American models, not American access to Chinese models.

Yes, they could — and that is achievable. They could block it. So they're the ones in the best position to block it. If distillation, if industrial scale distillation is a national security threat, they're the ones who need to stop it, because that is the place where distillation occurs. You have to stop it at the source. Once you allow Chinese companies to distill, the horse is out of the barn.

Yeah. And the reality is that I think that what's happening here is that in their lust for growth, Anthropic has done a very poor job at stopping distillation. I mean, they're saying that distillation is occurring at industrial scale. Okay, if it's industrial scale, it must be pretty obvious to see.

Yeah, the way it's happening is waves of accounts being created by students, rolled up and sold on the dark web, you know, in those kind of channels. So you got people in Manila, in the Philippines, I understand, and India signing up for all those accounts and then sending them to the dark web and selling them, using IP addresses from America.

Yeah. So that's how it occurs. Sure, but the more industrial scale it is, the more obvious it is to see. And Chamath has been saying for a while, why don't you KYC your customers? Well, they know that if they KYC their customers, it'll slow their growth. So instead, what they're saying is, hey, ban our competitors. Well, that's ridiculous. I mean, they're in the best position to stop the distillation. I think that they're negligent about doing that. Or I mean, if they really think it's that big a threat, they should use a few points of their 90% gross margins to do that. What you don't do is then say that American developers cannot use everything that's in the public domain.

So it seems to me that this debate is all backwards, that the question should be on Anthropic to explain why it's doing such a bad job, not on the whole American open source ecosystem to be punished for Anthropic's failure.

二、蒸馏、KYC 与商品化：Chamath 的诊断

All right, Freeberg, I have a really good question for you. But before we do that, Chamath, can you give me maybe a little bit of what you're hearing on your sales calls for 8090? You're talking to enterprises. They're hearing all these reports, whether it's you, Dario, this pod, other places talking about, hey, open source is ready, this is the moment, get control, AI sovereignty, etc. They must be calling you up and saying, hey, okay, we're ready. Like, how do we get these things on-prem? How do we do it? So what's happening on those calls you're doing with the enterprise? And then can you maybe give people an idea of what distillation is and why it's so important here?

蒸馏到底是什么？

Chamath: Let's start with the second thing. Distillation is when you fire up a model and you ask it a question and you observe it and you take its output and you use that in training of your own model. Now multiply that behavior by tens of millions, and what you exfiltrate is essentially trillions of questions and answers.

And Sacks is right. If you really care about distillation, you implement KYC. You force people to make an account, not just with a username and a password, but with some form of identification, maybe with a bounded credit card. There's all kinds of steps that you can take that would frankly slow things down in terms of revenue traction, but would solve the distillation problem on its face. So that isn't really a thing. It's a bit of a red herring.

谁没蒸馏过谁？——蜘蛛侠指指乐

(1) 蒸馏其实是各行业通用的产品学习法

I think the three things are really around distillation. I don't think distillation is just about AI. Distillation is a process whereby you look at the end product that someone else has produced in thinking about and learning about how to engineer your product. It is a common technique that is used across every product category in every industry. One car maker will look at how the other car maker's car operates, and they will use that to help them design a better car.

You know, at Google, in the early days, we would submit millions of search queries to Yahoo and Microsoft search engines to see what the result sets were, and we would compare our results against their results as a way of improving our search engine rankings and our algorithm. It was a very common technique. It doesn't mean we were stealing their algorithm. We didn't go into their servers and steal their software. We looked at the output of their software and used that to improve our software.

It was called benchmarking, right? It was benchmarking. You can call it — there's been a million terms. Exactly right.

That's not copyright infringement in a classical sense.

And so I do think from a distillation IP argument perspective, it's the output, not the process, that matters. So the question is, are they taking copies of copyrighted software and using it? And then my third point is just: open source is better for the world. To Chamath's point, this is a hundred times cheaper. That is better for the industry, for enterprise. The beneficiaries are going to be the economy, the consumer.

Fundamentally, if you look back on the internet, in the early days, Netscape made a proprietary browser and a proprietary server software, the Netscape software. And they went public and they were the first to do this and it was super valuable and profitable. That company ended up getting crushed because of open source. The Mozilla Foundation was formed to create an open source web browser called Firefox. And then Google ended up hiring everyone and made it Chrome, but it was still open source. The Apache Foundation set up the first HTTP server as an open source product rather than having to pay Netscape or Microsoft or Oracle for their server software.

Anyone with a computer could download the Apache software and make a web server and be on the internet and create a website. And what ended up happening is the value accrued to the internet. It didn't accrue to the small number of software providers that controlled the gate and the portal of the internet. Basically, everything got open sourced. And Google took off and eBay took off and Etsy and Amazon and all the millions of small websites and all the millions of small businesses and everyone that benefited from an openly accessible, open sourced internet.

If the internet was closed and there was proprietary software gates and portals throughout the internet that everyone had to pay to get through, the internet would not have taken off and the economy wouldn't have grown. And all these jobs would have been created.

It was called AOL and CompuServe. Like, literally, we had that.

And, gosh, it seems to me giving all this money back, buying back in the form of buying back your shares, you know, or giving tons of dividends — I think it's great that tech companies are now saying, wait, we have something to invest in. The next big thing is on-demand intelligence, and there is no upper bound for intelligence, or I don't think anybody — I certainly don't see, you know, anytime in the next 10 years, people saying, I got enough intelligence, I've got it, I've solved all the problems in the world. I think they're going to keep wanting it.

So what do you think about this incredible change? And, you know, basically $100 billion, $200 billion, you know, depending on the company, just going into CapEx. This seems like a savvy move, right? This is that all of us think this is a good thing.

Friedberg: 若你怀疑 Google，就别持有它

Freeberg: I mean, if you want to bet against Google's deployment of capital into infrastructure, because you'd rather have them give you cash for your shares today, you shouldn't own the stock. Someone else will buy it.

I think Google wins in a lot of different ways. There's just so much to Google. There's the consumer business, which is a lot of stuff. There's also YouTube. There's also GCP. There's also this portfolio of other bets, which, by the way, includes 10% of SpaceX and a good chunk of Anthropic that they own and so on. Way more worth $120 billion. I think they just took a $100 billion write-up on Anthropic in the quarter. So they had a $100 billion mark-to-market on Anthropic just in one quarter. And they own a piece of all these businesses.

So there's a lot to like about Google. But just on GCP, I think that there's probably no better-suited enterprise layer than GCP to take advantage of capturing value with AI for that enterprise setting. I think you're just so much better, because you have so much of your enterprise data — all your email, your Drive, a lot of information that you would want to have AI have knowledge of and have AI have access to to improve workplace productivity. And then they're model agnostic. I mean, you can run any model you want and you can run any workflow you want and you don't have to be tied in. A lot of other cloud service providers, cloud SaaS, they're kind of model dependent to run in a certain way. With Google, you can better tune your system how you want to tune it.

And what's the worst, worst, worst case scenario? The worst, worst, worst case scenario, they have the lowest cost infrastructure in the world to run other people's models as a service. Like Elon did with Grok, with the Colossus. Elon Web Services seems to be doing pretty great, and look at the return Elon's making on the Colossus install.

So I think if Google in the worst-case scenario, none of their application layer stuff works, none of their network effects work, and they don't have any good models, they're still going to have the world's best infrastructure they can print cash on for years if you believe in AI. So if you want to bet my AI, I think the best public market stock to own is Google. And by the way, you also get YouTube, you also get the consumer, you also get everything else. The multiple is kind of ridiculous right now.

Apple 与"Apple Web Services"的假设

We talked about this on a previous issue. I think, Chamath, you and I were talking about, like, what Apple should do next. And I think we both came to the conclusion, it's like, why not have Apple Web Services? They have such great relationships with developers. They have the App Store. They have this deep development relationship. It's not so easy, because you have to build a cloud service provider, you have to build some critical infrastructure. It's taken Amazon, call it 17 years to perfect it. It's taken Google, call it 12 or 13 years to mostly catch up.

But the minute that you sign up to be a web provider, Jason, and a cloud service provider, what you're really signing up for is five nines of reliability and uptime. And that is just extremely expensive. Getting to the first two nines, you know, 99% uptime, if you're hosting something for a pharma company or a defense company, you can probably do it for relatively cheaply. Getting to the third nine, 99.9, probably costs you in the billions. Getting to the fourth nine costs the tens of billions. But getting to that fifth nine costs hundreds of billions. And that takes a real investment and real technical skill. And there's only three games in town.

Yeah, I think Tim Cook's not the guy to do it. But this new CEO might be, since he's an engineer. But they've returned in the last decade, they could buy anyone at scale, approximately $900 billion — $755 billion in buybacks and $140 billion, Sacks, in dividends. Just let that sink in. $900 billion. If they had invested that in Anthropic and SpaceX and other things, they just could have found some good uses for that money.

But Sacks, any thoughts here on what's happening?

Sacks: Sorry, but who's to say that the investors that got that money didn't find a good use for it? Oh, yeah. So on society level. But I just think Apple could have been more ambitious if they just spent half that money instead of on buybacks and dividends on creating new products and actually releasing their car, maybe buying some interesting companies.

I think they think it was very much a "do no harm" capital allocation strategy, which worked for the stock. It's going to be really interesting to see if John Ternus flips the script. I think he does. I think he's going to be like engineer guy and yeah.

十、"社会主义角"：Mamdani 与"驱逐即暴力"

All right. Enough on the markets. The market's going to do what markets do. We will talk about Iran and other stuff like that when there's more news for venture capitalists to comment on. Right now, it's just on, on. I know everybody keeps asking. I don't think there's much for us to say on it.

I do think there's a lot for us to say in socialism corner, our new reoccurring theme here, Friedberg. Every week, there's more news coming out of socialism corner. I'll show my videos on socialism going back six years.

Let's add to the Friedberg socialism rants. Earlier this month, New York City dictator/mayor Zohran — Mamdani —

Don't misuse that term, please. Come on, Jason.

— a rental rip-off hearing at New York City's Tenement Museum. After the hearing, he introduced a rental rip-off report: - Bars landlords from charging applicants for credit checks - It's going to let landlords require a credit check OR the 40x rent income standard, but not both - Legally recognized as tenant unions - And more.

He's obviously frozen the rent for a year.

At the hearing, an activist wore a COVID mask and referred to evictions as "the violence of evictions."

Here's your 20-second clip:

"The Mamdani administration is emboldening us so that we no longer tolerate the violence of evictions as a matter of business as usual."

What were we just watching? Is that the — Sacks, do you remember the guy from Fat Albert who had the hat like that? Can we pull that guy up? Remember the guy from Fat Albert who had the hat? What's his name? Oh my God. It's still happening. I thought COVID was over. No, she just got a poster — that was like a super duper mask. That was a super duper mask. That just wasn't like a little cloth one. That was one of these — whoa. Those big ones. I mean, combined with the hat, it was — that was pretty — there it is. I remember that guy from — what is going on?

Wait, we're going to give Friedberg a chance to do a rant? Yes. I mean, I could do a rant on this. No, no, let's give Friedberg his rant. This is Friedberg rare meat.

Friedberg: 私有财产权是自由的基础

Friedberg, what are your thoughts?

Freeberg: In 1787, John Quincy Adams published a work called A Defense of the Constitutions of Governments of the United States of America. And in that work, he had a comment:

"The moment the idea is admitted into society that property is not as sacred as the laws of God, and that there is not a force of law and public justice to protect it, anarchy and tyranny commence."

And then in 1791, he made the statement publicly:

"Property must be secured or liberty cannot exist."

In an essay series.

Can you unpack it and explain why he said that, do you think?

Fundamental to the foundation of the United States of America was this idea of private property rights. Because if you think about where everyone that came to America was coming from — there were these tyrannical governments, monarchies or whatever, where some overlord or some cabal could decide at any point to take the things that you have. You had no private property rights as an individual. They could come in, they're like, that farm is my farm. You're actually a serf. I'm the lord. That thing is my thing. You have a right to use it because I vest you that right to use it. I am the all-powerful. I am the tyrannical overseer of these lands. And it was that stasis that drove so many to come to the United States and say, we want a place where individuals, one person, can say, I own something and no one can take it from me.

Private property rights are the foundations of liberty in America. This idea that you can then claim acts of violence, that you can then claim circumstances of extraordinary extravagant wealth and say to that individual, I now have a right, the government now has a right to take your private property, ultimately leads to this tyrannical form. And it starts out as being anarchic because — and remember, anarchy is a temporary state. It's always in between one state and another. All anarchies end up in tyranny. Groups of people fight each other, they're all stealing from each other, everyone just goes and takes and gets what they want, and eventually people coalesce, they form groups, and those groups become the more powerful groups, and the powerful groups end up winning, and they become the tyranny over the mass. And that is why all anarchies eventually evolve into tyranny.

So anarchy and tyranny are one in the same. And fundamentally, what's going on with these socialist principles is that we are taking your private property and you no longer have rights on your private property. Whether you are a landlord or whether you are a wealthy person that we've deemed to have too much wealth, we now will have the rights to come in and take your property and control it and take it from you.

And it always starts with this framing of moralistic intent. We are good. You are bad for the following reasons. You have committed violence against the people that live in your building. You have taken too much wealth and none of us have wealth. We have a right to go and take your wealth from you. It has always started from this point of view that you are bad. So the first framing is that the private property owner is evil. And that the private property owner has committed an act of injustice against those who don't have the private property. And that is the justification for taking away their private property rights. And it is the beginning of this transition towards a tyrannical system, which will ultimately be what I call this kind of great American politburo or whatever socialist framework gets set up by the cabal of the socialists and what they're trying to put together.

So all of these little acts, while seeming ridiculous and insane and inappropriate, in aggregate are the same thing. They're a transition away from private property rights, which is the foundation of the United States of America. That's why I think we should all be so shocked. And to John Quincy Adams' point, we need to vehemently defend those rights. As soon as those rights start to slip away, even in the tiniest way, it is a cascading effect. And everything will become tyrannical and it will be very ugly in the United States of America.

Sacks: 无法驱逐坏邻居，最受伤的是老邻居

Sacks, what are your thoughts here on Comrade Mamdani?

Sacks: Yeah, I just want to add a layer to this idea. You know, these DSA socialists say that evictions are violence and they basically want to stop them. I think Freeberg's making the point that this deprives the landlord of their property, and that's true. But I think we also have to stop and consider what this means for the other residents in these buildings.

I mean, first of all, if the landlords aren't making income because they got a bunch of delinquent tenants in the building, they can't now pay for upkeep and maintenance. And so these buildings become more dilapidated and that affects the other tenants.

But also, I have a friend who manages these apartment buildings, and he makes the point that it's often these squatters, these delinquent tenants who should be evicted but can't, who make the worst neighbors. So when you think about the problems in an apartment complex where you've got people creating noise at night, maybe they're playing loud music, or you have people punching walls, or there's disgusting smells coming from apartments, or they're misusing common areas, or you have drunken and disorderly behavior — I mean, this is all the kind of stuff that happens in these rent-controlled apartment buildings. And you have to remember that there's long-standing residents, a lot of old people who can't afford to find a new place. They depend on the rent control. And when you can't evict that unruly tenant, yes, it affects the landlord, but it affects the neighbors even more because now they're stuck in a downward spiral.

奢侈信念与工人阶级的现实

And I think this is a problem with the progressive mindset across the board is that these DSA types are always these like highly educated and often affluent types, and they can afford to have luxury beliefs about public spaces, because they never use them. Right? They don't use the bus or the subway or parks. And so when they get taken over by homeless drug addicts, they always defend the addicts as opposed to the middle class. And what an easy thing to do if you don't live in the Tenderloin.

Right, exactly. And it falls the hardest on the working class, because they actually need these amenities. They need the parks for their kids, or they need to use a subway, right? And it's really a problem when you get people shooting up or doing drugs or, you know, defecating in a subway. You're walking your kids to school. Like the person in Marin County who has these luxury beliefs or on the Upper East Side — they just don't — they're abstracted from this. They don't need to deal with it, right?

We talked about this. And it's no different with these rent-controlled apartments. I think that's the important point here — is that if over a period of several years you can't evict anyone, no matter how problematic they are, you effectively turn these apartment buildings into the equivalent of housing projects. And that really affects decent people of modest income who have nowhere else to go, and their quality of life suffers. And look, the private equity wives in their gated communities will still feel good about themselves because you know they prevented these evictions, but it's the people in the building who are going to suffer the most.

Well, at least — and they're traumatic — these people are not just — thinking from first principles: if you want to solve the housing problem, anybody with any basic understanding of economics would just say, well, increase the supply, and the price will go down. And it actually doesn't matter which supply you add. It doesn't matter if it's luxury units, or multifamily or single family — as long as there's more housing, and there's transportation to get to it and to move people in and out, it'll be fine.

J-Cal: 东京、德州、佛州都懂了

As I am sitting here in Tokyo, like they figured this out a long time ago — just build up and put more units in. They figured it out in Texas, Florida, Nevada. The only people who can't seem to figure this out is New York, LA, and San Francisco — just happens to be liberal elite enclaves.

It's not hard on a conceptual basis. Just allow people to build some more units and different types of units, and then the price will go down.

Chamath, any thoughts here?

Chamath: The data from Austin says once you relax the permitting constraint, you'll get more units built. And for every unit that comes online, it literally drives down the rent. So if you want low rent, you need to have more units. If you want more units, you need to permit more aggressively. That's it. So it's just a decision. The same political will that it would take Mamdani to pass this law, he could actually pass some permitting reform and it would do a lot more good.

The thing on private property — the reason I asked Freeberg to explain it is I really believe what he's saying is really important. It's like funny to me this idea that at the limit — let's just say you're driving your car, and all of a sudden somebody jumps in it. And they're like, well, you know, now I'm here, you can't kick me out. Or, you know, you go outside, you leave your door open to go get a FedEx package or Amazon box, and somebody runs in and sits on your couch. And now all of a sudden, you can't kick them out. And it sounds so ludicrously dumb.

If you force the owners of physical property to not be able to credit check and differentiate who they rent their apartments to, what's going to happen is rents will go up even more. So I suspect that what they should do is they should pass this law and they should observe what the outcome is. And then you can do a pretty scientific A/B comparison between New York City and Austin, and you'll know what works and what doesn't work.

Yeah. I mean, here's the problem, is the socialists never learn. I mean, we already got rid of rent control in Argentina. Rents went down. Yeah, yeah. I mean, this is a problem with, Chamath, is that, look, if the socialists ever learned from their failed experiments, you wouldn't have Chicago. You know, it's just like we don't need New York to go down the tubes to know this isn't going to work, because it's happened in so many other places already. But somehow it just never seems to stop. They never seem to learn.

So they should run the experiment and learn. I mean, what's crazy is you'll be learning and it'll be a failure on the grandest stage possible. You're talking about the biggest, most complicated city. Yeah, my gosh.

房东的处境与"幽灵公寓"

Yeah, I mean, and Sacks, what happens if a landlord cannot raise the rent reasonably well? They have no incentive to invest in new units. They have no incentive to upgrade new units. And there's this trap in New York City specifically, they have made this regulations for apartments such that if you do a renovation, it has to hit certain codes, and there are a ton of codes. Okay, so that means it's incredibly expensive. So now you have ghost apartments. Yes, now the housing stock becomes dilapidated.

And look, they're doing something even worse now, I think, which is they are banning landlords from doing credit and background checks on potential tenants. And they say that you can't look at their income. So you can't vet whether they can actually pay the rent. So they're banning a landlord. No more landlords. They're banning eviction. And then they're preventing you from doing the diligence to see if this is even a tenant who will pay the rent. We've lost the script.

So what are you supposed to do?

Chamath: The interesting question is, if you were forced to live under these rules, the landlord, what would you do? And the obvious answer is you'd start rent three or four times higher, and you force people to sign up to a multi-month prepayment, and you'd slowly ease those conditions until you find a market clearing price. That's the only way to do it. So rents will not go down. Rents will go up. So run the experiment. And let's just observe what happens.

That's a really good point, Chamath. Let's say that X percent of tenants are going to become delinquent, right? And by the way, what's their incentive to pay when they know they can't be evicted? Zero. So actually a pretty significant percentage of people could just decide, I'm going to make rent optional. And so now the landlord has to absorb those losses. And that means they have to pass on a higher rent to everybody else.

You're going to set the rent 3x higher and you're going to slowly meander it down. And like I said, you're going to have to wire in the first full year of rent. Okay, good luck. How is that more affordable?

It's even worse, Sacks. Not only do the landlords keep the dilapidated apartments, in some cases, it's better for them to just leave apartments — housing stock — empty. So somebody leaves, they are forced to renovate it, and it costs more, you know, hundreds of thousands in renovations. So they say, you know what, I'll just leave it empty for now. And so you have 50,000 ghost apartments according to reports in New York City.

Well, that's an Airbnb problem. That's like — no, they banned Airbnb in New York. You cannot get an Airbnb. Oh, really? Yes. So now that's really interesting. Yeah, look, if you're a landlord, okay, I mean, I guess one thing you do is to sell and go to another jurisdiction. Another thing you could do is just wait this out. Because it's not profitable to run an apartment building. You can't raise your rents. You can't evict people. You can't diligence the tenants. So maybe you just leave the building empty and you wait this out.

I mean, that's assuming you don't have too much debt on it, right? More ghost apartments, yeah. And then you have ghost apartments. Yeah.

收尾与广告

All right, listen. You've been thinking about coming to the All In Summit. This is your year. Speakers are world-class. The events, the parties, the networking — 80% of the people that are founders, investors or high-level operators. This year, greater focus on networking, musical performance. Yes, I mean, in the past, we've had the food, the drink — rhymes — Diplo. Diplo. We've had so many incredible people. Go to theallinsummit.com.

All right, everybody. It's another amazing, all-time legendary episode of the All In Podcast. Love you, boys. Bye.

Let your winners ride. Rain Man David Sacks. And it said, "we open sourced it to the fans and they've just gone crazy with it." Love you, Westies. I'm the queen of kids. Westies are back. Dog taking a mission in your driveway. Oh, man. We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy because they're all just like this like sexual tension. But they just need to release somehow. You're the beat, wet your feet. We need to get merch. I'm going all in, we're going all in.

item.description:
## 一、表面之下：这不是"开源之争"，而是一场关于"知识经济时代终结"的葬礼预演
大多数评论把这集当作"美中AI博弈"或"Anthropic的监管俘获"来看，但真正令人不寒而栗的洞察藏在 Friedberg 最后那段几乎被忽略的独白里——**中国的开源战略并不是为了赢得AI，而是为了让AI这一整个赛道"贬值归零"**。
想想这个反直觉的结构： - 美国过去50年积累的财富，本质是"把一个比特转换成另一个比特"的知识经济溢价 - 中国用20倍的制造产能、8倍的电力产能，长期押注的是"分子转换经济" - 如果开源让"智能"变成像自来水一样的公共品，那么美国最擅长的那一层价值就会像2000年前后的电信带宽一样瞬间坍缩
**这里有一个让人不适的类比：Anthropic 和 OpenAI 现在的处境，像极了1990年代末的 Encyclopedia Britannica**——不是被更好的百科全书打败，而是被"百科全书这件事本身不再值钱"打败。他们向政府求救的动作，本质是在为一个正在消失的商业形态申请"临终关怀"。
## 二、跨领域连接：Anthropic 的"IP盗窃"话术，是一次法

item.title: [Business of Sport] Has Football Finally Cracked America, The Story Behind Golf’s Hidden Superpower, & NRL’s $5.3bn Deal
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：RNA 是体育治理界的"隐形寡头"，它证明了不透明才是最持久的竞争壁垒

节目里两位主持人对 R&A（皇家古老高尔夫俱乐部）的态度非常有趣——他们一边揭露它是一个由苏格兰老绅士在会所里啜饮红酒运营世界高尔夫的"影子组织"，一边又忍不住"脱帽致敬"。这不是矛盾，而是揭示了一个被现代体育治理话语彻底遮蔽的真相：在一个人人要求透明、多元、问责的时代，最健康、最赚钱、最少丑闻的全球性体育治理机构，恰恰是那个最不透明的。

对比一下：FIFA 高度公司化、透明化，却陷入无穷争议；Jockey Club 一旦"民主化"就迅速崩坏；ATP/WTA 用委员会治理，反而让球员为奖金池比例撕破脸。而 R&A 用一个"信托前台 + 私人会所后台 + CEO 兼任双方秘书长"的三层结构，把治理权、商业收益、会员分红全部锁死在同一群人手里——没有人抱怨，因为没有人真的能看清。这与英国宪政的"未成文"逻辑高度同构：模糊本身是一种权力技术。当一切规则都写下来时，规则就变成了博弈对象；当规则藏在传统里时，规则就是空气。

二、跨领域连接："百球板球" × "补水暂停" × "R&A 现金堆" ——三件事其实是同一件事

表面上这期节目谈了三个毫不相关的话题：ECB 的 The Hundred 缩短比赛时长成功了、世俱杯的补水暂停被证明是伪装的广告位、R&A 坐拥 2 亿英镑现金却只象征性地投资青训。但如果把它们放在一起，会看到一条被忽略的产业主线——

"注意力单位（Attention Unit）的证券化"。

  • The Hundred 把 3.5 小时的 T20 压缩到 2.5 小时，本质是让一个"注意力单位"更接近足球比赛这个全球标准长度，从而使它可以被同一批广告主、同一套播出窗口、同一份家庭日程"复用"。
  • FIFA 的补水暂停不是为球员，是在同一场比赛里凭空多铸造了 832 个 30 秒广告位——把 90 分钟的比赛"切碎"成更多可售卖的注意力片段，Fox 光这一项就近乎回本 4.85 亿美元的转播费。
  • R&A 拒绝把奖金池提到营收的 22%，坚持只给 8%——是因为他们理解一件深刻的事：Open 的品牌溢价来自"稀缺 + 传统"，一旦奖金军备竞赛化，注意力单位就会通货膨胀，反而贬值。他们宁可把利润变成现金堆在银行，也不参与这场膨胀游戏。

换句话说：足球在做"注意力单位的通胀扩张"（QE），高尔夫的 R&A 在做"注意力单位的通缩紧缩"（收紧货币）。两种货币政策，两种未来。哪一种更长寿？看看谁在 270 年后还端坐会所里就知道了。

三、Chelsea 与 NRL 的镜像：同一种"过度杠杆"，一个在俱乐部层面，一个在国家联赛层面

节目里 Chelsea 又花了 1.17 亿英镑买 Morgan Rogers，主持人半嘲讽半困惑；NRL 则刚签下 53 亿澳元的历史性转播合同，对英国 Super League 展现出"施舍还是收编"的暧昧姿态。这两条新闻看似风马牛不相及，但骨子里是同一种"资本势差"的显影。

Chelsea 靠 6 年摊销把巨额转会费"未来化"——今天签下的 1.17 亿，会计上只是每年 2000 万，用未来的收入抵今天的赌注。NRL 对 Super League 做的事情，逻辑一模一样：NRL 每家俱乐部拿到的转播分成，比整个英超 Super League 联赛的总转播收入还多。当财富势差达到 20 倍时，"合作"这个词就丧失了对称性——它必然演化成"殖民"，只是包装形式各异（联合品牌？球员双向租借？IPL 式的多联赛股权？）。

这里有一个真正令人意外的连接：cricket 的 IPL 已经通过"同一批老板控制多国联赛的同一支球队"实现了全球化（Mumbai Indians → Mumbai London → MI New York）。节目最后一句轻描淡写的猜想——"也许我们会看到同一批人同时拥有 NRL 和 Super League 的俱乐部"——其实预示着一个更宏大的模式：21 世纪体育全球化不再是"国家队 vs 国家队"，而是"跨国俱乐部联盟 vs 跨国俱乐部联盟"。国家变成了地理标签，真正的作战单位是横跨大洲的品牌资产组合。板球是先行者，橄榄球联盟正在跟进，足球（曼城的 City Football Group）早就在做。

而 R&A 在这一切喧嚣之外，安静地坐在苏格兰会所里——他们已经用另一种方式（rulebook + 品牌 + 现金）实现了同样的事，只是没人注意到。真正的全球治理，从来不需要 5.3 亿美元的新闻稿。

But effectively what Super League in this country is asking for is please please please give us a helping hand here because our TV deal seems to be going down over time and our commercials going down to the point now where the kind of total wage bills that we're looking at in in British rugby league about 2 million quid a year. Um, now I'm not saying that professional rugby league super league players in this country are exactly pleading poverty, but it is getting to the point where if any of them do have the opportunity to go to Australia, they would be absolutely crazy not to take that opportunity.

Well, to put it into context again, it basically means that you're you're likely to get and they haven't fully disclosed, but let's say you're likely to be getting 25 to $35 million from this deal per club. Yeah.

Per year.

Yeah.

Right. So more than the entire broadcast deal in this country. per club.

We know what the finances are generally used for in sport. If you can go and get the best talent and the best players from the other league and bring them here because that's the marketplace for it. And as well, we've talked about this before, right? The the sport in Australia, as you said, is huge. Here, it's a band of the country. People have got very upset with us talking about rugby and saying rugby union, rugby league, you know, not specifying. You have an amazing audience in the UK. It isn't a well spread one. It's not a diverse one. is a very specific group of fans who have been following and you talked about generational fandom who have been following these clubs and the stories behind it which we've discussed on previous shows is fantastic.

Been numerous attempts haven't there to sort of get a proper London team going. You've got the Broncos um who have been tried with many times over the last 20 years and there's been more investment coming into the Broncos.

Exactly. So look what I want to get back on to this proposed deal. No one quite knows what's in this proposal. I looked around everywhere and I spoke to various people and you know the rugby football league in this country is keeping its cars pretty close to its chest in terms of what that deal looks like, what the proposed deal looks like. They've been careful to say it's not a we're not proposing a take over a takeover. We're not saying that the NRL should take us over.

The CEO of the NRL has been very clear on that. public communication.

But but that is a PR point cuz if you then look into what what the underlying likelihoods are for the last whatever it is 20 or 30 years rugby league in this country has been being played in in the summer months. Y — right it used to be a winter game. It was put into the summer months so it didn't have to compete straight against um against football. Um but of course the thing is is that in Australia rugby league gets played in their winter which is our summer months. So, if you're going to start proposing a partnership between the two, our rugby league would have to go back to our winter months, right? To to to make sense out of that, you wouldn't want to have or the NRL would not want to have be in partnership with organizations effectively scheduling rugby matches at the same time as their own rugby matches.

Yeah.

Um, I think you'd have to be thinking about um, you know, what investment the NRL could be making into rugby league in this country given that they've got a lot of money and what they would get in return for that. You know, what would be their why would they do it? Why would they bother getting out of bed to do it?

Um, now they've said quite clearly in the statement, the chief executive of the NRL, he has said, "I don't want to simply take all the best players from Britain. Otherwise, what product would we be left with in Britain?" M right.

So the challenge then comes okay so what's the transfer of money going to be like to enable rugby league players to be able to be paid more money in this country but also could we end up in a situation where some stars start playing in a bit of both — right so if you think about I'm I'm just thinking laterally here what in cricket we're seeing the same franchise owners starting to own franchises in the IPL um now in in in our in America, in various other cricket jurisdictions, the same people.

I wonder if that's kind of where this might end up going, where you might see the same groups owning a a franchise in Australia and in this country. And you might start to see some of the superstar players — um being able to play at least part of the season in both to try and sort of boost sort of um interest in it.

It's all speculation. No one quite knows, but the bottom line is that when the NRL's scooping TV dealers like that, they can kind of do whatever they want. And it's just to be hoped from the prospect of rugby league in this country, that what they want is in a way to grow the game worldwide because otherwise it is kind of just an Australian game. If it if it doesn't flourish in England, which is the second biggest jurisdiction for rugby league, then you are losing it as a global game.

Yeah. And you want to have that, right? We've talked about this with India and cricket. India could monopolize cricket. They need to have a few teams competing with them on at least an international test level. Yeah. To maintain a lot of that interest.

If you do this in rugby league, they need to have just about enough of competition where they get a bit of variety, but not enough to eat into the success of the of their own product.

The challenge I would have is is a conversation we have regularly. What's the value for the NRL to prop up, if we want to say, create this partnership with the Super League?

Charlie, I just want to ask you a question, right? Which is if I'm running the NRL and I've just maxed out my Australian audience and I'm getting the TV deals that reflect the fact that I've maxed out my Australian audience and I'm thinking, where in the world are there more eyeballs that can watch my product, the NRL? Well, you'd start with Britain, wouldn't you? Being the second biggest rugby league geography. Um and therefore it is potentially an expansion moment for the NRL itself.

Yeah.

Now they might very well regard Brit British Rugby League as being effectively under capitalized. Right. Which is the le the rugby league itself and the clubs within the rugby league are so poor that they just don't have the money to do the stuff that needs to be done to really push the the sport forward. Now you and I might well push back saying okay it's pretty competitive landscape. you know, you've got rugby union, you've got football, you got cricket, you got all sorts of different other sports and rugby leagues only in one particular part of the but the NRL might say, "We believe in our sport. We believe that our sport is the absolute top top premium spectator offering. It's just in this country, it's not being promoted in the right way." So, they might just view this as a big expansion opportunity.

We've talked about the challenge of club rugby in rugby union, right? and and and their issues with developing consistent and continual fandom that turns up every single week — in to some degree while in competition with so many other things that happen. Now, if you add another thing to that in this country and you go, as I said, you know, your audience in rugby league, you know, you've got that core, that's not in question. The the question would be, can we build it?

Can we develop it? Because why would Sky pay more money — for a deal right now when they can pretty much predict — how many people they're going to get based on the Rugby League?

So if you were the NRL looking at it, you'd say, "Right, we're going to put massive money behind getting this right in London. We want two franchises in London, right? We want to put lots of money behind them because that's a key part, you know, even in terms of there are so many people who are originally from the Northwest who are living in London, right? So we're going to have to get really get the marketing going to get them into the stadiums to watch this."

I I think it's just think it's going to be fascinating, you know, and sort of watch this space.

尾声：三则"成功案例"的意义

It's interesting on today's show we've discussed what in a in a way three triumphs you know so often we end up discussing stuff that's gone wrong and here we discussing stuff that's gone right talking about the ECB's creation and effective sort of actualization of the hundred as a concept and the value accretion that's happened as a result of that then you've got the masterful governance of golf by the ra and ancient golf club of St Andrews um with all that that has meant over the last 100 to 200 to 300 years and then you got the NRL and them having mastered their own home market and made vast amounts of money from that and now thinking, okay, could we potentially do something in Super League which really starts to globalize a sport in a more ambitious way.

So, I'm going to be fascinated to read in the next 2 to 3 weeks what that deal actually looks like cuz it's bound to come out. There was a lot of mood music around the NRL is going to want to complete their media rights deal before they agree anything with the Super League. It almost seemed like a bit tempting fate to say, "Okay, we haven't signed the contract yet, but now let's start talking about how to spend it." Now they know they have it and now they've got the Super League proposed in front of them, whatever that looks like.

I'm guessing in the next two to three weeks, we'll find out what it is.

Oh, I agree. Fair play to them. Well done everyone involved. Um, if you want the other side of rugby, we're about to go and chat about the nation's championships and everything that's going on in rugby union. So, if you want to come and have that chat, come and join us on Substack. And if not, we will see you next week. Thank you, Charlie. Thanks Charlie.

## 一、最反直觉的观察：RNA 是体育治理界的"隐形寡头"，它证明了**不透明才是最持久的竞争壁垒**
节目里两位主持人对 R&A（皇家古老高尔夫俱乐部）的态度非常有趣——他们一边揭露它是一个由苏格兰老绅士在会所里啜饮红酒运营世界高尔夫的"影子组织"，一边又忍不住"脱帽致敬"。这不是矛盾，而是揭示了一个被现代体育治理话语彻底遮蔽的真相：**在一个人人要求透明、多元、问责的时代，最健康、最赚钱、最少丑闻的全球性体育治理机构，恰恰是那个最不透明的**。
对比一下：FIFA 高度公司化、透明化，却陷入无穷争议；Jockey Club 一旦"民主化"就迅速崩坏；ATP/WTA 用委员会治理，反而让球员为奖金池比例撕破脸。而 R&A 用一个"信托前台 + 私人会所后台 + CEO 兼任双方秘书长"的三层结构，把治理权、商业收益、会员分红全部锁死在同一群人手里——**没有人抱怨，因为没有人真的能看清**。这与英国宪政的"未成文"逻辑高度同构：**模糊本身是一种权力技术**。当一切规则都写下来时，规则就变成了博弈对象；当规则藏在传统里时，规则就是空气。
