And what sets Excel different from these static expression models, such as SGV or geneformers, is that we actually, instead of training on gene expression datasets, we train on causal datasets. We train on massive amount of genome-wide perturbation datasets, so that it learns better about the dynamics of the interventions.

And in our preprint, we extensively compare with linear model as well. And as you mentioned, linear model totally failed to extend to unseen cell types. You can quickly imagine why. And I believe that foundation model or other more complicated AI models that train on the right data will outperform these linear models in harder tasks, particularly in generalization tasks. And that's why I keep mentioning the right dataset with the right AI model will lead to huge improvements. But I think the field still needs to see more biological validations to be more convincing than the virtual cell direction is the right one.

[Xi Chu] Yeah, I think the field suffer from a lack of consistent and uniformly accepted benchmarks. What gets measured will get improved. And in our paper, we measured, I think one of the metrics that we put a lot of thought into and saw the model really shine is metrics around gene expression changes. So in Pearson Delta, the similarity between predicted changes and ground truth changes upon a perturbation. That's very hard to cheat on. You have to really get the changes right.

And what really blew my mind away is when I saw the model make prediction, just print out the heat map of the gene expression changes, look at the actual raw data and line up the linear baseline prediction, the ground truth and the XR prediction altogether. It's visually very clear to see that XR prediction is very much more similar to ground truth than the linear baseline.

[Bo Wang] This is a wow moment I was talking about in the beginning.

[Xi Chu] And it's not hard to understand why when we put, so this is the first time that someone can put together not just one perturbs, but seven genome-wide perturbs campaigns together. Something that jumped out to us, biologists right away is that some of the perturbations are context universal, meaning that the genes do the same thing in regards to the cell types you experiment in might not be surprising to you that these are your housekeeping genes, right? Of course, they do the same thing every cell.

And then there are all of these other clusters of genes that have very context specific functions, they do different things in different cells. Again, not hard to imagine why in iPSC in our stem cells, we saw developmentally relevant genes, that are important for neural differentiation. They only light up in iPSC experiments, of course, right? That makes sense.

So if you think about biology, it's so complicated that you have to capture these, you know, context universal perturbation effects. You also have to somehow learn the context dependent perturbation effects. It's not hard to then see why a very sophisticated nonlinear model is able to capture and learn all of those biology much better.

单基因扰动的局限与组合空间

[Brandon] Are your perturbations always single gene perturbations? Or do you have more? Because my understanding of regulatory networks is oftentimes, sometimes it can be a single gene does a ton of things. For example, I think males are just differentiated due to one gene being enabled at like day seven of embryo development or something. And that differentiates everything is this one gene. But then sometimes you have large networks of genes, which all are very redundant, which allows for more subtle feedback mechanisms and so on. So I could imagine a lot of single gene perturbations as being kind of irrelevant. And that you might want to start having a more commentorial strategy here.

[Xi Chu] Yeah, that's a great question. And Bo and I have thought about this a lot. Actually, it's interesting that you brought up reproductive biology in, I studied a lot of in female cells, the compensation, the dosage compensation mechanisms. There are female cells have two X chromosomes, male cells have one X chromosome to match the dosage output from the X chromosomes strategy that the mammalian cells employ is one gene that produce a RNA that does not encode for any protein, just a non-coding RNA. That RNA wraps around one of the female X and turns down most of the gene expression from that chromosome, shove it away in the corner of the nucleus and it's called the bar body. It is never heard from again.

And so I absolutely agree with you, one gene can do a lot. But in biology, you also have redundancy, you have compensation, you have all kinds of mechanisms where knocking down one gene is not sufficient to always see a phenotype. What if four genes redone only do the same thing, right? Taking out the RNA is not going to be sufficient.

So where we started with one cell type at a time, loss of function, single gene perturbation, and look at only RNA expression as the output, we're expanding the platform along all of those axes. So that's what we do today to build a scaffold of the data for training models like Excel. We are now beginning to grow in all three axes of the platform, going beyond transcriptomics alone to like a multimodal data, going beyond just one gene perturbation alone to look at also pathway activation and inactivation, turning on and off entire cascade of chain reactions. And also going beyond just cell lines, monocultures into more and more complex translationally relevant systems into primary cells, into organoids, doing even direct in vivo perturbation swings. So we believe with all of that expansion, that data will be all the more exciting to train models on.

[Bo Wang] This is also why we incorporate PPI networks as the prior knowledge into our model. And although the model right now are trained on single gene perturbations, but once the model is trained, you can actually predict combinatorial perturbations just on the model in only silico, right? So in the sense that we can just perturb the tokens of two genes at the same time and see what's the response. Certainly without training the actual combinatorial perturbation data sense, the accuracy may not be there, but at least with the existence of such models, we can start to generate hypotheses using in silico perturbations.

AI 时代的科研角色与学界生存

[RJ] How do you see the role of the scientists changing in the age of AI? And you may, because you're not using, your focus is not language models themselves and agentic science and things like that, then you may have a different, slightly different take. You're building these very specific models, but still one, how are you and your students able to maintain such a high pace? And I suspect it may have something to do with generated by AI partly, but also, and how do you see the role of the scientists, the academic changing?

[Bo Wang] Yeah, that's a great question. So my official split of time is 80% on the era, 20% on my university affiliations, but turns out the reality is 100% on the era, 100% on the university.

[Brandon] You invented a time machine, that's the answer.

[Bo Wang] So the way I try to keep up is something we, my lab use lots of agentic AI trying to monitor all the AI papers every day. And which every week we have lab meetings, we're trying to discuss different topics in AI for biology, AI for healthcare, et cetera.

And it's, to be very frank, even as a professor, I find it's extremely hard to catch up. The pace of AI is just so incredibly fast. And to the point that sometimes I feel anxiety, waking up says, "Oh my God, so many people published and what happened to our existing on-purpose work." And suddenly, you can imagine students probably face 10X anxiety.

So sometimes I try to encourage students to really kind of using different tools, trying to stay focused, and find the niche areas that we become experts on. But with the era of generative AI, now agentic AI, I find the way people, at least academics, does science are extremely different now.

Overall, most of professors or students in academics start to be very struggling in terms of fundings, in terms of the pace of publications. And that's why you can see lots of major breakthroughs come from industry, like Alpha-Fold, for example.

So how academics survive or even thrive at such era of agentic AI is certainly something everybody is thinking about. We see lots of faculties left university and join industry simply for the reasons of resources. If you are doing research on AI, do you have enough GPUs at your school? It's the first question you should ask when a student joined a professor's lab. The first question they often ask is, "How many GPUs do you have?" So suddenly, in that sense, industry has a major advantage over academic labs.

But I think what academics labs have advantages on is really the pace of innovations and also the niche areas of this specific academic lab can be extremely expert on. So also having the freedom of thinking sometimes also makes you easier to innovate on ideas that maybe industry people didn't even think about.

Overall, I think the whole field needs to be a lot more innovative to catch up and hopefully with the help of different tools and hopefully the government starts to invest more into academia because I still deeply believe that academic is the main source of innovation for the whole field, and particularly when it comes to biotech. So hopefully we see more investment into academia so that we stay afloat.

为什么学界仍然重要：教学、自由、公共基础设施

[RJ] I agree with you, but why? Why should the money just go to industry? Why should the government put any money into academia?

[Bo Wang] I still believe the power of academic freedom. This is actually the original motivation we have, the existence of academic professors who are the only we teach, and there's also benefits of teaching and research at the same time in the sense that when you teach a subject, you actually have to become the experts and that force you to keep updating your knowledge base and then find easy ways to convey your knowledge to students. And by doing that, you actually start to innovate on different ideas.

And myself, for example, I teach a big class at the University of Toronto about deep learning and neural networks. It's a gigantic class with 600 students every year. And by teaching that, it forces me to update the slides, lectures every year, and myself reading lots of materials, trying to update myself so that I can find ways to convey some of the knowledge to students. So that's how I keep updating myself whenever there's transfer. I remember vividly we have GPT-2, we updated the lectures, and then different language models, how the multi-thread GPU communication is used in training, largest scale neural networks, et cetera. So I force myself just update the models.

And by talking to different students, we really generate lots of novel ideas to apply the cutting-edge AI models to very specific niche areas in biology or in healthcare.

Maybe it's unique to Canadian academic system. By being a professor in academic, we also have access to lots of healthcare data sets, which are very hard for industry to access due to many illegal reasons or regulatory reasons. And that's why you see some of the papers we published through academic hospitals in Canada, where we developed some of the state of arts foundation model for ultrasound images. So that's what I mean that there's certain level of freedom of academic thinking that really drives lots of innovations.

And I still believe, maybe it's biased, but myself still believe that having certain level of freedom of academic thinking will lead to lots of kind of innovations that is unthinkable in industries.

[Xi Chu] I 100% agree with Bo there. So just thinking about the lab workflow that we do, a lot of these are building upon innovations that were first pioneered in academia as well. CRISPR, of course, was discovered in academia. CRISPR applied to mammalian high-throughput screening, also demonstrating academia first. scRNA-seq, this kind of drop-up encapsulated scRNA-seq first demonstrated in academia. Then different companies tried to build it up into commercial offerings. Putting all of these together to do Perturb-seq at first, also pioneered in academia, right? CRISPR lab Jonathan Weissman's lab, Aviv Regev's lab, many of the pioneers in academia.

And then I think these, especially on the lab side, these innovations take so long, and the discovery process can be so accidental, right? That it's perhaps not ideal for a pure industry to take on. But once they show early promise, scaling them and robustifying them, and generating data that's not only massive but high quality, especially for AI scale, I think that's something that can be very well done in industry, both the mindset, as well as the kind of the resources that we can support. That sometimes can be hard for academia labs to match.

开放科学与学界应聚焦何处

[Brandon] Xaira has been very generous with releasing your data sets and your models. You've been, seem to be very committed to open science. Given some of the things you were just talking about, and this discussion about what is the best, most important data strategies for virtual cells, or understanding human biology, where do you think academia should go next, now and next? Since Xaira has probably a budget comparable to probably dozens or hundreds of bio labs right now, what do you think that if you are an academic, a professor, especially in a wet lab, what would you want to be focusing on?

[Bo Wang] First of all, myself is a deep believer of open science. That's why all the models we talk about here, that are open source. You can find all the data weights from my lab GitHub. It's very thorough. Yes, thank you.

The reason I believe open science is that, as you mentioned, most of the time, academic lab, we started an idea and we prototype it. It's not scalable, it's not even a good product, and industry can take it to scale things up. This is also why SDGPD quickly becomes one of the most widely used single cell foundation model in pharma companies. That's very encouraging to us.

This is why Xaira also started to open source some of the data sets, some of the models. Part of the reason is that we believe virtual cell is such an early field, and it doesn't help to withhold certain data sets or certain models because it's so early. A better win-win situation is everybody gets to in this field start to contribute models together to exchange ideas so that this field can move forward in a much faster pace.

We see successful examples in protein space because of the availability of open source data sets in PDBs. Therefore, we have models such as alpha fold, rosetta fold. Again, alpha fold is also open source. Therefore, we can quickly iterate different models. That's why you see a booming situation in protein space. We want to do the same thing for virtual cells. Let's put all the data sets together. Let's have the same standard protocols to generate high-quality data sets. Let's put all the resources together to generate next generation of virtual cell models.

When it comes to academic labs, then you can comment on what lab, how what lab academics can survive. From Joy Lab's perspective, I do encourage all the Joy Lab AI researchers in universities start to collaborate with industries so that they can get more resources to develop their own ideas. With the era of HNT AI, now everybody can code. It's more important to have a right taste about your project so that you don't just burn tokens without purpose. We want more academic students, academic professors to have a taste of research so that we make the right utility of HNT AIs.

[Brandon] As a professor, your job is to have taste, obviously, but as a student, how do you develop taste as in a world where so much of the thinking scientific process could be essentially outsourced to an LOM or a, you know, some there's not a world where you're forced to bang your head against something and you're forced to take a taste by the hard way.

[Bo Wang] This is why we need academic training where you get into a field you know nothing about and hopefully after you graduate become the expert about this particular topic in the world, right? This is why you have to go through different programs to talk to your peers, talk to your professors to get an idea about what's a good taste to begin with.

But more importantly, I always teach students that the best way to learn something is to just program it. By programming, you kind of know what's the details hidden in all the mathematical equations in the paper, which often you omit.

But in the era of agentic AI, things are slightly different in the sense that we used to spend lots of time coding, a little bit of time just debugging. But now we let the agent do most of the coding, but we spend most of the time debugging, which seems to be definitely interesting to me. And we had lots of discussion with the students in the lab what's the best way to spot bugs by by AIs. So how do you find places where AI is particularly good at? Also, how do you find places AI are still limited at? You need lots of China era as well.

And in the end, you still need to kind of validate your model using real world evidence, right? So that's why collaboration with wet labs, collaboration with clinical teams to validate your model, provide feedback signals to your taste, as we discussed, is certainly a very important training program.

[Xi Chu] On the wet lab side, academic has extremely important roles to play. I think we'll enter a field of symbiotic innovation and cross-pollination of ideas. Just like in AI field, I think we have great ideas coming out of academia still all the time. But industry now increasingly are contributing new ideas on architecture, on all of that as well.

In the wet lab side, certainly industry seems to be able to scale these type of data generation quite well. But biology is so much more than just cell-based perturb-seq. Beyond RNA-seq, we would like to measure many other analytes, right? Proteins, metabolites, lipids, protein-protein interactions. How do we do that at scale? Beyond individual cells, we would like to be able to measure cell-cell interaction, spatial, cell in their native context, or even whole animal level in vivo perturbations. Again, how do we do that at scale with lots of great innovation coming out of academia? Actually, just one great paper last week.

And so how do we connect all of these together? I think we have many years of work ahead of us to fully crack data for all biology. And that I think we need to scale the industrialization, the innovation from industry. We also need that from academia. I think we'll together move this field to the next level.

魔法愿望：如果能解决一个瓶颈

[RJ] One question that we've been trying to ask everyone is in your field, which you could say maybe is AI and sort of high throughput experimentation, or however you wanted to find out. If you could wave your magic wand and have a bottleneck removed for you, or a key problem solved, what would that be?

Chu 的愿望：高通量蛋白质测量 Protein.

[Xi Chu] If there is a way to do protein sequencing or high throughput protein measurement, the same scale that we can do genomics, that would be amazing. I'm training genomics field, but if I can do that, I would incorporate that technology in a heart beat.

RNA is amazing. It foreshadows which proteins are going to get made. But protein by and large are the functional units in a cell. Not only does their abundance matter, their post-translational modification matter, their localization in a cell matter. If you can measure all of those things, their conformational states, their modifications, their abundances, their localizations at scale, single cell, or even spatially, I think such data sets would be incredibly useful to train the next generation of initial models. I know there's a lot of innovations in that direction. Can't we just see that become a come of age?

Bo 的愿望：同一细胞的时序测量 [Bo Wang] My hope is I hope to see a breakthrough in sequencing technology, not just the reduced cost, but sequencing technology that can sequence the same cells at different time points. I think this is much lacking right now because you have, in order to sequence the cell, you have to kill the cell.

Can we have a technology that can measure the cell states at different time points for the same set of cells? I think that will bring a very different dimension to the data set so that we can start to measure the temporal dynamics of cells. So far, everything we measure, everything we model is extremely static. Can we have a technology that measures different cell response at different time points for the same set of cells will unlock massive opportunity to model the dynamics of cells. To me, that is a real virtual cell.

[Brandon] That's a really interesting idea. I never would have thought about that. Wow. Would you be okay with even just partial small snippets of genes or maybe three prime regions of a small number of transcripts?

[Bo Wang] Yeah, we can start with a small set of gene panels to begin with, right? But eventually, since we are talking about the magic, eventually, if we can have a system that observes how cells evolve at different time points and we have enough data to actually model such development, I think that would be a real virtual cell model.

[Xi Chu] There are small attempts, also earlier attempts, in just, for example, sucking out portions of the cells, taking almost biopsies from the cell to do a fraction of the cytoplasm measurements. So that might be similar to the idea you talked about. There's also work from a public in this lab to have the cells secrete little vesicles and they harvest that in the cell culture media to measure what the cells are producing longitudinally. But there hasn't been technology that can let you measure the entire cell's transcriptome while still keeping the cell. You can't have the cake and eat it.

结语与招聘

[Brandon] Cool. Yeah, thank you for taking the time to chat with us. It's been great. We've learned a lot. It was a lot of really interesting discussions. I especially really appreciate your commitment to open science and all of the cool models and data, if you're at least. Is there any last thoughts you have or anything you'd like the audience to know? Follow up on that.

[Bo Wang] Overall, I think virtual cell is such a new and fast moving field. We hope to have more and more people join us and our Excel paper is out and we look forward to receiving your comments and feedbacks. And also we're hiring.

[Xi Chu] Yeah, we are always looking for talented engineers, technologists, biologists, drug hunters, AI scientists, computational scientists. So look on xaira.com. Look for the open roles. We'll be happy to chat with you.

[RJ] Thank you. Thank you very much. Great.

[Xi Chu] Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、意外观察：他们在“修改”细胞，而不是“书写”细胞
大多数生物学基础模型（scGPT、Geneformer）沿用了 ChatGPT 的**自回归范式**——像打字一样一个 token 接一个 token 地生成。但基因表达数据根本没有天然顺序！Bo Wang 团队做出的最激进选择，是把生成范式从"**打字**"切换到"**编辑**"——用扩散语言模型迭代式地精炼整个基因表达向量。
这里有个被访谈者本人没有明说的深层反讽：**整个 NLP 领域花了七年时间想把 Transformer 从"集合运算符"逼成"序列生成器"，而生物学领域正在反向走回去**——因为细胞根本不是句子，是同时炸开的 20000 维快照。Brandon 在采访里模糊地感觉到这点（"transformer 本来就是 set operation"），但没人挑明：**X-Cell 的成功其实在暗示——语言模型的"因果顺序"归纳偏置对语言可能都是次优的，只是被工程惯性锁死了**。生物学在这里像一个自然实验，暴露了 LLM 架构选择中一个被忽略的假设。

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Mark Cuban on the AI Bubble: Who Actually Gets Wiped Out?
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这不是互联网泡沫，这是风投行业的自我引爆

Cuban 抛出了一个反直觉的诊断：这场 AI 泡沫破裂时，出租车司机不会谈论它，普通美国人也不会受伤——因为泡沫的能量被封闭在一个专业阶层内部。这与 2000 年那种"人民的泡沫"截然相反。

有意思的是这里有个隐藏的对称美感：VC/PE 曾用"风险民主化"的叙事把散户从公开市场吸走（因为好公司都留在私募里），结果他们成功地把风险也留给了自己。这是一个自我实现的因果闭环——他们把公众隔离在外，最终也把损失隔离在了自己手里。这或许是资本主义历史上第一次，"泡沫破裂"变成一场行业内部的清算，而不是社会性的伤口。

跨领域的连接：这很像加拉帕戈斯群岛的进化陷阱——一个封闭生态里的物种因为缺乏外部选择压力，会朝极端方向进化（估值从 500 万一路飙到 6000 万而产品还没上线），最终一个外部冲击就能引发局部灭绝，而大陆生态毫发无损。

二、"前置部署工程师"是 AGI 神话的证伪证据

这是整场对话里最锋利的一刀，也几乎无人注意到：如果 AI 真的接近 AGI，Anthropic 就不需要雇 6000 个"前置部署工程师"去帮企业实施 AI。 Cuban 用一个逻辑短路揭穿了整个叙事——一个能"取代 50% 白领"的技术，怎么会需要人类工程师才能被部署到白领的工作场景里？

更让人意外的是：这个悖论和 Palantir 早年靠"前置工程师"建立护城河的商业模式是一模一样的。Alex Karp 的焦虑不是"AI 会取代我们"，而是"这些 AI 公司在盗用我们十年前发明的商业形态"。也就是说，前沿 AI 公司正在悄悄地从软件公司退化成咨询公司——一个远古的、劳动密集型的行业形态。这是"技术进步"外壳下的商业模式退化。

跨领域连接：这就像 19 世纪的电力革命。电力本身很快就发明了，但让每家工厂真正用上电、并重构生产线布局，花了整整 40 年。真正的瓶颈从来不是模型智力，是社会技术界面。

三、大模型将成为算法喂养时代的解毒剂——这是本次对话最反常识的政治预言

Cuban 顺口说出了一个几乎没人在讨论的悖论：社交媒体的货币是"参与度"，大模型的货币是"正确性"。这两种货币系统正在同一个用户的注意力里打架。

反直觉的是：大多数人担心 AI 会加剧信息茧房，但 Cuban 说的正好相反——LLM 有一个结构性动机去"求真"，因为一旦用户发现它撒谎，产品就死了。而算法则相反：用户越愤怒、越沉迷，产品越活。所以我们可能正在见证一场媒介之间的自我制衡：一个媒介让你困在信息里，另一个媒介让你从中逃出来。

这里有一个更深的系统性洞见：AI 的商业模式恰好和民主健康所需要的"共同事实基础"是对齐的。这在人类媒介史上极其罕见。报纸靠订阅（真相有点重要），广播靠广告（娱乐重要），社交媒体靠参与（愤怒最重要），而 LLM 是第一个把"给出准确回答"作为核心商业指标的媒介。这不是道德胜利，是商业结构意外与公民健康对齐——这种对齐是稀缺资源。

跨领域连接：这类似 20 世纪初 AT&T 的"通用服务"承诺——一个垄断者为了保住信任而不得不承担公共品性质的责任。垄断者的商业模式如果依赖"被信任"，就会自愿地行使"准公共品"的克制。LLM 可能正走上这条路。

一个额外的、埋在对话里的信号

Cuban 反复告诉他的 portfolio 公司"go public, motherfuckers"——这不是投资建议，是他在为即将到来的 AI 并购潮做准备。逻辑链是这样的：AI 会让"小而快"的公司具备颠覆性能力 → 大公司必须收购它们才能自保 → 而收购需要股票作为货币，因为现金太贵 → 所以现在不上市的公司，等于放弃了参与未来重组的资格。IPO 从"退出机制"变成了"进入机制"——这是一个悄悄发生的、几乎无人察觉的资本市场语法翻转。

📝 转录文本

关于 AI 泡沫：这次和互联网泡沫不同

Jason： You and I live through a couple of bubbles. We've seen this movie before. Um, and this wave seems very different than dot waves. So, let's talk about that. Are you concerned about a bubble? We're seeing bubbly-like behavior. People —

Mark Cuban： It's not, it's not the traditional dot bubble, right? Because back then there was companies going public getting crazy valuations and people are buying them and the stock would go up, you know, 50% 100% with companies that had no revenue, no traffic, no nothing. And you'd go get a cab back then and people would be talking about them. Yeah. And you don't, you don't see that at all today.

So, it's not a bubble that's going to impact most people in the room, right? Or most people um across the US, but it could just destroy a lot of VCs and a lot of funds and a lot of PE, right? Because they're going all in.

I'm going all in.

[广告：AppLovin — App 111 started with an $8 domain and no VC funding and became one of the largest ad platforms in the world. Now that same engine powers AppLovin ads for e-commerce. Mark Cuban： Well, that's why we come to these things in Europe, right?

Jason： Yes.

Mark Cuban： Because great talent, right? Smart people. Obviously, you guys are geniuses for being here, you know. But at the same time, there's a different vibe in every European country and India and the whole rest of the world, right? And I think you're starting to see some entrepreneurs leave us —

Jason： Yep.

Mark Cuban： To come here. And that's scary. And hopefully, you know, large language models seeking the truth will help educate people away from what the algorithms tell them.

对美国、乐观主义与领导力

Jason： Yeah, I think it's important. You optimistic now? It's been pretty chaotic, but we're seeing such great progress. You optimistic?

Mark Cuban： About — let's start with America and then we'll go to humanity.

Jason： Yeah.

Mark Cuban： Yeah. No, I mean, you know, like every country, we have our issues. Ours just happen to be kind of insane.

Jason： It is pretty wild.

Mark Cuban： Yeah. [laughter] But the good news is, you know, we have term limits for our president.

Jason： Yeah.

Mark Cuban： And —

Jason： Yeah. And it seems like 12 — three terms is going to be the one for president. I mean, you're going to run. I mean, I hope you do, man. I would love to be your press secretary. That would be a — we'd have so much fun.

Mark Cuban： We'd have fun.

Jason： We would have fun.

Mark Cuban： Well, if he decides to run for a third term, then I'll run. But he's —

Jason： Yeah. Okay, that's good. That's breaking news. I mean, I, uh, honestly, if you think about what we need, I think, in leadership — executives who can, I think, you know, who are post-money, post needing to make a living. Um, that no — I'm not going to even go there. [laughter]

Well, and then maybe who are doing it for love of country and maybe some amount of civic pride, or —

Mark Cuban： No, I get what you're saying, right? And it's just like — you know, in the US, what — the Democrats don't know how to actually do anything, right? You know, they know how to take whatever happens and extrapolate that to the end of the world and the end of democracy, right?

Jason： Yeah.

Mark Cuban： But and the Republicans on the other hand, you know, do crazy shit, right? Like they don't care about the people in the country. There's no connection to people. There's no empathy. And so, you know, we're — in the short term. But I think as we get past this next — the midterms and the next presidential election — I think we'll get back to normalcy. I think we'll get — I think people wanted —

州治理对比：德州 vs 纽约

And you know, the thing that has been really eye-opening for me having lived in New York, California, now Texas — you know, in Texas, we spend half as much money per — sometimes less. I think it's two and — 2.2 times as much is spent on each citizen in New York. And we spend half as much, right? $67,000 per person. They spend like 14 or something, 12 to 14. And quality of life's better.

But on the flip side, New York contributes more to the federal treasury, right, than Texas does. And you would think it should be the opposite, right? Just because of the business and how things are run. So there are trade-offs.

Jason： Yeah. But it's changing. Like what do you think about all of us moving to Austin and like Texas? You got —

Mark Cuban： Smart, obviously, for obvious reason — particularly, you know, like the wealth tax shit is just dumb-dumb crazy.

Jason： They tried it here. Everybody works, and they did it for about two years in France.

Mark Cuban： Did they? Yeah. I don't know. But you know, when Elizabeth Warren first proposed the wealth tax and she said, "Well, we have these models and everything," so I found the economist at UC Berkeley and I said, "Would you share your model with me or at least tell me about it?" I'm like, "Was it more than one year?" And he goes, "No, it was just one year." I'm like, "Did you do any behavioral analysis to see how people would respond to the changes?"

Jason： Yeah.

Mark Cuban： No. And so, you know, whether it's Mamdani, Elizabeth Warren, whether it's California, it's showmanship more than reality.

Jason： Yeah. And I think people are forgetting that people are mobile, you know.

Mark Cuban： US.

Jason： Yeah, in the US it's pretty extraordinary. You got Travis, Sachs, myself, Elon — just a bunch of folks have all of a sudden just shown up.

Mark Cuban： I was there first.

Jason： You were. I remember talking to you about it. And the thing that's amazing to me is, you know, in California, they won't let you build anything. And then I come to Texas, I buy a ranch, and I asked the guy, "Hey, can I put a solar farm in here?" He's like, "On your ranch?" I'm like, "Yeah, here." He's like, "Oh, son, it's your ranch. You can do that." It's like, can I build like —

Mark Cuban： Trust me, in the cities themselves — try doing that in the city of Austin.

Jason： I mean, but just outside of it, you build. And housing prices have gone — three years in a row housing prices and rents have gone down. When you build a company in Austin now, and I'm sure it's like that in Dallas and Houston and San Antonio, when I have founders move there, the entire pressure is released. People can own a home. And I was like, wow, is that —

Mark Cuban： Why do people still go to Silicon Valley? That drives me pissed.

Jason： I think if you're a first-time founder, nothing better in terms of soaking in it. But when you're a second-time founder —

Mark Cuban： Soaking in it, but what they don't tell you, the shit is, right?

Jason： Yeah, it's tough. I think second-time founders have now realized: if I build it in Texas or Nevada or Florida, I'm going to — just all the talent's going to come.

Mark Cuban： In Silicon Valley just sets people's heads so wrong. Yeah. Right. So whether it's Travis, Mike — by the way, I've known Michael Dell since we were 22. Yeah. And I used to do business with him way back when. But in Texas, it's just like build your company and go.

Jason： Yes.

Mark Cuban： In the valley it's like, so are you series A? Are you series B? Are you series C?

Jason： A lot of distractions.

篮球时间：纽约尼克斯、独行侠、以及联盟规则

Yeah. 25 years I've been waiting for my Knicks to win a championship. And you played a significant role.

Mark Cuban： No, the Spurs — significant role. [laughter] They should have kicked your ass.

Jason： And why didn't they? Why didn't they?

Mark Cuban： I think it was coaching, lack of experience. Yeah. You know, cuz you're — put aside the 29, right? You're up in the fourth quarter of every game. WBY throws it into the back of some guy, misses two free throws. Dear Fox goes the wrong way.

Jason： Lot of mistakes.

Mark Cuban： Yeah. And you would be talking about firing Mike Brown. [laughter]

Jason： I mean, it was — we were concerned when he got hired and getting rid of Thibs. Oh my god.

Mark Cuban： Thibs. But JB was the real deal, right? Was my Indiana boy OG, right? He, you know, he saved you guys. So —

Jason： Yeah.

Mark Cuban： Uh, and you had Jalen Brunson.

Jason： Yep. He left and that was kind of destiny. His family wanted to come.

Mark Cuban： That's what he wanted. I mean, I could show you a text where his agent, you know, texted me. He says he wants his own team.

Jason： He wants his own team, right? Yeah. He was ready to go before.

Mark Cuban： And I texted or emailed you and I said, "What's the story? Is this what we're going to base the franchise on?" You said he's really good. He's the real deal.

Jason： You know what I love? He's a great guy. That's the best part about JB. He's just really a good human. I was there for the fifth game, six rows behind the bench.

Mark Cuban： That's cool.

Jason： And, man, I just cried. I just cried. It's been so many years. And you got your chip, too, with Dirk.

Mark Cuban： Yep.

Jason： It's so amazing how sports plays such a role in so many people's lives.

Mark Cuban： Yeah. Especially now — look at the World Cup.

Jason： I mean, it's just like sports has just changed everything. And you know, like I've been to four World Cup games in Dallas and I hate soccer, football.

Mark Cuban： Right.

Jason： I hate it. But just the whole scene, the vibe, the energy — you can't beat it. It's like going to a Knicks game, going to a Mavs game. Same thing.

Mark Cuban： Yeah.

NBA 全球化与规则变化

Jason： And the NBA — is it peaked? It sounds like —

Mark Cuban： It's hard to say. I mean, you know, for fans, no. Because it just grows on social media, you know. I went — I was walking in Paris and there was a basketball store, you know, and it had Wembanyama jerseys and Gobert jerseys and everything. And so, I mean, it's just growing globally.

Jason： Yeah. Is Wemby the real deal?

Mark Cuban： Yeah. He got humbled though.

Jason： Yeah.

Mark Cuban： Which is good for him. It's like Dirk in 2006 — got humbled and came back better. He'll come back bigger, stronger, better.

Jason： Yeah. It's amazing how he went from this like incredibly — I don't know, there was a magic about him — to, no, he's a villain, and he turned into a villain.

Mark Cuban： Because it was New York and it was 50-some years, right? And just the circumstances. And you know, San Antonio thought they had it in the bag. Everybody — it's like I went to Indiana University, right? And if anybody here follows college football in the states — like we were the ultimate underdog. We had not won 10 games. We beat more top-10 teams last year than we did in 100 plus years of the program. And so that just changes people's attitude.

Jason： You were very much involved in rule changes. And we're going to get on AI next, but it's just great to talk to you about this since we're both such super fans of the NBA. Seems like the rule changes, the apron and how punitive it is, has created a lot more parity in the league. And nobody knows who's going to win, like —

Mark Cuban： Well, because you have to break up your team, right? Because at some point, OKC will have to break up their team. That's why they collect all their draft assets, because you can't have three max players. No. And if one of them turns out to be hurt or not what you expected, then you're in deep, right?

And so the second apron is just a complete game changer. And you have to be so much better at putting together a team than you were before. And you have to get lucky. Like the Spurs have — went beyond a rookie contract, you know. OKC has got, you know, Hartenstein on a rookie contract. He's not on a rookie contract any longer. So they have to be even more careful. And so it really changes the strategy behind building a roster.

Jason： So we're going to see back-to-backs anymore?

Mark Cuban： No chance.

Jason： No chance.

Mark Cuban： No. I — maybe back-to-backs, but not a — what do they call when you have three — the three-peat.

Jason： Three-peat. Yeah, no more three-peats.

Mark Cuban： Can be back-to-backs. Like, you know, if Jalen Williams — JDub — hadn't gotten hurt for OKC, I think they would have beat San Antonio and I think they would have beat the Nets —

Jason： I was worried about them versus the Knicks. I knew we could beat the Spurs but I was concerned about —

Mark Cuban： I did not know you could beat — I knew — we beat them two out of three of the games of the year. We spanked them. I knew it would be like a — I said Knicks in six. It was Knicks in five.

Jason： You guys barely beat the Hawks and then —

Mark Cuban： Oh, come on now. We were tweaking the offense and we just had to get Cat to buy in. Us — points.

Jason： Let's talk AI.

Mark Cuban： Let's talk AI.

尾声：冠军与球队估值的新逻辑

Jason： But it is so great to be a champion. God, it was — where's your ring? They didn't give you —

Mark Cuban： They didn't yet. No, I'm going to get it at the ring ceremony. [laughter]

Jason： I, you know, I always was like, man, I got to follow Cubes and get, you know, a piece of —

Mark Cuban： You always told me you wanted to buy a team.

Jason： I always wanted to get like a piece of the Knicks. And now it's like my net worth doing great, the value of the team disconnected from reality. I mean, my only chance is to call like Elon and be like —

Mark Cuban： Part about the valuations is it's not driven by attendance. It's not driven by wins or losses. It's driven by subscriptions to streaming services. And it's going to be interesting to see. Because it used to be we looked at ratings — TV ratings — and people said the NBA was underperforming versus everybody else. Now, the Knicks play, obviously there's some pent-up demand there, but what really matters is the number of subscribers Peacock gets, ESPN gets. It's the ratings sales, but it's more subscribers.

Jason： I mean, I literally had to subscribe to like, I think, one or two more services.

Mark Cuban： Well, that's the whole point, right? And did you keep them is the question.

Jason： Yeah, I'll keep them. Sure. I mean —

Mark Cuban： But there will be churn. If there's churn, who knows what happens with valuations. If there's not, valuations keep on going.

Jason： Wow. So crazy. All right, listen. There's your 45 minutes with Mark Cuban, the one and only.

[music]

Mark Cuban： I'm going all in.

[music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、这不是互联网泡沫，这是**风投行业的自我引爆**
Cuban 抛出了一个反直觉的诊断：这场 AI 泡沫破裂时，出租车司机不会谈论它，普通美国人也不会受伤——**因为泡沫的能量被封闭在一个专业阶层内部**。这与 2000 年那种"人民的泡沫"截然相反。
有意思的是这里有个**隐藏的对称美感**：VC/PE 曾用"风险民主化"的叙事把散户从公开市场吸走（因为好公司都留在私募里），结果他们成功地把风险也留给了自己。这是一个自我实现的因果闭环——**他们把公众隔离在外，最终也把损失隔离在了自己手里**。这或许是资本主义历史上第一次，"泡沫破裂"变成一场行业内部的清算，而不是社会性的伤口。
跨领域的连接：这很像**加拉帕戈斯群岛的进化陷阱**——一个封闭生态里的物种因为缺乏外部选择压力，会朝极端方向进化（估值从 500 万一路飙到 6000 万而产品还没上线），最终一个外部冲击就能引发局部灭绝，而大陆生态毫发无损。
## 二、"前置部署工程师"是 AGI 神话的**证伪证据**

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Grant Williams: Gold Is Warning Us About What Comes Next
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：金本位不是"选择"出来的，而是被"逼"出来的

Grant 在这里颠覆了整个货币改革叙事。所有的评论员都在争论"金本位好不好、要不要回去"——这本身就是一个错误问题。真正的机制是反向的：社会动荡 → 政治动荡 → 金融市场动荡 → 巨型去杠杆事件 → 被迫用黄金重新稳定系统。

这里藏着一个更惊人的推论：2020 年那几万亿凭空印出来的美元，可能是"最后一次掷骰子"。因为它成功阻止了那次"巨型去杠杆事件"——也就是说，它推迟了通往金本位的最后一道触发器，但代价是把系统里的通胀压力封存起来，让它现在正在"试图挣脱"。换句话说，我们没有避免那一天，只是让那一天变得更贵。

二、跨领域连接：AI 时代的"懒惰陷阱"，与 Grant 从进攻转向防守，其实是同一件事

Grant 说"人类的所有发明本质上都是让自己更懒的方式"——这句话表面上是在批评有人用 ChatGPT 替代尽调，但把它和他自己的资产配置从 70/30 进攻变成 90/10 防守放在一起看，一个更深的模式浮现了：

过去 40 年，"懒惰"是被奖励的。你可以闭着眼睛买指数、买房、拿国债，甚至倒着摔进任何东西，只要拿住就赚钱。这是一个允许"外包判断"的时代——外包给美联储的看跌期权、外包给全球化、外包给下降的利率。AI 恰好在这个"懒惰红利"耗尽的临界点出现，让人们在最不能偷懒的时刻，获得了史上最强的偷懒工具。

这就是为什么 Grant 60 岁的"防守转向"和年轻人用 AI 找十倍股，看起来无关，其实是同一枚硬币的两面：一个人在识别范式转移，一个群体在用新工具加倍押注旧范式还会持续。

三、被忽略的信号：Bessent 的"语言学"，比 Fort Knox 里有没有金子更重要

大多数人只关心"Fort Knox 到底有没有那 8133 吨黄金"。但 Grant 抓到了一个更微妙的东西：财长 Bessent 措辞上刻意的距离感——"我没去，但我团队的人去了"。作为财长，他本可以说"黄金都在那儿，我亲眼见过"，但他没有。

这是一个语言学层面的信号交易。它和欧盟从"廉价货币的共同决策"（人人都爱）变成"紧缩的共同决策"（土耳其不会投票支持圣诞节）是同一种现象——当一个系统的一致性依赖于正和博弈，任何轻微的语言退让都是结构性裂缝的先兆。

四、China 长游戏的真正逻辑：不是为了锚定人民币，而是为了做"最后站着的人"

主流叙事说"中国囤金是为了给人民币背书"。Grant 的洞见更冷峻：中国根本不需要用黄金背书人民币。他们在囤金，是为了等到美国、欧洲、日本被债务危机逼着重新引入黄金的那一天——那时候，谁的黄金多，谁就是新的金融世界之王。

这个逻辑和围棋的"厚势"概念惊人相似：你不是为了当下的这块棋，你是为了三十步之后的全局。西方的四年选举周期天生无法执行这种策略——民主政治的时间贴现率太高，只有能"不需要每四年被再次选举"的体制，才能玩这种五十年的博弈。

五、真正意想不到的连接：DFW 的鱼缸寓言 → Grant 的日元套息 → 你的思维盲点

Grant 引用 David Foster Wallace 那个著名的"水"的寓言——鱼不知道自己泡在水里。他把它用在日元套息、NATO、联合国、"黄金很无聊"这些"二战后 70 年的默认假设"上。

但这里有一个更深的含义值得停顿：你无法通过思考跳出鱼缸，你只能通过被伤害跳出鱼缸。因为鱼缸的定义就是它是你所有思考的媒介。Grant 说得含蓄，但这是残酷的：那些正在读这个转录的人，大概率已经在鱼缸里想过"要不要跳出鱼缸"这个问题——但仍然没跳出去。真正让人跳出去的，从来不是洞察，而是成本。所以他给自己的解决方案不是"想得更清楚"，而是结构性地降低试错空间（90% 防守）。这才是他真正的答案。

📝 转录文本

开场：金融系统的重置

"This idea that the entire financial system is about ready to reset. Will it be reset or will it naturally reset? I don't know. Nobody chooses to go back to a gold standard. It's the other way round. You have social upheaval, you have political upheaval, you have financial market upheaval. That leads to a giant deleveraging event and the answer is to bring back gold to stabilize the financial system.

And you know, we've had social upheaval, that's clear. We've had political upheaval, that's abundantly clear. We almost had financial market upheaval in 2020, but we conjured another several trillion dollars out of thin air to paper over those cracks. So, we avoided the giant deleveraging event. But in doing so, that was perhaps the last roll of the dice."

主持人开场与足球寒暄

Welcome to the Microscopic Podcast. I'm your host, Alexov. And today I'm joined by my fellow English brother from — uh, let's say a football brother that has — uh, let's just just the two of us. We were just talking about the fact how much we're in pain this morning. Uh, our our respective teams have lost uh in a bit of way. I would say French definitely out you on that. Uh —

Grant: Yeah. Well, look, look — let's — the the good thing you have is that you have those extra stars on your jersey and you've you've had as much pleasure as you have pain. We've only had pain. So I I refuse to believe there is a sporting nation in the world that have suffered more pain than the English. So I'm afraid I'm going to call dibs on this one.

Alexi: What was even more painful was I had an interview with Michael Oliver a few days ago and I was actually wearing my French jersey and I had to post it the day after we lost. So that was even more painful.

Grant: Yeah, that hurts. That hurts.

Alexi: And now — it's football.

Grant: It's football. It hurts you more than it shows you love. So what are you going to do?

Alexi: Football is life, as this great character in Ted Lasso said.

过去 8-9 个月最重要的转折点

Alexi: Apart from that, obviously like we haven't talked to each other I think since eight months. That was last time it was in Switzerland — and as we all know there's never a dull day in the macrosphere. Things happen almost on a weekly basis. It really feels like just confirming what you've been also telling us last time that we're in this very transitionary phase of different systems, not just one system but many in different levels.

So I would like to first maybe begin the conversation with asking you: what do you think were the most important turning points in the last 8 to nine months since we actually spoke last time? What surprised you the most?

Grant: Well, it's a great question. I've tried very hard to find a way to not be surprised by anything. And I think that's been important for me because I think we're at one of those turning points where really big change is happening, which we spoke about last time.

And I think anytime you get into this place where there are big changes happening, you can find pockets — and we had this in the '90s, where markets, because the world was on a trajectory of, you know, post the Berlin wall of more peace and more cohesion — and yes, we had 9/11 and we've had these various little kind of skirmishes, but the world in general was on a trajectory towards more peace and more cooperation and tighter knit and globalization and all these things. So you had that period where being ready for anything wasn't as important. It's always important to be prepared but it wasn't as important.

Now I think trying to find a way to let go of all your preconceptions about how the world works — that's not to say you completely change how you do everything. But you have to be more nimble and you have to realize that the kind of change that's happening is going to lead, by definition, to more unexpected outcomes.

从"可能"到"概率"

So I think that's how I've tried to approach the last couple of years. And so when you get the war with Iran — which obviously, I mean people could say they've seen it coming for many many years as the rhetoric's ratcheted up — but when it actually starts, it still catches you by surprise. And those kind of conflicts, conflicts involving China, trade wars, all these things for me have become probabilities rather than possibilities now. And so that shapes the way I think about them.

系统重置的临界点

And then there's the big one — you know, this idea that the entire financial system is about ready to reset. Will it be reset or will it naturally reset? I don't know. But I feel like that's now the big thing that people need to be conscious of. And again, it's not a definite, but 25 years ago, it was a definite that it was not going to change. The financial system was not going to change. It worked for everybody. Yeah, there were some parts of it that you could see, particularly around the debt, were starting to get a little bit out of hand. But now I think we are in the sweet spot where it needs to change, and anytime something needs to happen, it tends to whether we like it or not.

So that in a nutshell, that's for me the important thing. It's a mindset for us to say: right, we can't assume the world will work tomorrow the way it works today. And what does that mean for how I think about investing? How I think about whether I allocate my capital for growth or I allocate it for maintenance of my purchasing power?

投资组合的重塑：Rick Rule 的自然资源大会

Alexi: So maybe a blunt follow-up question would be then, what would that then be exactly, and how would you paint this, let's say, the portfolio construction that you just mentioned now? What would be, let's say, your first step right now in assessing which asset you would own in this kind of environment, and how would you then also question what you own at which step of the way?

Grant: Yeah, it's funny. I've just been at Rick Rule's conference in Boca Raton, Florida, which is always great. This year was particularly good. And this was a question that I found myself either being asked directly or in discussions about.

It was very interesting because you know the conference — it's a natural resource conference and you've got a lot of great companies there exhibiting and showing gold mines and tin mines and silver mines and uranium and every kind of natural resource on the planet, which I do believe is a space that's going to be in a bull market in the years to come. So you've got all these companies that are looking to raise capital, they're looking to find investors, and you've got an audience that are hungry to make money. So it should be, for both sides, like shooting fish in a barrel.

一位名叫 John 的先生

I sat down with a gentleman — really nice gentleman called John — who saw me and grabbed me and said, "I would really like to talk to you. Can you spare some time?" So I said, "You know, of course, let's sit." So we sat and chatted for a while and he asked me this exact same question. And the answer I gave him was this one:

"Look, I'm pushing 60. I'll be 60 in a few months time. And so my challenge now, having worked for 40 plus years and got myself in a position where I'm okay — you know, I don't live an extravagant life, but I'm okay now. I have the money I need, if I'm careful with it, to be fine now and to leave some money for my kids and do all the things that I set out to do when I started work 40 plus years ago.

商品作为"必需品"

So resources are a great way to make money in a bull cycle because commodities are "need goods," right? The world needs commodities. People don't pull stuff out the ground for fun. And the price of the companies that do it will also reflect that — at the ebbs and flows of regulation and price and supply and demand.

So putting money into commodity stocks I think is a really good idea if you are at the right age, you have the right amount of interest and the right amount of time to spend monitoring the companies, and you have the right risk tolerance and you don't get your position sizing wrong.

AI 与尽调：一个被外包的危险

A subject that also came up quite a lot was AI, understandably. And the point I was making on one of the panels is — for me, with regards to that second type of investing, AI is potentially incredibly dangerous because it feeds that insatiable human desire to be lazy.

Humanity is lazy. Every invention mankind has ever come up with, essentially, is a way to do less work or to lighten our workload and get the same output. That's the story of progress, the story of humanity. And what AI does is it gives people the misguided belief that they can outsource their due diligence around companies, around positions they own, to AI.

And people are coming saying, "Well, you know, I've got Claude or I've got ChatGPT, and I've set up different GPTs to act as mining analysts for me to find the companies that I need to buy."

There is no substitute. None. I don't care what AI is capable of doing, of going to an event and meeting the management of the company, meeting the CEO, meeting the geologist and sitting and talking to them and asking them pointed questions about the company. And then once you've decided that you like the asset, you like the management, you like the jurisdiction, all the things you have to do, and you invest your capital — leaving the maintenance due diligence up to AI is, I think, a massive mistake.

You have to read. You can set it up to give you alerts, but you have to be reading the press releases. You have to be understanding what a certain headline at a mine can mean, because the guys who've made money in that space understand that and they know which 50% drawdown is a massive buying opportunity and which 50% drawdown is halfway to zero. They're distinct and they're very important to understand.

历史坐标：黄金覆盖美国债务需要多少价格

More importantly to me is if you look back at a chart of — let's assume the gold is there. Let's assume Scott Bessent's people were right when they went to see it and they told him what they'd seen — if you look back through history at the amount of the US debt that gold covers and the price you need for gold to reach those levels once again, there are three dates. There's 1917, there's 1940 after World War II, and then there's 1980 when we had these spikes in the gold price.

  • Currently we sit at, let's call it $4,000
  • To match 1980 coverage: gold would need to be $30,000 an ounce
  • To match 1917 levels: I think it would have to be $60,000 an ounce
  • To match 1940 levels: it would have to be $72,000 an ounce

That would be — and by that I mean to have the same amount of gold backing for the debt. You've got the same amount of gold, obviously, and at different prices it backs a different amount of debt. So those are levels: $30,000, $60,000, $70,000. We're currently at four.

And at some point, in every instance where a country starts to have the spotlight turned on its debt and the affordability of the debt and whether that debt will ever be paid back — those are the points in time where you say, "Well, what is that debt backed by?" And through history, it's been gold.

Now, people will argue that the United States debt is backed by its military, or it's backed by national parks and all these great assets that the United States has on its balance sheet. But it doesn't count. No one's going to be able to swap a billion dollars of treasury bonds for a nice little part of Yellowstone National Park. So it's a spurious argument. And yes, the military backs it — and if you kind of try and take it, they've got a lot of guns and aircraft carriers — but gold is the barometer. And so given the debt and the amount of gold that we have supposedly in Fort Knox at $4,000, it's way too low. Simple as that.

核心论点：没有人"选择"回到金本位

I talked about this in my presentation "Cry Wolf" in 2018, which I just kind of went back to at Rick's conference and did an update on it. The commonly accepted wisdom and the way people talk about a gold standard is this: they say, "Well, nobody would reintroduce a gold standard because if you do that, you have a massive deleveraging event that leads to social upheaval, political upheaval, financial market upheaval. So the gold standard is not coming back."

And the point I made in 2018, which I make again this year, is that that's not how this works. Nobody chooses to go back to a gold standard. It's the other way round.

You have social upheaval, you have political upheaval, you have financial market upheaval that leads to a giant deleveraging event, and the answer is to bring back gold to stabilize the financial system.

  • We've had social upheaval. That's clear.
  • We've had political upheaval. That's abundantly clear.
  • We almost had financial market upheaval in 2020, but we conjured another several trillion dollars out of thin air to paper over those cracks. So we avoided the giant deleveraging event.

But in doing so, that was perhaps the last roll of the dice, because now we can see the inflation that's now embedded in the system is trying to break loose.

So to me, we're a giant deleveraging event away from being forced back onto a gold standard temporarily. This isn't the answer to our problems, because it does create problems having a gold standard. But the problems it creates are actually solutions. The problems it creates is that it stops politicians promising and spending. It stops you spending money you don't have. So that's the solution to the problem that got us here. But it creates the problems that you go through when you try and set a system like that — it does create deflation, it does create all the things that the gold standard creates, but we need that now to purge the system.

So ideas like Judy's of this gold-backed bond, I think, are great. And I think they will come. But they won't be a choice made to celebrate anything, let alone the 250th anniversary of the United States. They will be a choice forced in times of trouble, when you need people to buy bonds and they won't buy them unless they're backed by gold. And that's where I expect us to go back to — even if it's only for the short term to stabilize the system.

David Foster Wallace 的鱼缸

And it takes an ability to step back. If you continue the David Foster Wallace analogy about the water we swim in, you've got to try and find a way to step outside the fishbowl if you want to see the water for what it is. It's just this contained environment with the fish swimming in it. If you're in it, you can't see it. You've got to find a way to step back outside the fishbowl in order to see it.

And if you can step outside the fishbowl, you can see that the water is different. And whether you want to stretch the analogy and say you can see that the water's got a different color to it, or a different viscosity, whatever it may be, if you step outside the fishbowl you can see that it's changed. And because it's changed, you need to change.

You need to change the way you think. And only by changing the way you think can you get to the point where you can understand whether you need to change the way you act. And you may be set up correctly for this new environment, in which case you don't need to make massive adjustments to your portfolio. But it's not until you change the way you think about the water that you will have enough information to work out whether you need to change the way you act.

欧洲：本应是巨人的第三方

Alexi: And now there was also something else I was asking myself — that as we see those great powers, and this is mainly, we don't know, as you said, change is constant and you need to readjust more than you used to before because the foundation of this new game is being rewritten, the rules are being rewritten. But the players are kind of known, right?

And in this case, where I see the biggest weakness in, let's say, the reconstitution of the world order, is the role that Europe will play. And in this case, I can speak for myself, I can also speak for you as Europeans — we just look from both sides and we just seeing in one way or another, we're getting squeezed. We are between two giants trying to fight for their survival, or at least impose their view on the world in one way or another. How do you see that, especially — because you have kids as well, grandkids — what are the thoughts that go into that process for you?

应该有三个巨人

Grant: Well, look, it's a great way to put it, but it's also, if you actually stop to think about it, part of the problem — because there should be three giants. Europe should be a giant, right? It should be.

The European continent is bigger than America, more people than America. It's a massive market for China. It's a massive market for America. But it isn't a giant. And that is part of the problem.

You know, the EU was a project that was designed in good faith to avoid more conflict on the European continent, but also to create a giant. And so I think what you said there is again important, because people in Europe again have to step outside the fishbowl to understand that Europe is not what they believe it to be.

I think if you talk to any Europeans who are pro-Europe, pro-European, pro-the EU, their perspective on what Europe is and its place in the world will be very different to how people outside Europe look at it. And again, in Europe you've got multiple distinct countries, distinct cultural identities, distinct ways of looking at their place within the European Union. So it's very difficult to get an accurate perspective on Europe unless you are removed from it.

Even the Brits, who are now technically removed from it, they struggle to have a really good perspective on Europe because it's always "what-aboutism," right? It's always "we left and we're doing so much better than Europe," or in the same country, "we're screwed because we left Europe, we should have stayed in Europe." It's impossible to get that perspective.

从外面看进去

If you step outside to America or you step outside to Asia and you look at Europe dispassionately, you can see what a mess it is, and you can see that without the right sort of coordinated policy — primarily energy policy, which is a complete shambles across Europe — the Americans and the Chinese will be looking at Europe thinking it's almost a third world power. Which is crazy, because it absolutely shouldn't be.

The policies that it's embarked upon have made it weak. And so at some point Europe is going to have to find the strength to push back against the policies that have weakened it. Largely, you know, net zero policies; largely the kind of micromanaging of the EU and a lot of the subsidy culture. There are so many things wrong with the EU as a project. It's an admirable ideal, but there are so many things wrong with it that are actually hurting it and creating this kind of weak mass at the center of the world.

依赖美国防务的代价

The Russia war and Trump's comments about NATO have exposed that for all to see. Europe has become weak because it believed that it could rely on the United States to fund its defense forever. And so all that money that we could have spent on tanks and guns and missiles and defense systems, we can spend on social programs. Lovely, right? But two problems: you've created a weak bloc, and you've also created a culture of dependency. And until you can tear those up, which means reshaping the way the EU allocates its budget in a way that is going to lose votes right across the bloc, you've put yourself in a checkmate position.

So Europe is in a mess, I'm afraid. And it's not to say it can't get out of that mess. Europe has a tremendous history of culture and advancement and civilization and invention and all these things. But they're all unfortunately being hamstrung by an ideology that is about the ends rather than how do we fix the problems. It's about how do we get to a certain end — this "socialist utopia." And I just don't think that's possible.

And the dying of that ideal and a return to pragmatism is vital for Europe. Germany is the poster child of this. Germany is being forced into pragmatic decisions now because the idealistic ones that put it in this bind — where it's now virtually the sick man of Europe, has gone from the strongest country in Europe to the weakest almost because of these policies — they're having to rethink them. And this is why the AFD are doing so well, because they're the party that's come along and said, "You know, screw net zero. Our standard of living is going down, and we're not going to stand for that and we need to do something about it."

So Europe is a mess. It's a complete mess. And that's not — I'm not saying that as a Brit poking sticks at Europe. I'm saying that as someone stepping outside the fishbowl looking at Europe and going, "This is a complete mess. And the sooner you do something about it, the better." Because you will be forced to do something about it sooner rather than later.

欧盟的死结：从"廉价货币"到"紧缩"的不可能过渡

Alexi: On one side it seems like it can go either direction, but in extreme violent ways. On one side there's this trend of confederation of Europe, making Europe even stronger, removing unanimity — like the veto rights of certain voting countries. Now in that was the case with Hungary, for example, in packages for Ukraine that actually revealed the system within the decision-making of European countries — now okay, now we need to actually have a hard decision-making process, China-like, "okay, now we do this and we all do it, there's no blocking in the way." Or on one side, what you just described as well with other parties that are more on the right spectrum, extreme rights some would say, that say, "Well, we actually need to disengage totally from this project, this is not working at all." And there's no in-between in a way.

唯一能达成的共识：给所有人低利率

Grant: I think you're right, Alexi. But importantly, that first idea is unworkable. It's just unworkable.

If you think about it, the original — "let's have one decision, let's have one policy" — that the EU was essentially built on when it came into being in the late '90s. Obviously, we can go back to the Treaty of Rome and the way that the EU and the Steel Commission, all those things built. But if we go back to 1999, the introduction of the euro, which is probably the most important part, the one common idea that it was founded on essentially was: low interest rates for all. Right?

That's what we can agree on. We're going to take Greece and Italy and Spain and we're going to give them Germany's interest rates.

When the one common decision is free money for everybody, it works really, really well. "Surprise, we're all Europeans. We love Europe. Let's all be European."

When the decisions that need to be made are, "You know, less welfare, we need to cut immigration drastically," we need to — all these things that, as we rode that tide of cheap free money for 30 years, 25 years, we have to reverse all the things that we did there. Suddenly it becomes unworkable when the one idea that we now need to coalesce around is effectively austerity. "We can't afford migration. We can't afford social benefits. We can't afford all these things now. So we're going to have to reverse them." It's unworkable. It's absolutely unworkable. Because turkeys don't vote for Christmas, right? No one's going to vote to have things taken away from them.

一个无解的僵局

So I see that as an intractable problem for Europe. And they will arrive — ultimately, it's not going to be good. I really don't see how this doesn't end. Not in conflict between Europe, but countries in Europe finally standing up to the EU and saying, "No, no, either we're not going to pay for that, or we're not going to let you take this away from us." And then we're going to go back to having a whole series of national conversations about, "Okay, what is our place in Europe? Do we want to be part of this project now that it's not a tailwind for everybody? Now that it's more of a problem, do we want to be a part of it?"

And I suspect when push comes to shove, the answer is going to be no. Because people are very happy to take, but they're not so happy to sacrifice or give. And it's just human nature. That's just the way it is.

Alexi: Yeah. It's like organizing a huge open bar night with all your friends and comes and then no one's like —

Grant: "I didn't have the chicken tender. I didn't have the chicken tender." Yeah, exactly right, exactly right.

欧洲增长为何停滞

Alexi: So it's but it's also a bit of — I mean coincidentally, I wonder as well, why the European Union — I mean for the first maybe 10 years its GDP growth was actually quite good overall, right? As a bloc it was quite strong. But then the 2008 crisis happened, and it added just barely 5 trillion to its GDP in the last then 10 years, while the US added at least double of that in that same time period. China, let's not even talk about it. So what then revealed or got hampered its growth since the last 15 years? Is it just like all the regulations and net zero that you just said, all the policies, or is something else?

Grant: Well, I think that's a big part of it. But I also think that the amount of debt that's been saddled on these countries — you look at Greece and Spain. What Italy — what do you think they're going to do when interest rates go from 11% to 3% overnight? There's going to be a massive borrowing binge. There's going to be a massive misallocation of capital. Of course there is. That's not a surprise to anybody.

Margaret Thatcher 早就预言过

So Europe, as I said, Europe was a fantastic ideal. But if you go back and listen to Margaret Thatcher's last speech to Parliament, she laid out exactly what would happen if you have European Union but you don't have a common treasury. She laid out exactly what was going to happen. This shouldn't be a surprise to anybody. Because the one beautiful thing about human nature — as erratic as humans could be as a group, human nature and the way we respond to incentives is undefeated over time.

And so we're exactly where Thatcher said that we would be. And she didn't get to the point of saying what happens next, because her thrust was, "We don't want to be a part of that, cuz I can see where it's going."

So it shouldn't surprise anybody. And the fact that, as you say, GDP growth has been poor is because you're trying to carry different countries at different points in time. You're trying to pay for massive social programs. You're trying to do an awful lot of things that any one of these countries individually, if you'd given them low interest rates, they'd have got themselves into the same trouble. But getting out of them on an individual basis and finding ways to grow would have been easier. But now, obviously, Italy can't devalue its currency. Greece can't devalue its currency. These countries that are struggling can't do the things that as individual sovereign nations they could do to try and change things because they're part of the EU.

It worked great when everybody was lowering interest rates together — it's brilliant. It doesn't work so well once all the goodies have been taken off from under the Christmas tree, right? All you got left are the needles all over the floor. And that's kind of where we are.

Alexi: Yeah, it's a bit of a "one-size fits none" type of thing.

Grant: Yeah, it is now. Yeah, exactly right. Great way to put it. Great way to put it.

数字欧元、CBDC 与净零：意识形态政策的反噬

Alexi: But then what is then — because I mean on one side, and I see also the way the European Union tries to still consolidate that power, which I said would be one direction by, for example, putting in this digital identity, forcing Europeans then to having to log in online to track activities under the false pretense of, "oh yeah, we need to catch those pedophiles" and so on so forth. And then introducing the digital euro, because "you know, cash is bad, we need to have a system that is against those Visas and Mastercards from the US, we need to be independent" — while actually only strengthening any grip that the European Central Bank has over its own money. But then also making it kind of like a Chinese surveillance type of — yeah, well, a CBDC type of scenario. And now the question is how far will Europeans actually comply and go with this or not, right?

投票箱的反抗

Grant: Yeah. And those are the questions that we are going to find out at the ballot boxes, because these are the kind of issues that will be front and center in elections to come.

You know, it's interesting — people have been talking about CBDCs for a long time and digital currencies, and this idea that "this is where we're going, cash is going to be abolished." And the assumption has been made that "that's just the way things are going to happen." They've also been talking about net zero — "and this is just the way things are, we are going to go to net zero."

And what's been interesting in the last couple of years, as those insane net zero policies have actually caused real-world problems, people are refusing to accept it. Electric car sales are down. The politicians that are pro-net-zero are now finding themselves on the receiving end of a lot of abuse and a lot less votes.

You know, we saw this week in the UK, Ed Miliband, who's the net zero czar, saying, "Well, I'd be willing to compromise my net zero goals if I could be made chancellor."

生活水平是最后的红线

So digital currencies, net zero, all these idealist policies that are designed to create a much better world — once they are proven to actually lower the standard of living of people, people get very animated about them and refuse to vote for them. And it horrifies people that there could be people out there suddenly voting for more coal power, or whatever it may be. But the history of humanity has been a constant improvement in the standard of living. That's what we've done. We've improved the standard of living for thousands of years. And the policies that are in place that are demonstrably going to reduce the standard of living of people who have a vote — you're going to find they won't vote for a lower standard of living. No one's going to do that.

And when — you know, the — we've talked about this 40-year period of tailwinds where cheap money and stock markets are going up, your house price is going up, everything's going your way. "Wouldn't it be great to have net zero?" Brilliant! Yes, absolutely.

Now you're at the point where it's, "Wait, it's going to triple my energy bill? Well, no no no no no, I'm not voting for that. No. I'm not so keen on net zero anymore."

I think every human being on the planet, if you said, "We could have net zero and it would not impact your way of life" — go. We're all for that. There's not anyone that's going to vote against that. But "We're going to force net zero on you and it's going to lower your standard of living" — no, people are not going to go for that. A few will, a few will be willing to sacrifice, but in the aggregate, a population is not going to be pleased to see their standard of living go down. And that's just the reality of it.

收尾：足球，时间机器，与两年后的欧洲杯

Alexi: Fair points. Grant, I think we've covered a lot today. Is there anything else that you think is worth sharing on a concluding —

Grant: Yes, I'd like a recount of the England-Argentina game last night. I want to find out if maybe if England could find two more goals somewhere and win 3-2. I would be happy if you can arrange that for me before you and I meet each other on Saturday night in the third place playoff final, which nobody wants to watch. Then that would be great. But otherwise, no.

Alexi: Well, that's something that only a time machine could fix, but yeah.

Grant: I think everything we've talked about today can only be fixed by a time machine. But maybe that time machine needs to go forwards. We'll see.

Alexi: Yeah. Well, there's still the Euro to go, so it's not all all over for the —

Grant: Two more years. Two more years.

Alexi: And the French. So — well, talking about the Euro and the Euro Cup and the European Union and all that.

Grant: We'll see you in the final in two years.

Alexi: At least there's still football to kind of get our minds off all those other big shifts and complex topics and all that, and we can be monkeys hitting balls again, you know.

Grant: There you go. Amen.

Alexi: Grant, as always, a pleasure talking to you. Also if it's online, obviously much better face to face, but this does the trick as well.

Grant: Likewise, really enjoyed it as always. Good to see you.

Alexi: Thank you. All right.
