一、核心结论：历史性的天然气赤字正在逼近

We are headed into a place where we see a historic deficit in natural gas supply available in the United States, which which does portend some pretty serious consequences.

Natural gas, which is over 40% of US power generation, has become or is imminently going to become the most important fuel in the country. It's overtaking petroleum given the amount that we use now for generation.

Our work suggests that 26–27 natural gas is appropriately supplied. But as we get into 28, and you plug in this compute and you assign gas to very specific assets as they're plugged in as well, and you continue to export LNG as we're planning to do with known projects, we start to eat into our working gas storage — which is the nexus of supply and demand in the country.

I think we will come to the conclusion that the upside risk price of natural gas is both unbounded and convex. Where you will feel it the most acutely will be electricity prices in 28, 29, 2030 based on our work.

这仅仅是数据中心的问题吗？

主持人： How much of this is just attributable to data centers — like, just purely we're building a lot more data centers, that's just for AI — like is it that simple, or is there something else going on as well?

Matt： The die was cast long before AI compute came to the scene.

二、页岩革命之后的天然气版图

If I may set the stage a little bit — US gas was plentiful starting in about 2010 when shale started to really change, come to the scene and change things. We had been importing natural gas to satisfy consumption on top of what we produced domestically. Shale started to be very productive, surprised to the upside, and became this abundant source.

And as natural gas became more abundant, we started to export it. Starting with Cheniere, we've gone from that early Cheniere exporting to today we're exporting about 15 BCF a day of nameplate US export capacity.

Now that 15 billion cubic feet is on a base of about 110 to 112 BCF a day of natural gas production in the US. So if you think about it, it's become about 12 to 15% of the US daily ability to supply the market.

LNG 出口的加速

As this abundance continued, more and more facilities projects have been announced. As of today, we're scheduled to export up to 35 BCF a day by the end of 2030 — and in that case the die has been mostly cast.

To build an LNG project you need various approvals. They're project financed, you site and permit many, many years in advance. Most of these projects that get you from 15 or 16 BCF a day nameplate to 35 are well on their way. That's the primary incremental demand driver in the country over the last 10 years, and will be at least for the next five.

需求侧的转折点

We had moderate population growth during the 2010s and teens into the 2020s. We went through a period of stagnating electricity demand — energy efficiency and some other things driving down electricity demand. You had more demand for gas-driven generation, but it's really in the recent past where compute has started to pull incrementally. Before that, you had LNG as the main driver of demand.

三、供需缺口的量化

Now let's put those together.

I just shared that we're going to go from about 15 to 35 BCF a day of incremental LNG exports. After evaluating every producing gas well and the entire pipeline and processing and gathering system, we have the capacity to add about 20 BCF a day of gas production.

Even without AI compute, we had sources and uses matched between our ability to deliver new natural gas from Appalachia, Haynesville, Permian, and that which is supposed to leave the door through LNG.

AI 算力的叠加

Now, in AI compute — so many different power-generating ideas in order to power compute, given this value of "time to power" that folks talk about so much. It sort of goes from the large-scale most efficient assets — which are Geova combined cycle — all the way down through the distributed generation assets, which we'll call fuel cells (we'll adieu Solar Turbine or Caterpillar solar turbines). There are various local field-level behind-the-meter assets that are also relevant.

We have had to assign, with an outside partner, probabilities to all of this stuff.

P50 基准情境

So we'll start with our base case, which we'll call P50 — everything with a probability of 50% or more (50% being: they have some approvals, they have usually a PPA — someone planning to buy power from them under contract — they usually have some sort of interconnection agreement or they're in process with an interconnection agreement). Those are the assets we've taken seriously in our base case.

When you do that, it's about 5 BCF a day of very credible incremental natural gas demand associated with mostly AI compute.

Now importantly, there are multiples of what we are considering seriously in our base case that have been proposed that will consume natural gas. Every solution today involves more natural gas.

6-series Bloom Energy — kind of latest-gen fuel cell — will take 150 million cubic feet a day of gas per gigawatt. The market has been assigning a high probability on them obtaining 2 gigawatts a year of manufacturing capacity, and that's likely to ramp to 5 gigawatts, for which there isn't gas unless you take it from something else.

主持人： In the extreme case, how high does that number get?

Matt： If you start to move it down and say P30 or P20, that number can more than double and be 12 to 15 BCF a day by the early 2030s if unmitigated.

四、为什么不能"直接关掉出口"？

主持人： One naive way to approach this is to say, like, this doesn't sound like that big of a deal. Like — 12 new [BCF] in the extreme case, just shut off the exports. Like, who cares? We didn't export natural gas for a long time. People domestically are not going to tolerate skyrocketing energy prices, especially when they think the simple solution to this is just to stop shipping it out of the country and just use it for ourselves. Like, why is the solution not just shut off exports?

Matt： It's more complicated than that.

Contract law. There are rules. There are really good reasons why we're exporting, and these projects have tens of billions of project financing and contracts that are attached to or associated with these LNG projects. As the US will be about a third of global gas supply in several years, our allies and other FTA and increasingly non-FTA countries are reliant on…

主持人： What's FTA?

Matt： Free trade agreement.

So the answer is that it's both: because it's a third of the global supply that's really important for the rest of the world, and domestically there's just contracts and investments — and it could be stopped, but it'd be very complicated.

建模的出发点

Let's step back for a moment. You have to have a starting place for a base case, which typically starts with signed contracts. What do the words on the page say? What's allowed? What's not allowed?

When we set out to build the firm, we've had about 16-plus months to start to model almost every asset at the atomic level. Along the way, there are numerous constraints and rules and regulations and contracts. When we set out to build this, it was about acknowledging those constraints for what they are, assuming that contract law would be followed.

Then as we go through and build, all of this can flex up and down based on the choice to send less LNG out the border or out of our terminals, for instance — or slow AI compute growth, which is one other solution which we're not really willing to propose because we know that there's insatiable demand. It's not popular to say "slow AI compute growth," but to the extent that would happen, that would be another lever to reduce the pull or strain we expect in the system as the decade goes along.

五、地下有多少气？——资源 vs. 交付能力

主持人： It's your view that in the bad-to-worst case scenarios, this is like a full-blown crisis. This is not a small thing. This is like the story in the country.

So underneath the United States right now or North America, there's a certain amount of gas just objectively. And I'm trying to understand — how much of this is that we are literally going to run out of the gas that's under the ground, versus it's just a problem of how quickly we can find out where it is, get it out economically, process it, store it, transmit it, use it, etc.?

Matt： Starting with what we'll call resource in the ground —

There's tremendous data availability. We can measure where we are in the exploitation of most of the major gas-producing basins. It would be:

  • Appalachia — primarily the Marcellus plus the Utica
  • Haynesville — a key swing basin
  • Permian — and to a lesser extent the Eagle Ford, which are oil-directed plays where the decision to drill and produce is driven by oil, and gas is a byproduct

In each of these plays there are some stacked pays or zones where well penetrations' output can be measured with a lot of data. When you digitize the acreage controlled by each one of these companies with polygon shapes that use a bunch of lat-longs to drop in and associate a well with an area that's controlled, you can figure out what's left.

The reality is: there is gas. As part of our analysis we've produced the gas that is logically captured and can be produced from wells from existing acreage positions of all these companies. There is gas. We're assuming it gets developed here. That's how you get to our 20 BCF a day of growth. But there are other constraints.

主持人： It's unbelievably cool that we can literally know at this precision what is underneath the ground — often deep underneath in hard-to-reach places. It's a technology story. But it doesn't sound like the actual problem is that we are literally running out of the stuff underneath the ground. We've also had a history of just finding new stuff that we didn't know existed before. So it sounds like the problem is more our ability to serve the demand in this kind of time frame, not that we're literally going to run out of the resource over the next 20 years.

存量 vs. 流量：一个关键区分

Matt： So, it's a little more complicated than that.

We get through most of the existing captured inventory of companies in the next four or five years. When you bring on a new well, it has a decline rate, and each well as it's stacked on an existing companywide portfolio decline… a lot of these companies' decline curves are maturing.

主持人： They're pretty steep in natural gas, right?

Matt： It's steep initially in natural gas, but Expand Energy and others have such mature portfolios, the replacement is less costly today than it would have been 5 years ago.

When you stack all of these wells based on existing acreage on these companies, assuming they're going to drill optimally based on their forward curve (which is depressed and we'll talk about that), you get to this 128, 130, 132 BCF a day of maximum deliverability.

We are assuming that all of these companies develop the rest of their acreage.

主持人： But that's a flow metric, not a stock metric.

Matt： It's a flow metric. What is possible when you use known well performance parameters to maximize production before you get to midstream and other surface-level constraints — which we'll talk about.

更高价格能解锁更多资源吗？

There's resource. We are depleting the known resource. If you were to assume prices go up meaningfully, you may unlock additional basins that are legacy known basins. We know a lot about most of the rock in the US. There are other known gas basins, but they have been uneconomic. And furthermore, there isn't infrastructure to really accelerate drilling and activity in those basins.

This is [not] software — you don't press a button to solve this.

常见反驳：库存真的够吗？

A common pushback as we have gone through this is: "there's plenty of resource available to us in the Permian. There's plenty of resource in Appalachia." A number of companies describe themselves as having a lot more inventory of wells to drill than we can justify with facts. And I'll just leave it at that.

When folks meet with companies, they should ask to understand exact engineered locations on a map — where do they have not just the ability to produce, but plans to have infrastructure on the surface to allow it to flow, for instance? And the ability within financial parameters to invest and produce the resource in the ground?

We're fairly far along in understanding it. We've accounted for all of the major productive basins in the country, and I do not think we're likely to be surprised by some new major shale find. At this point, knowledge of those things is pretty mature.

主持人： So to say it back — there's a lot of resource, but at this rate, we're depleting the known resources quite quickly.

Matt： We are advanced in depleting the known resources. Especially as we move to the next layer, which is infrastructure.

六、地面基础设施：处理、集气、干线管道

主持人： There's a bigger longer-term question about, is this just a parenthetical period of time between 2010 and now when we were awash in gas? Prior to that, we really weren't, and maybe after this, we really won't be. Let's talk now about: OK, we get gas out of the ground. It still has to go get processed and transmitted and used. What are the most important rate limiters in that part of the equation?

1. 处理（Processing）

In some cases it's processing — the natural gas flows to the surface with natural gas liquids embedded therein. In some cases there's sulfur or nitrogen that has to be dealt with. In some cases it comes with oil, so you have to have surface-level infrastructure to produce the oil, which is different.

Gas primarily has to be produced into a pipeline system, and there's a certain spec on regulated pipelines — kind of 1030 BTU is the spec. So you have to remove enough of these other hydrocarbons to get it to pipeline spec to be able to produce it into the system to be consumed by folks downstream.

Processing is the first major constraint. There are a couple of basins with a little bit of extra processing. We'll fill it up pretty quickly. We do not have processing yet to get to our assumed 20 BCF production target that's necessary.

Processing would be something it takes 2 or 3 years to build at the midpoint. We generally know what processing investments are being made and projects have been announced by Permian processors or by Appalachian processors. We know where the materials- and liquids-handling throughput capacity will be in 27–28 at least.

You really would need, in the near term, even to get to our 20 BCF of incremental gas production we're willing to estimate, you need to have more processing built.

主持人： Build stuff now.

Matt： Build it now, imminently.

2. 集气（Gathering）

Gathering — small-diameter pipes. Gathering is what takes it from the wellhead to processing or the pipeline system. There is a fair amount of disclosure around processing systems being expanded and built, and we would posit — we have put all those on a map on top of every one of these wells at their lat-longs — in order to grow even a fraction of where we must have natural gas production go in the US, gathering has to be invested in very materially over the next imminently to get to the place where we can achieve 130 BCF/day of production in the US.

3. 干线管道（Interstate Pipelines）

The last one is interstate gas pipeline system. And this is where I come back to your answer on LNG — lots of rules and regulations around these things. Pipelines are monopolies for the most part. Local distribution companies that deliver gas to your stove — those are monopolies or oligopolies.

In the last 10 or 12 years we've really built one interstate gas pipeline — that was Mountain Valley Pipeline, connecting Appalachia to Mid-Atlantic. The various environmental permitting, the regime changes…

主持人： Things are a nightmare to build. Yeah.

Matt： It's been made very difficult to build interstate gas pipelines. This administration has been trying to reduce the barriers to building interstate gas pipes. We've started to see some more progress to that end. But there is an urgency to build more connectivity to wield gas around the country to serve this incremental AI compute load if it's going to happen. That's necessary.

七、如果什么都不做，2030 年会是什么样？

主持人： Before we keep going through this sequence, can you just say what you think the state will be? Let's assume there's roughly inertia in the system and nobody listens to this. Nobody does it. I think hopefully some people, a lot of people will listen to this and have ideas. But what is going to happen in the world? What will the state of the world be like in 2030 if none of this starts getting addressed sooner than later?

Matt： There is a tremendous inertia around natural gas being the primary fuel to power AI.

The market has been focused on understanding the power shortage and trying to solve that and generation generally — power generation, which could be solar and batteries, wind, nuclear (whether large scale or small modular reactors — SMRs), or natural gas.

Natural gas is well supplied today, 26 and 27. The result is that nobody is investing in gas. In fact, EQT is shutting in natural gas right now because they think it'll be more valuable later. The rig count, the things that we can see real-time to figure out if the market is on to this tightness in 2029 or 2030 —

主持人： No one's on it.

Matt： It's not apparent today. It's perpetuating this view that most Americans have — which is: there's plenty of natural gas, because for 15 years it's all we've been [seeing] — abundance.

复杂性的沉睡

There's a complacency that's developed, and we think that complacency is going to take us right up to the point where it's too late.

We do think the die has been cast where gas — which is currently at $3.50, $3.60 — going out to 26, 27, in 28, the curve is flat. 2029, 2030 the curve is flat because people believe the gas is abundant. That's despite all these AI compute announcements, despite what all of the companies are doing for their investments. Gas has lulled everybody to sleep.

2028 中的临界点

But what happens is: these structural things start to fall in place in 27, 28, and we start to draw meaningfully in the middle of 28, as early as early 28, on the gas system like we've never drawn before.

As we look at 2028, 29, 2030, we start to cut into the US working gas storage — which is about 4 TCF total gas storage. There's a range of high and low for that storage seasonally as we draw in summer and winter and then build in the shorter months in the spring and fall.

  • Middle of 2028: we start to break very materially below in a historical way where gas available in storage has ever been before.
  • By 2029: we drop below all known historical storage evidence.
  • By 2030: we get pretty close to where we think, ceteris paribus, gas storage looks very, very low.

At that point in time, because it's not happened before, we're forced to look at where gas price has gone during shortages.

历史参照与"结构性"的区别

We can look at Russia–Ukraine — gas went to $8, $9, $10 an MCF because we send a lot more externally to Europe. We've seen various weather anomalies — polar vortex in '14, in December of '22 — and those prices have gone to $6 or $8 or $10. But those have been transitory.

What we're talking about are structural drivers of demand against a known possible production of gas, and they don't match up. You pull in a very historic way starting in 28 to the point where the deficit gets really convex and unbounded.

主持人： Meaning the gas prices could be 20 or something like this?

Matt： I would hesitate to even put a price target on it. But at $8 or $10, we think you potentially shut off some of the US exports where there are spot cargoes and they are leaving the border to capture uplift in Europe or elsewhere. Those spot cargoes may not be lifted, and then that gas is left in the system, and we've tried to account for that in our model.

But spot cargoes alone can't solve this. You would have to get into shutting off contracted cargoes leaving our border via LNG to really start to mitigate some of this. And it's hard for us to count on the choice to shut off contracted cargoes where there's some Japanese utility counterparty who has counted on it for provision of electricity.

八、赢家与输家

主持人： In crazy convex outcomes like this, can you tick through who you think the biggest winners and losers are?

上游赢家

There are some clear natural gas producer winners.

Expand Energy is probably at the top of that list. They probably control 70% of remaining core Haynesville wells of the very closely known parameters of rock where we know it to be very productive. So Expand we think is far and away the biggest winner.

Uniquely, Expand is CEO-less right now. There was some turnover in the year — they're going through a search. The stock has plummeted over the last six months as part of that search, and it's trading at 4x EBITDA on a forward curve where no one believes what I'm telling you to be the case.

Even though we think modeling the facts gets you to a much higher gas price, the stock has dropped. The assets have not changed. It has some of the highest quality rock in the country.

Highest quality upstream company in Appalachia is probably Range. Range has significant room to grow production and materially grow returns to investors. So those would be the upstream companies.

太阳能：意外的边际收益者

It's not going to be obvious in the first pass through this equation for most, but natural gas sets the marginal fuel for the next-in-line power-generating asset in each power market. As natural gas goes, power prices go in the country.

If you think about the dispatch curve of different generating assets in the country, there are some where the fuel is free — that would be solar, to a lesser extent wind, hydro. Solar assets have been growing meaningfully — they've been 90% of the interconnect queue with batteries in the last 10 years in terms of new assets coming on, other than gas.

Solar assets stand to benefit from a windfall where electricity prices are going up because gas is setting the margin of plant taking fuel where the price is increasing, while sun costs the same.

We think there are some companies positioned very well for margin expansion for no incremental capital cost:

  • XPLR (ticker XIFR, formerly NextEra Yield Co) — an interesting set of assets. They have a windfall coming in the latter part of the decade, in early 2030s, ceteris paribus, because they mark their PPAs to market at much higher values without any capex.
  • Clearway Energy — another similar circumstance.

So solar assets at the utility scale, especially, stand to win.

住宅光伏的静默复兴

Maybe more interestingly as it relates to some of our discussions of the past: residential solar, which has been suffering from really the first removal of tax incentives to install residential solar since the late '70s.

Residential solar assets are really one of the only ways to protect yourself from what's going to happen during the time of 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. once gas gets really tight in the electricity markets — what you pay for electricity at your house.

We think residential solar grows exponentially from here. Even without tax incentives for the first time, it's very economic with where electricity prices are likely to go — to install solar, especially when it's coupled with batteries which make the electricity much more available round-the-clock.

核电：唯一的长期解决方案

主持人： I think it's important to say — you're an investor, you have money behind this work. Beyond those two categories, are there any other surprising winners? What about nuclear? What about Westinghouse or places like this?

Matt： What we're talking about is a complex dynamic system where there will be choices to consume electricity or not at different times. As I go through this, I want to make sure I acknowledge that there's no silver bullet solution for what I described as a convex situation with natural gas — and therefore electricity prices — as the decade closes.

There's no bridge fuel other than solar and wind, because currently natural gas is the only flex fuel to get us to when we can bring on nuclear.

We have spent a fair amount of time in the nuclear ecosystem. To us, large-scale nukes are the only solution that makes sense — which points us primarily to the AP1000 Westinghouse units.

主持人： Don't those take like 5 years to build or something?

Matt： More than that. But at least they have a story.

Past and very brief history: we've built two nuclear reactor units in 30 years in the US — Vogtle 3 and 4. Around that time we also tried to build one in South Carolina called VC Summer — another nuclear project at the time nearly bankrupted SCANA, which was later pushed into the arms [of Dominion] and the project was shut.

The muscle memory from trying to build large-scale nukes — especially in the back of Fukushima in 2011, Chernobyl, Three Mile Island — for three decades, nuclear engineers and scientists and companies…

主持人： Gone to do other stuff.

Matt： And then the Vogtle 3 and 4 experiment, where it cost 3x as much and took, I don't know, 15 years from birth to commercial service. That's the recent memory of building these nuclear units.

But if you go out to the 2030s, what I'm describing in terms of gas deficit only gets worse in 31, 32 and beyond. So in our mind, the only viable solution is to build large-scale nuclear as fast as possible — which would mean it needs to come on in 2033 or 2034, which is as soon as it can come on.

Regular utilities, hyperscalers, regulators should all align around that goal. But because people don't really believe that gas is in short supply as the decade goes along —

主持人： They don't believe in the problem.

Matt： — and they don't like the solution. So they need to be convinced of the problem.

The country has a history of building pipelines to solve problems that exist today, not problems that will exist in 5 or 10 years. So we're trying to get out ahead and see where the puck's going. And where it's going is: we are going to need large-scale nuclear by 2033, 2034.

SMR 为什么不是解？

主持人： You don't think SMRs can be a solution — where you use smaller reactors to power individual data centers behind the meter, and this just never touches the system?

Matt： Many of the SMRs are still science experiments. The NRC and the US government are actually doing a fair number of things to break down the barriers to bringing those to fruition — to see if they work or not and what the cost will be and whether they can be scaled or not.

But many of these SMR companies are not set up to manufacture and truly scale for the solution that's needed to solve this problem, which is tens of gigawatts as you go into the 2030s. That points us to these AP1000s.

Since Vogtle 4 came on, Vogtle 4 experienced very material improvements from Vogtle 3. In Georgia today, China is building 39 plus-or-minus nuclear reactors. 34 of them are 1 gigawatt plus. I think a third of those are modeled after the AP1000. We know a lot more today about building large-scale nukes than we did when these mistakes were made.

Large-scale, to us — where it can be commercialized on a known timeline, where the costs are probably better — vs. where we don't even know if we can scale the businesses yet in terms of SMRs. Large-scale versus small — probably wins in our mind.

Two companies most levered to that would be:

  • Cameco — owns 49% [of Westinghouse]. Brookfield 51%. You'll probably find that the US government agrees with what I'm describing. They seem to really be lining up and trying to facilitate commitments and early procurement, which will de-risk some of the supply chain and help put timelines on this. When the Westinghouse comes public, and it's deeply undervalued within Cameco today — so that's an interesting one.
  • BWXT — a super interesting company. They're the primary supplier of nuclear for the US Navy. They significantly benefit from the coming nuclear cycle as well, and lots of dollar content in the AP1000s.

输家：消费者、涡轮机制造商、分布式发电

主持人： Who are the big losers do you think in this future?

Matt： Sadly, the biggest losers of this would be the US consumer.

If we're even partially right, electricity prices rise — which you can see some of on the forward curves in these different markets. As electricity prices rise, you start to think about the trade-off:

  • Are we going to export natural gas to foreign buyers?
  • Are we going to use it for AI compute?
  • Or are we going to try to keep consumer electricity bills [low]?

It's an awful trade-off. And I think it will probably start to contribute more to the public dialogue — the NIMBYism that we're seeing already pop up in some places.

We think AI is tremendously transformational. We're not anti-AI. But it consumes a lot of power. We need to really focus on the 2030 to 2035 period. The US consumer is probably going to pay the bill in the meantime.

Please note that most of the solutions being proposed by the government are to consume more gas because everybody believes it's enough.

"Bring Your Own Generation" (BYOG) is a thing today. That's what the hyperscalers are being asked to do — to site their data center in a certain lat-long. Well, that means more gas, not less.

Every time you read a press release from Bloom or from GE Vernova —

主持人： Think more gas.

Matt： Just think more gas. And you can use the energy efficiency of each one of those units and understand exactly how much more incremental gas beyond the base case that I just shared is dangerously tight.

涡轮机制造商：又一轮周期泡沫？

Another loser — I want to be respectful — some of the biggest winners so far, at least in the stock market, have been the manufacturers of gas turbines or distributed power gen sets.

When you think about those companies, it's been somewhat boom and bust. In the early 2000s, there was a boom to build as many gas plants as we could. The capacity was overbuilt, and the industry really languished for a long time — until now. You've had just tremendous profitability and equity returns come from these companies over the last two years.

But as you look at 2028, 2029, most of them are adding more capacity again just like they did in the early 2000s.

  • Caterpillar — I think they're doubling their Solar Turbine capacity between now and the end of 29, which I would judge is just at the exact wrong time, when people may be questioning whether they even want to deploy those assets because the gas is much more expensive than they planned.
  • Bloom Energy — has been topical recently because of other things folks are talking about (the rare earths they use in their manufacture, for instance). For us, we don't think that Bloom Energy's assets at 2 gigawatts or more will be able to get natural gas in competition with all of the other assets that are being deployed that will consume gas, given the scarcity that we see.

Those are two we'll call manufacturers of distributed generation or BTM generation that we think are probably more poorly positioned than investors appreciate.

And then it really doesn't make sense to us beyond 2029, 2030 to build large-scale natural gas generation until we ramp up production meaningfully and you can make sure we have the security of deliverability of supply of gas that's consistent with our model.

We could see orders slow very meaningfully for natural gas generating assets even at large scale as 26 progresses. Those could be some of the losers — it may just not make sense to use gas for power generation for new or incremental assets after a certain point.

超大规模厂商：类比 DRAM 短缺

主持人： It seems like sort of like this whole memory shortage thing that we're going through right now, that hyperscalers might also be people that are in trouble here if this is a key input to what they're doing. Do you think that's a big problem for them?

Matt： So as we've been socializing this a little bit — trying to learn more and have people poke holes — shared this with one of your recent guests. He listened. They said, "Well, this sounds like DRAM 2 years ago."

Slowly at first, and then all at once. The lack of investment in capacity expansion is going to come up to bite us. I think that's where the analog starts. When we think about the way this plays out and other analogs, that's probably the best one.

When we think about the cost of the hyperscalers right now, energy is budgeted to be about 10% of their cost. Depreciation's the highest. Certainly memory and other things factor into that as well, but total cost of energy is supposed to be about 10%.

If you plug in all of this compute and it's gas-powered, and we think gas could double or triple structurally even without weather, it could end up being 20 or 30% of the cost of compute by 2029. So we do think it becomes a much more material issue.

The levelized cost of energy (LCOE) as it's referred to takes into account capex, cost of fuel. Everybody making decisions in this moment is using the forward curve for natural gas — which is flat, a little backwardated, mostly flat out to the 2030s, in the mid 30s. That is a very attractive low-cost fuel for the hyperscalers to commit to when they're focused on solving everything else, like how do I get compute in place to manifest in this revenue growth in Anthropic or elsewhere.

For us, we're just focused on modeling objectively — when you plug in this compute, or this power gen source here and there, what does — how exactly does it pull on the system of companies that we focus on?

九、魔鬼代言人：什么情况下 Matt 会被证明错了？

主持人： If you're forced to play devil's advocate and come up with the set of circumstances such that this is all much ado about nothing, and we're sitting here in 2030 and gas costs three bucks — what do you think is the most likely reason? Is it that data center power requirements are much lower because we make performance breakthroughs, or AI demand isn't what we think it's going to be? What is this most sensitive to such that they might be wrong?

Matt： So after we did most of our work, we went on a bit of a listening tour to target conversations with who we think are the subject matter experts in that thing — energy storage, hyperscaler compute deployment and energy consumption.

反驳一：Permian 会拯救我们

The common pushbacks we've spent a lot of time understanding are: Permian is an oil play. Oil is high. Permian has lots of gas in the ground associated with it. Why can't Permian productivity just fix problems?

So our base case model already accounts for the 7-plus billion cubic feet a day of pipelines that are already being built or developed that come on between 26 and 2030 in the Permian. If there were a new gas pipeline that would come on between now and 2030, we would know about it — because of the regulatory processes and the way, the time it takes to build these pipes.

We have mitigated the risk of being surprised by the Permian by moving into the midstream to understand the bottlenecks, constraints — and so beyond the deliverability of the resource or the gas in the ground itself, how much can actually get to market and either leave via LNG export terminals or be consumed in Texas or nearby. We've already included that in our base case model.

But that will be one of the pushbacks: "there's plenty of gas in the Permian." I would posit — this may be controversial — there was plenty of oil in the world before the Iran conflict surfaced. Eventually there will be oil aplenty again. It's why it was at $55 a barrel before the Iran conflict.

In order to make more Permian natural gas, you also have to be incentivized to make more per barrel. Those incentives didn't exist until Iran. In order to produce a lot more Permian gas than even these seven-plus BCF pipelines being built that we're already modeling, you'd need much, much higher oil for longer — which only exacerbates this consumer crisis that we are concerned about.

So we don't think the Permian solves the problem.

反驳二：就地发电

The other one is: "well, you can locate a bunch of behind-the-meter local Permian power generation." Which is happening. But we are modeling what has been announced and proposed. If it's going to consume local Permian gas, that means it's not going to make it into the pipeline downstream — so we can accommodate that with our model.

反驳三：颠覆性技术（电池）

The only other one, and this is hard to handicap for — in any case, we always try to think about technologies that can disrupt and change structurally the need and consumption of natural gas. It often leads us to focus on battery technologies.

There's sodium and other battery technologies that are currently not commercial but folks are working on. People getting a bit more enthusiastic about. The vast majority of economic battery deployment today is lithium-ion. It has a fairly fast discharge cycle, and those are being deployed in earnest across the system. Yes, we are also modeling known battery deployments as part of modeling this generating system across all fuel types.

Step-function battery technology change could be something that would affect this — it would affect some of these pieces that I described (winners and losers) in meaningful ways. It would be a watershed moment that I would welcome, because it would solve a problem that we're pretty concerned about.

[广告间歇：Vanta / Ridgeline]

Vanta automates security and compliance for over 16,000 fast-moving companies like Ramp, Cursor, and Harvey, keeping them audit-ready around the clock. It's the number one agentic trust platform, and it now helps companies like yours watch for the risks that show up between audits — across your vendors, your AI tools, and your whole environment.

Every new tool your team signs up for, every vendor that turns on AI features is an opportunity for something to go wrong. Most security programs weren't built for AI's pace of growth. The Vanta agent works like a 24/7 GRC engineer in the background, finding issues, drafting fixes for you, and cutting vendor assessment time by up to 50%. Whether you're a fast-growing startup or a global enterprise, Vanta helps you earn and prove trust. Invest Like the Best listeners: get a special offer for $1,000 off at vanta.com/invest.

Ridgeline is the first end-to-end system of record with embedded AI for investment management firms — running portfolio accounting, reconciliation, reporting, trading, and compliance on one unified platform. Firms are moving off legacy technology and onto Ridgeline because of how far ahead Ridgeline's AI features are compared to anything else in investment management software.

I've been hearing from a lot of investment managers about AI, and they fall roughly into two camps — with some unsure of where to even start, and others convinced they can build their own order management system over a weekend. The reality is that running an investment firm will always require governance, controls, and a single source of truth for your data. And no amount of AI enthusiasm changes that requirement.

Ridgeline is built on exactly that foundation, which is why I believe that firms that come out ahead in the AI era will be the ones running on Ridgeline's unified platform. If you're serious about your firm's AI strategy, Ridgeline should be part of that conversation. You can request a demo at ridgeline.ai.

十、如果你是"沙皇"：解决方案剧本

主持人： If you were czar for a day and you had to decide everything that gets started to solve this problem, what are all the things that you would do to most solve and mitigate this?

政府层面：立刻启动 2–4 座 AP1000

Matt： If I were the US government, I would find a way to build entirely from beginning to end two to four AP1000 nuclear plants — nuclear reactors. That would de-risk the supply chain. It would open up doors to folks who want to see somebody do it first before they do it.

主持人： With the hopes that we get more China-like and build 30 of them.

Matt： Currently there are 10 to 20 envisioned by the US government through different groups in terms of nuclear reactors to come on, but no one wants to be first. I think we're close to a few stepping forward.

But if the US had said, "Hey, we have $260 billion to spend at the Loan Programs Office" — now the EDF, it's $260 billion, I think, to spend by the end of 2028 — we need to build four nukes with this. That would de-risk this materially, and I think you would see it jumpstart the nuclear equation.

Energy and resource availability, egress, and knowledge we think are the biggest bottlenecks to productivity and deployment of all this incredible technology that America has really been the leader of developing.

That's why we — when we set up our firm and started building a team — things are happening pretty quickly in AI and especially with regard to power. So we didn't set out to understand the now. It's important to understand now, but we set out to understand where the puck is going. And where it's going looks like it will meaningfully diminish growth if not dealt with. That's why it brings me to the nuclear solution as maybe the most viable long-term.

个人层面：屋顶光伏

My comments on solar are probably the most important thing that I would do. I think everybody should get a solar system on their houses. It won't be perfect. It will deliver electricity when there's sun out. It may not deliver electricity when it's cloudy, but it's a way to protect yourself from very high peak power prices from 10 a.m. until 6 p.m., which are the biggest part of your bill.

I would incentivize people to study your state's rules and try to put incentives in place to really start to grow residential solar faster than what's been a stagnating industry the last year, after some incentives are removed. That would be one place to be reinvigorating solar incentives, because they're going to be needed in a few years.

加拿大能救场吗？

主持人： Could we build like a giant pipeline from Canada or something? Try to tap our neighbors to help us solve this problem.

Matt： Canada is an interesting partner of ours. They have the capability of delivering about 11 or 12 BCF usually in January, periodically. And there are meaningful pipelines from Canada to the US. Largely it's seasonal — and it helps us solve winter. But otherwise, they're net imports most of the year. We're not really set up to take from Canada year-round.

There are a few reasons for that. One is Canada has limited storage — it's about half a TCF, about a fourth of the US storage.

If I think about this on a 3 to 5 year-plus basis, Canada by far has the deepest and richest resource of economic gas in the ground — but it's been trapped behind pipe.

I would build a 1 to 2 BCF a day at least pipe into the US Midwest, the MISO power market, and then wheel it around — MISO, PJM, SPP — and try to satisfy this demand, because I really don't want to see demand slow. I really don't want to see consumers' bills go up.

十一、全球影响

主持人： We've really focused on the US here. What are the implications of this for the rest of the world?

Matt： The US has become the leading provider of natural gas — with our exports going from virtually zero to starting in the mid-teens, and now we're 15 BCF/day; that'll be 35. Many countries in the world are building gas generating assets that are dependent on our delivery of that gas to them.

Now there are lots of political conflict-related tensions or bottlenecks today — Russia–Ukraine. Russia used to be one of the biggest deliverers of gas to Europe, for instance, and we filled the gap.

To the extent we cannot deliver our 30 to 35 or more BCF a day of gas to the global consumer, rebalancing will be required. You probably impact Europe meaningfully, and they're left with a trade-off of taking Russian gas or or much higher-cost US gas because they can't produce it domestically themselves enough to satisfy their need.

Asia is a large consumer — the largest consumer until Russia–Ukraine of US natural gas — and they probably will be, at some point, the largest consumer again with some of the outages in the Middle East.

We potentially hurt important allies at a time where we really want them to be allies, if we can't send them the gas they need. So it is pretty important that we don't curtail LNG — although that will certainly be one of the levers as we go out to the late decade that we will be forced to think about to deal with rising electricity prices in the country.

十二、什么让 Matt 最感意外？

主持人： Anything that we haven't talked about that has surprised you in this year-and-a-half-long analysis? Obviously we've covered the big conclusion which is scary and hard to deal with even if we start acting now. Anything else that surprised you either in your work or in people's reaction to it as you've started to share it?

Matt： Really, for the last two or three years, the phenomenon where CEOs and CFOs of companies — all of whom have really been asked by their investors or their products lend themselves well to deploying products to capture AI compute rent — what CEOs have said versus what is possible from the system, I think, is an interesting study that will happen over time.

The amount of capital made available to companies to make investments that are really shortsighted in the context of our work — like the incremental distributed natural gas gen-set. It's an inefficient, high-heat-rate or high-cost, inefficient asset that really should only serve as backup generation in any context outside of this fast-time-to-power setting where AI compute needs the power. Now, over four or five years, those assets may not even run.

You've had tens of billions flow into these distributed power assets, all of which are short and will consume natural gas.

一个奇怪的沉默

We really haven't seen anybody — including firms we really respect — question at any point whether there will be enough gas and what the cost will be when the time comes. It's been surprising.

Enough folks haven't put pen to paper to then start contracting gas to make sure they have supply certainty. We haven't seen more financial contracting. 28 is somewhat illiquid, which is why we really haven't seen the forward curve move. We think that's where the action starts.

As soon as utilities turn the page and start to really hedge or buy gas in 28, and we start to see all these natural gas generating companies start to think about securing supply — you're going to see a knife fight to secure natural gas physical in 28 like we really haven't seen before.

It's been surprising we haven't really seen any of this yet, because 28–29 the physical market tightens materially — depending where you are — and the amount of money that's gone into unproven, untested [assets]... the amount of capital being raised for things that really may not happen until 2035.

Maybe that's been surprising, especially as it relates to: you've got Expand trading at 4x EBITDA, a low-to-mid-teens free cash yield on a gas forward curve that is complacent to all of the objective things that we already know are likely to get plugged in.

People are really not willing to look past summer heat or a slight outage in an LNG facility right now. But in six months, we start to see these companies roll forward to look at 28. In 6 months, you could start to see the forward curves really move up materially.

Investors are not willing to look past near-term appropriately supplied gas market, but they're willing to pay for something in 2035 that is totally untested or unproven. That's been surprising — the assumptions and the inconsistency across sectors and industries, even among the four sectors we follow.

十三、结语：给 CEO 的健康挑战

主持人： So maybe in closing — what would be the healthy challenge to pose to anyone out there whose business has as an input, directly or indirectly, energy prices? How would you encourage the CEOs — what question should they ask of themselves or their business?

Matt： Make sure when your assets are deployed that you understand exactly what the source of your natural gas will be. Make sure you have physical supply locked up, and that you understand your counterparties and what will likely be very meaningful counterparty risk in two or three years.

Counterparty risk isn't something we've really talked about during the last couple of years in the AI boom. But when it comes to parties being long and short something that is moving a lot — imagine being short memory a year ago or 18 months ago and finding out all of a sudden you're short memory. That is what this natural gas market looks like to us — not two years out, but six-plus months out.

Making sure you understand the physical provisioning of gas for your assets is important:

  • For hyperscalers and for the buyers of simple-cycle and CCGT large-scale plants
  • But especially for fuel cells — we are very cynical whether you can deploy fuel cells at scale, because there isn't the gas in the system to power those 24/7 365. So we treat them in our base case that I described as backup gen. To the extent you were to deploy fuel cells as base-load gen, that only pulls forward and is additive to the convexity that I described.

For CEOs and partners on projects — whether you are the EPC company trading at 25x cash flow, which is a historically high multiple for an engineering-construction firm, and your main business is building natural gas plants — we may not be able to build or deploy more gas plants at a certain point in 2029, 2030 because gas is much more expensive and you may have regulators asking questions. The focus for you should be on how do you do accretive M&A to backfill and diversify your business so that you're not entirely beholden to natural gas generating asset build.

For hyperscalers — I know memory has been a pain point. Natural gas could be 20, 30, or 40% of their cost of doing business at a time when they're supposed to be reaching escape velocity with profitability.

Performance per watt is probably a compute metric that we're going to care more and more about.

I would say that the questions or the challenges for each pocket or industry of companies is a little bit different, but it's all focused on making sure you're managing risk and you understand exactly when your plans play out, how it can go wrong — which in this case means: what if gas is not $3.50, but $10 or more? What happens if physical gas is questioned? What happens when consumers, and regulators therefore, start to ask questions? Do you have a backup plan? What's your backup plan?

结束语

主持人： Matt, I love talking about the energy system with you. This was an especially fun one on the back of so much of your work. So fascinating and interesting. I hope, as the US has been very good at doing historically, that lots of people listen and start to imagine solutions, and also create the right amount of urgency to get those solutions in place — and that we emerge from this more resilient, more capable, more efficient, all these things. Thanks so much for your time.

Matt： Thank you again for having me.

[片尾广告]

You know how small advantages compound over time? That's true in investing and just as true in how you run your company. Your spending system is your capital allocation strategy. Ramp makes it smarter by default. Better data, better decisions, better economics over time. See how at ramp.com/invest.

As your business grows, Vanta scales with you, automating compliance and giving you a single source of truth for security and risk. Learn more at vanta.com/invest.

item.description:
## 一、最深的洞察：这不是能源危机，是"信念结构"的时间套利
表面看这是天然气供需失衡的故事，但真正令人震撼的是Matt揭示的**认知层的错配**：物理世界里，2028年的短缺几乎已成定局（LNG合同、井筒物理、管道审批周期都是刚性的），但金融世界里，2028年之后的天然气远期曲线仍然是"平的"。
**这是一次由"复盘偏差"造成的集体幻觉**：过去15年美国人被页岩革命宠坏了，形成"天然气永远充裕"的直觉锚点。市场并非不理性，而是被"最近15年的样本"锁死了先验分布。这跟2022年前的欧洲天然气市场、2020年前的芯片产能、2007年前的房价预期是**同一种认知病理**——用"稳态期"的方差去定价"相变期"的风险。
真正的机会不在天然气本身，而在**"人们何时会醒过来"**。Matt说的"6个月内曲线会开始移动"——他实际上在交易一个**认知拐点的期权**，而不是一个商品。
## 二、令人意外的跨领域连接：AI训练的Scaling Law，正在撞上地质学的Decline Curve
这里有一个几乎没人注意到的深层反讽——
AI界最神圣的规律是**Scaling Law**

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] OpenAI是AI泡沫的雷曼兄弟，泡沫剛剛被中國戳破了？【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这不是 AI 泡沫，这是"负债驱动的循环献祭"

大多数评论者把 OpenAI-Oracle-CoreWeave-Nvidia 的关系描绘成"AI 生态"，但如果你把资金流画出来，会发现一个让人不适的真相：这根本不是生态，是一条闭环的自我引用债务链。

  • Nvidia 投资 CoreWeave → CoreWeave 借钱买 Nvidia 的 GPU → CoreWeave 把算力租给 OpenAI → OpenAI 承诺给 Oracle 300 亿 → Oracle 先借钱建数据中心 → 数据中心里塞满 Nvidia 的芯片。
  • 钱在这个环里转了一圈，最后落回 Nvidia 的营收报表上，被市场当作"AI 需求真实"的证据，推高 Nvidia 股价，让 Nvidia 有更多市值继续投资 CoreWeave。

这在会计上叫"vendor financing"（供应商融资），在金融史上有一个不太光彩的先例——1999 年的朗讯（Lucent）。朗讯借钱给电信客户买自己的设备，把借出去的钱当营收入账。市场兴奋了 18 个月，然后一夜崩溃。视频把 OpenAI 类比雷曼是抓错了参照系——雷曼是流动性危机，而这一次更像是"营收本身是假的"的朗讯式危机。这才是真正让人后背发凉的地方。

二、你以为中国在打价格战，其实中国在打"标准战"

视频把 Kimi 的威胁描述为"更便宜 + 差距不大"，但这个框架完全没抓到重点。真正的杀招是开源——而开源不是慈善，是一种非常古老的战略武器。

跨领域连接来了：这一幕曾经在 1990 年代的操作系统战争里完整上演过一次。当年 Sun 的 Solaris 昂贵而封闭，微软的 Windows NT 也昂贵而封闭，然后 Linux 出现了——不是因为 Linux 更聪明，而是因为它把"操作系统"从一个可以定价的商品，变成了基础设施般的公共物品。结果不是 Linux 打败了 Windows，而是整个操作系统层的利润消失了，价值向上迁移到了应用层（Google、Facebook 就是这样长出来的）。

Kimi、DeepSeek 开源做的是同一件事：它们不需要打败 Claude，它们只需要让"模型层"变得无法定价。一旦模型变成 commodity，OpenAI 那种"每年烧 200 亿、期待未来靠 API 定价权收割"的商业模式，其底层假设就崩了。所以 Anthropic 要求政府"筑墙"，本质不是国家安全，是在守卫一个即将被开源蒸发掉的定价权。David Sacks 隐约看到了，但没说破。

三、被所有人忽略的、最诡异的一句话：David Sacks 的"FAA 类比"

视频里 Sacks 说 Anthropic 想做的是"AI 版 FAA"，然后一笔带过。但这里藏着一个堪称精妙的博弈论陷阱，值得单独拆解：

  • 飞机型号认证需要 5-9 年——不是因为工程复杂，而是因为先取得认证的公司自动获得了对后来者的时间垄断。波音和空客不是靠飞机好而稳坐寡头，是靠认证成本把新进入者挡在门外。
  • Anthropic 提议的"frontier model 认证"看似是安全治理，实际上是把这套"用监管周期换取市场周期"的手法搬到 AI。因为模型迭代周期是几个月，而认证周期是几年——认证本身就是把时间当武器，消灭速度更快的竞争者。

这里出现了一个让人啊哈的悖论：Anthropic 一边说"中国追上来了，我们必须跑得更快"，一边设计一套会让自己也跑不快的监管框架。这看似矛盾，其实完全自洽——因为他们的赌注是：中国被墙挡在外面，美国国内小玩家被监管挡在外面，最后场上只剩三家。跑得慢一点没关系，只要别人不能跑就行了。

而这也解释了视频结尾那个"没人敢先停"的资本开支游戏——当所有玩家都在跑，唯一能让人停下来的方式，不是自己刹车，而是让裁判判别人违规。Anthropic 想做的不是运动员，是裁判。这才是这场 AI 战争最不为人知的底层结构。

一个额外的观察，送给爱思考的你：如果 Kimi 用 2400 个假账号从 Claude 抓了 1600 万条对话，训练成本降到 1/3——这在数学上意味着什么？意味着"训练一个前沿模型"的真实成本可能远低于 OpenAI 公布的数字。也就是说，OpenAI 的万亿资本承诺，不是技术必需，是为了让门槛看起来足够高而故意抬升的军备开销。当中国证明"用 1/3 的钱可以做到 90% 的效果"时，被戳破的不是技术泡沫——是"AI 必须很贵"这个共识本身。而所有基于"AI 必须很贵"的估值模型，从今天开始，需要重写。

📝 转录文本

OpenAI 是 AI 泡沫的雷曼兄弟？泡沫刚刚被中国戳破？

开场

This is what mania looks like. Why are people starting to call OpenAI the "Lehman Brothers of AI"? Why was Oracle's credit rating downgraded? And why does this inadvertently expose the fact that the AI market is actually quite fragile—and did China just pop the bubble of the U.S. AI stock market? In the face of such fierce competition, the U.S. is left with...

Hi, I'm BY. Welcome to subscribe, and please share such major events with others who are also following the market.

一、Oracle 被降评，OpenAI 是最大风险源

S&P Global downgraded Oracle's credit rating from BB to BB- in July, just one notch away from junk status. There is even talk that OpenAI could be the "Lehman Brothers of AI," the key player that might cause the dominoes to fall.

OpenAI is Oracle's primary credit risk, meaning Oracle has bet its business heavily on OpenAI. If something happens to OpenAI, then Oracle will face trouble too.

Oracle currently has about 100 billion dollars in remaining performance obligations, meaning orders that have been signed but not yet officially recorded as revenue, and for which they haven't received payment. 30 billion of that is a five-year cloud computing contract signed with OpenAI.

This sounds like a good thing, right? OpenAI promised 30 billion dollars in business to Oracle. But the point is that Oracle must invest a massive amount of money upfront to build data centers before slowly recouping that cash.

二、OpenAI 的巨亏与万亿承诺

So, what is the risk? S&P Global doubts that OpenAI can afford this payment because, although OpenAI is growing rapidly, it is currently operating at a massive loss.

  • In 2025, OpenAI's revenue was 13.07 billion dollars, but its costs were 34 billion, resulting in a loss of about 20.9 billion.
  • Furthermore, OpenAI has committed to spending over one trillion dollars on Nvidia, AMD, Oracle, and CoreWeave.

If OpenAI cannot significantly increase its revenue in a short time or continuously secure new financing, it might not be able to pay on time. Once OpenAI fails to pay, Oracle—because it has bet so heavily on this specific business—could face a situation where the work is done, but the money never arrives.

三、多米诺骨牌：谁会被拖下水？

If these dominoes start to fall, it won't just be Oracle that is affected; companies like CoreWeave and Microsoft, which provide computing power to OpenAI, will be impacted as well. If that happens, these cloud companies will slow down data center construction, which in turn will further affect Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, and other companies involved in memory, networking equipment, cooling, and power infrastructure.

Wait, some might say that Microsoft and Amazon don't just rely on OpenAI for their AI, and NVIDIA has a massive client base too. That's all true, but the ones with the real risks are companies with highly concentrated clients, high debt, and that have already front-loaded massive capital expenditures.

四、Oracle 为什么这么脆弱？

That's why Oracle is constantly being brought up and discussed. It was originally a database software company. Its business was letting major firms—like banks, airlines, and governments—store their data in Oracle's databases, and Oracle would charge them software and maintenance fees. This business has very high margins because, once the software is developed, serving one more client doesn't cost much.

However, their traditional business is mature and saturated, so Oracle started pivoting, building data centers on a large scale, buying GPUs, and preparing power and networking to rent out computing power to companies like OpenAI that need to train models.

Now that their credit rating has been downgraded, Oracle's future borrowing costs might rise. If they get downgraded one more level, down to BB+, that's what's commonly known as junk status. Funds that are restricted to holding investment-grade corporate bonds would be forced to sell off Oracle's bonds, which would then drive up the cost of borrowing for Oracle in the future.

五、中国 AI 突然发力：Kimi 的登场

Now. The entire U.S. stock market, as well as the Taiwanese and Korean markets, are betting on the same assumption: that U.S. AI giants will be the biggest winners in the AI race. But is that really true? Is there no one else?

The common view used to be that the U.S. was 6 to 12 months ahead of other countries in AI, but on July 16th, China's Kimi k3 AI model took first place in six out of seven test categories. Former White House AI and crypto advisor David Sacks posted that this is exactly how the U.S. could lose the AI race.

六、Anthropic 的出口管制事件

Let's rewind another month: U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick suddenly notified Anthropic that their models, Claude 3.5 and Opus 3.5, were now subject to export controls, meaning foreigners couldn't use them.

Even if these foreigners were inside the U.S., as long as they weren't American citizens, they couldn't use them. Even Anthropic's own employees, if they weren't American, couldn't access them. Anthropic couldn't possibly check everyone's nationality in time, so they simply took both models offline for everyone.

For the first time, the whole world realized that the U.S. government actually has the power to shut down the world's most advanced AI models in such a short amount of time.

七、价格与能力对比：Kimi vs Claude

Several key points have recently emerged. The first is that while everyone assumed we could only use expensive US AI models, China has launched a new AI model called Kimi k 1.5.

This chart compares the average cost for each model to complete a benchmark task from Artificial Analysis.

  • For China's Kimi k 1.5, each task costs about $0.95.
  • Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet costs about $2.75.

In other words, under this specific test, Kimi k 1.5's cost is roughly one-third of Claude's, clearly showing that Kimi is much cheaper.

Also in the Artificial Analysis breakdown, Claude 3.5 Sonnet has an intelligence index of 60, while Kimi k 1.5 has 57; the capability gap isn't that large.

Usually, saying this sparks a lot of debate about whether A is clearly smarter than B. People argue endlessly, but what defines "smarter" is subjective, as different people and companies have different analytical criteria and weightings. But the point is, regardless of who you think is better, the two models aren't that far apart in intelligence.

This is why not only foreigners, but even Americans are starting to wonder: if I can get similar results for a much cheaper price, why should I stick with these expensive US models? If enough people feel this way, it could negatively impact the sky-high valuations of these US AI companies, which in turn would hit the US stock market, since much of the market is currently built on these high tech valuations.

八、开源 vs 闭源：真正的战略差异

Next, the issue is that Chinese AI models are choosing to be open-source, whereas US models are closed models—not open-source. What does this mean?

Open-source means they provide the model itself to users. You can pay to use the official API—for example, Kimi's official API—letting them handle servers, chips, and maintenance. Or, you can download the model yourself and deploy it on your own servers, or have other cloud providers run it for you.

So, open-source doesn't mean it's free; there will be costs regardless of which method you use. The difference is that because Kimi is open-source, you aren't limited to buying services only from them. You can choose who operates the model, where your data is stored, and how much you pay, meaning pricing power is no longer solely in Kimi's hands.

If we compare this to closed American models like Claude, which can only be run by Anthropic, companies are forced to send their data to Anthropic's system and accept their pricing.

Therefore, the advantage of open source is that it gives users choice, data control, and bargaining power. So, on top of these advantages, Chinese AI models are also cheaper. When these advantages stack together, it creates a massive threat to American models.

九、赞助商时间：Mtrade 平台介绍

As retail investors, how can you try participating in the investment market with a small amount of capital?

The Mtrade investment platform holds trading licenses from the world's four major regulatory bodies and offers a wide variety of products, including stocks, forex, cryptocurrencies, indices, commodities, and ETFs.

Mtrade is a CFD trading platform; you aren't buying or selling the asset itself, but rather trading the movement of its price. It supports direct deposits and withdrawals via credit card and USDT, so there's no need to convert to USD first. Trading is commission-free with low spreads, and leverage can be set up to 200x. Of course, you must, must be very careful when using this leverage.

Accounts come with default insurance coverage of up to $1 million, underwritten by an insurance company. On Mtrade, you can go long or short with two-way trading, meaning there are opportunities to profit whether the market rises or falls, and you can start with a minimum of just $5.

It partners with TradingView, featuring built-in TradingView indicators for free, and the platform also provides plenty of information, news, and trading strategies for reference. They are also the official sponsor of the Argentina national football team, and in 2025, they were recognized with awards like "Most Reliable Broker in Europe" and "Best Digital Customer Experience."

There is currently a channel-exclusive event; join via the link in this video's description to receive up to $1,300 in trading bonuses. If you profit, you keep it; if you lose, the platform covers it. If you want to try trading, you can practice risk-free—the link is in the description.

十、中美 AI 战争的两派：Anthropic vs David Sacks

How will the China-US AI war develop moving forward? Currently, the US AI scene is divided into two schools of thought: one side includes Anthropic, and the other includes former White House AI and crypto advisor David Sacks.

Anthropic 的立场：筑墙防中国

Anthropic's stance is that America's most powerful AI must not fall into the hands of China. In February of this year, Anthropic publicly accused three Chinese AI companies—DeepSeek, Moonshot (the parent company of Kimi), and MiniMax—of using about 24,000 fake accounts to scrape over 16 million conversations from Claude to supposedly boost their own models' capabilities.

There is an interesting irony here, because Anthropic's own AI models were also trained by scraping various books, internet data, and all sorts of content.

Anyway, Anthropic is asking the US government to "keep restricting China's access to the most advanced chips, don't let them have it, and limit Chinese companies' access to AI models. Prevent China from using 'theft' tactics to quickly copy cheap versions of models that cost the US so much to train." They also want strict safety protocols—essentially building a wall to block China.

David Sacks 的立场：行业自律

That is Anthropic's take, but David Sax thinks differently. He feels that if China is already catching up, the last thing the US should do right now is tie up its own AI companies with a bunch of restrictions.

He thinks a more feasible approach is for the US industry to come up with its own set of rules; definitely don't let the government, which doesn't understand this, write the rules. People within the industry should be the ones to write them.

Number one, I think the SRO has to have broad representation from within the industry, the AI industry. It has to include startups and open source. It can't just be the three biggest labs, you know, can't just be fixing it right. Yeah, exactly.

十一、FAA 类比：为什么强监管会让美国输掉 AI 竞赛

David Sax mentioned that the regulatory concept currently proposed by Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario is very much like an AI version of the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

One of the FAA's jobs is to approve new aircraft designs. Any new aircraft design, or any major maintenance performed on an aircraft, must first obtain a license called a "type certificate."

  • A new aircraft usually takes five to nine years to get this certification.
  • Even if you are just modifying an existing certification, if the changes are significant enough, it can still take three to five years.

AI systems today release new versions every few months. So, if we switch to total government control, and every model has to wait for government approval and every update has to go through certification, release times will drag from months to potentially years for a single update. If that happens, the US is definitely going to lose the AI race.

Number two is: I think that this body should only be reviewing frontier models, meaning the true frontier, the models that really represent an advance in the state of the art of artificial intelligence. And models below this level should not be held up from getting to market. And I do think that is a big risk under regulations is: that the leaders in the market use this as a way to tie up lesser models. And there's no reason, if a model is not at the frontier, to hold it up.

十二、监管背后的商业算盘

David Sax believes Anthropic's current push for strong regulation is actually just a business consideration. Because regulation is very favorable to big companies. If the government starts mandating that only a few companies are allowed to train the most advanced models, the ones capable of meeting those requirements in the end will likely just be giants like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google.

If it's not a step change, then how are you dealing with some new incremental risk, right? I mean, this is all about dealing with some sort of incremental catastrophic risk that could be introduced by some new step change in intelligence. And that brings me to number three, which is I think this body should be dealing with catastrophic risk only. And to my knowledge, those right now are cyber and CBRN, meaning it's, you know, chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear. So, it should not be things for example like disinformation or microaggression. regulation number works and because

Which side do you think will win out: strong regulation or self-regulation? If you have

十三、AI 投资的债务循环与 CoreWeave 案例

In the AI industry, when you hear about investment plans, they are usually astronomical figures; a lot of it is done through borrowing and cross-investment.

For example, CoreWeave is a classic case. They borrow heavily to buy Nvidia GPUs to build data centers, then rely on long-term contracts with major clients like OpenAI, Microsoft, and Meta to use future revenue to support today's investments. Nvidia is not only CoreWeave's chip supplier, but also their shareholder and customer.

As long as the demand for AI computing power continues to grow, this model can forge ahead at full speed. But if one day these major clients start delaying plans or decide to scale back their computing orders, CoreWeave will face much more than just a slowdown in revenue growth. They still have to pay interest, handle equipment depreciation, and cover data center rent and electricity costs; none of these expenses will vanish just because they have fewer clients or lower usage.

十四、无人敢先停下的军备竞赛

All tech companies are currently competing against each other.

  • If Meta announces a $35 billion investment for 2026
  • And Google announces $185 billion
  • Amazon will announce $200 billion the next day

It's just a race to see who invests more. Eventually, no one can stop; not only can you not hit the brakes, but even failing to accelerate is considered not good enough.

Because if they slow down, the market will say, "Gotcha! Look!" And then interpret it as, "Oh, AI demand must be weakening." Once one company stops, others will have an excuse, saying, "Well, so-and-so slowed down, so we'll slow down too." After that, the market will fall into a panic, much like a game where no one dares to be the first to drop out.

As long as everyone is still running at full speed on the field, the story can continue, but when and who will be the one to stop?

结语

If you want to keep hearing content like this, please subscribe to the channel. If you have any questions about operating the platform, feel free to join our free LINE@ to ask our staff; you can ask anything.

Next, I recommend you join the discussion on this topic. Let's keep working hard in the market. See you next time, bye-bye.

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Factory's Matan Grinberg: The Coming ‘Dark Factory’ Where Software Builds Itself
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"付钱送客"是最反直觉的护城河建造术

Matan 最令人震惊的决定不是那些看似大胆的技术选择，而是主动把已经到手的 $2M 收入退回给客户。这在传统商业逻辑里近乎自杀——但它揭示了一个被大多数创业者忽视的"信任的负熵原理"：

在企业软件销售中，信任是一种熵增系统。一旦客户开始怀疑你的产品，衰减速度远快于建立速度。他实际上做的是用现金购买未来的谈话权——花 $2M 买下了"12 个月后我可以再次敲门"的期权。这种反向嫁妆式的操作，比任何 NPS 调查、任何 CS 团队都更能刻画一家公司的品格。

更深层的跨领域连接是：这个动作在物理学上等价于"退火"（annealing）——为了让系统跳出局部最优，你必须先主动提高能量、破坏眼前的稳定态。绝大多数创业公司卡在 $2M–$10M 之间死掉，恰恰是因为他们不敢做这种"负梯度动作"。

二、Harness 的悖论：多模型让系统更强，而不是更弱

这是整场对话里最反直觉、也最少被注意到的技术洞察。所有人的第一直觉都是"模型和执行框架协同设计（co-design）"会带来最佳性能——就像苹果的软硬件一体化。但 Matan 戳破了这个幻觉：当你的 harness 只服务一个模型，它会过拟合到那个模型的怪癖上，从而在真实的分布外任务上变脆。

他给出的类比很深：这跟"个人 AI 应该只用你自己的数据训练"是同构的错觉——正确答案是"用整个互联网训练它才最懂你"。模型之于 harness，正如数据之于模型。 多样性不是妥协，而是唯一的正则化项。

一个更远的跨领域连接：这与生态学里的"中度干扰假说"（Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis）完全同构——单一物种垄断的森林（单一模型的封闭 harness）看似高效，但抗风险能力最弱；被多种干扰交替塑造的生态系统反而最稳定、最有生产力。Anthropic 和 OpenAI 都想成为森林里唯一的树，而 Factory 在下的赌注是：森林比树活得久。

三、"暗工厂"与公司即 AGI：一场关于组织结构的相变

Matan 预测 12–24 个月内 90% 的 token 消耗会变成异步（asynchronous）——这个数字比大多数人想象的激进得多。它的深层含义远超"效率提升"。

现在所有 AI 编程工具（包括 Claude Code、Codex、Droid）本质上还是同步的：如果所有工程师明天都病倒，token 消费瞬间归零。 这说明我们其实还停留在"AI 作为高级计算器"阶段。真正的相变发生在 AI 开始自己捕捉信号、自己开工、自己交付——那时候公司才真正变成了 Jack Dorsey 说的那种"AGI"。

而这里藏着一个几乎没人讲的观察：大多数公司现在用"直觉"（vibes）做 token 预算、做裁员决策、做资源调度。 Matan 把这个类比推到极致——"你不会用直觉做反向传播"。这暗示未来 3–5 年，会诞生一个全新的岗位类别，姑且叫"组织权重工程师"（Org Weights Engineer）——他们的工作是把整个公司当作一个神经网络来调参，用真实的 outcome 做反向传播。

跨领域连接：这其实是运筹学里"经济调度问题"（Economic Dispatch）在组织内部的复活。电网每 5 分钟就要决定哪个电厂多发一点、哪个少发一点；Matan 描述的 token router 几乎是这套数学的直接翻版。人类花了 80 年优化电网调度算法——现在同样的问题以"每一美元该投给人还是投给 token"的形式，在每个企业内部重新出现一次。谁先解决它，谁就是下一个时代的杰克·韦尔奇。

彩蛋：埃隆的"命名反噬定律"

Matan 随口提到 Musk 那句——"你注定会变成你名字的反面"——是整场对话最诗意的一击。Factory 这个名字预示着它的终局形态其实是 Artisanal（手工的）。这是一种语言学层面的战略预言：极致的自动化最终释放出的，恰恰是极致的人类手工艺时间。

这也是为什么"程序员会消失"的说法完全错误：当所有琐碎工作被工厂吞掉，剩下的每一小时都是艺术家时刻。

反直觉的 Harness 悖论：多模型让 harness 更强

What goes into building a great [harness]? And is it a great harness? And it seems like there's almost a lot of FUD in the ecosystem of "my harness is better than your harness," and, you know, "you need to own the model to have a good harness," or "actually you have a better harness if you don't own the model." Yeah. So a couple — some general things that matter are, um, the way you do caching. So, you know, cache tokens end up being like a tenth as expensive. And so one big piece of performance for a given harness is what is your rate of token caching.

Um, another example would be how do you perform while in compression or compaction. So typically when you're dealing with a long session, you're going to exceed the context limit of the model itself. And so the harness will do some sort of, you know, summarization, compression, compaction, whatever you want to call it. And the way that you perform during that compaction is a big determining factor of how good your harness is. Um, and tests that they do for that are like, you know, they call it "needle in the haystack," where you have some long thread and maybe there's one piece of information that's really important. How often will your harness preserve that through compaction?

Other examples are like tool use or how does it use the environment to validate whatever work that it's doing. Um, these are things that you can kind of have individual metrics on, and that we kind of have our own internal benchmarks to measure: how do the out-of-the-box agents do versus how does Factory perform.

I think one thing that um, naively everyone believed initially was: if you train the model and you build the harness, you're going to make them better together.

Yeah.

And much to the chagrin of many of my friends at OpenAI and Anthropic, this is not true. If you build a harness that supports different models, that harness will be better.

What's the — like my intuition would be model-harness co-design makes you better.

Yes.

What's the intuition for why it's actually not?

It's very analogous to the idea, maybe like I don't know, 10 years ago of: if you were to be like, "Hey, I want to train my personal AI back in like early ML days before like GPT-3. I want to train my personal AI. I'm going to give it all of my data because I want it to know me." Turns out the answer was: train it on the whole internet and it'll be so much better for you than if it were just trained on your data.

So there's a sort of analog that emerges where what data is to a model, models are to a harness. Where the more models you expose to a harness, you avoid overfitting that harness to the nuances of that model in particular. And there are certain intricacies about different models that you can learn from and then improve different models' performance in your own harness.

And this was why — for example, we kind of stopped doing it because terminal-bench got so benchmaxed — but initially when every new Opus or GPT model would come out, it would perform better on terminal-bench in Droid than it would in Claude Code or Codex. Um, which is — and this is something that I think was somewhat frustrating to — because ideally, like from a lab perspective, you ideally want it so that it's better together, because then it means you have to use their harness and you can't use a different one. But I think the reality is having that multi-model harness ends up getting kind of frontier on all those.

Token Maxing 的四个阶段与 Factory Router

So we talked about one type of maxing, benchmark maxing. Let's talk about token maxing, because it feels like the world has changed a lot. We've gone from token maxing to now cost rationalization. What does that mean for Factory?

Yeah. So um, maybe I'll lay this out just so we're all on the same page of the way that we see what's led us to this token maxing.

So loosely there was like this phase one where — maybe phase zero was like no one believed in AI. Then phase one, everyone believes in AI and then boards were like, "Mr. CEO, what are you doing about AI? What's your AI strategy?" And Mr. CEO is like, "I don't know, like what's our AI strategy? CTO, make sure everyone goes and uses AI."

And so then phase two is, you know, CTO is like, "Okay, we got to make sure everyone uses AI. Let's start putting it in performance reviews. Let's make public rankings of who's using tokens the most" — because everyone's stubborn. No one wants to use this stuff. They're all skeptical.

And then we enter phase three, which is everyone sees these ratings. They see that it's part of their perfs, and they're like, "Okay, I'm going to use AI for everything." And that's kind of phase three. It's this token maxing where people are using like Opus for literally everything. Like, "What's the weather in SF? Opus tell me. I don't know." Like there are banks that we are working with where they are spending literally hundreds of thousands of dollars a month on people asking things like literally, "What is the weather?" or "Tell me about Python" — like trivial questions that you could Google, people are asking Opus.

Um, and the reality is this happened because we were so worried about adoption that we overcorrect, and we're like, "Adoption by any means necessary." And I think that's actually — it's a decent approach. Like it's probably faster to do that and then curb usage or make usage more responsible than it is to start limited and be like, "you know, you can only use it for this thing" — because when you have people that are stubborn, first you want to just prove that it works and then you can get kind of more mature about it.
