So, you know, if you're asking what the weather is, you probably don't need the very frontier of human intelligence to answer that for you.

Or or you really do.

I mean, it depends. I don't know. It depends on what kind of answer you're looking for. Um, you know, giving you like a full down to the molecular level of what's happening.

But um, uh, you know, allowing that — but also more importantly, for every enterprise, something that no one's dealing with yet but 12 months from now is going to be the case is: not everyone needs the same tokens. Having a blanket token cap for every individual in some large bank, let's say, makes no sense.

So every CIO is going to need to answer: for every incremental token, where do we put it? And right now it is super not obvious how you would do that. Like right now we're saying, "Oh, you know, the PMs who are vibe-coding dashboards get the same token limits as the engineers who are building critical infrastructure." That's probably not the best thing to do. Or similarly, you might be dealing with COBOL codebases where Opus is not the best model to use, but instead maybe some fine-tuned model on that codebase in particular.

The point of the router is that we can accommodate these different constraints, where maybe you say, "You know what? This part of the org, they're just vibe-coding, they can use Gemini Flash. This part of the org, they're doing COBOL, we fine-tuned this great model to work on COBOL. Let's route to that when we're working on that part of the codebase. Maybe this other part, we really care about reliability, so let's generate the code with OpenAI, test it with Anthropic, review it with like Gemini," things like that.

And we can actually take in your routing procedure instructions in natural language. So, you could even say things like — it's not purely deterministic — it can even be like, "Hey, you know, Pat, I don't know. Like, I don't know what he's doing. Like, give him Flash." Like, I don't know. [laughter] Or, "You know, I think we really need to avoid having them use open models because, you know, whatever reason, we don't like the way open models perform here." Um, and we'll do internal benchmarking to know which models are better at which of these tasks.

开源模型：Frontier-Minus-One

How close are the open models at this point? Which one's the best?

GLM 5.2 is incredible. Um, it's at the point where internally we have no token limits for our engineers and like half of our tokens are open to open models.

Wow.

Yeah. Because they're just faster and they're cheaper. They're just as performant. And I think the thing that everyone gets wrong is everyone is comparing like GLM 5.2 to the latest model like Opus 4.8 or GPT 5.6. But really they should be compared to Opus 4.7 or GPT 5.5.

Why?

Because generally the open models come later and they're kind of a generation behind. And that's kind of the — the frontier models will be frontier. The question is: are the open models getting as good as frontier-minus-one? And the answer is unequivocally yes, which I think is a really really interesting outcome.

It's great for consumers — and by consumers I don't mean like individuals, I mean the consumers of the APIs — because if you're a business that is doing in AR software engineering, your job is at a very high level to solve problems. And if we can allow you to solve those problems faster and with cheaper models that are just as performant, that means you can solve more problems. Like that is a good thing. And it is a very good world where there is not a monopoly on intelligence, but instead kind of a garden of intelligence that you can pick and choose from, um, you know, when you'd like.

Something that we joke about on this intelligence allocation thing: if you're trying to get a tutor for your daughter in algebra, you can probably find someone cheaper than Albert Einstein to be that tutor. Now, it might be that she eventually goes and becomes like a leading, you know, physicist or something — in which case, yeah, maybe let's get Albert Einstein in there. But most likely you can get, you know, a high school student or something like that. Um, and it's probably much more cost-effective for you as well to do so.

模型使用份额：从 <1% 到双位数

Since you guys do the model routing, if you look at, you know, if there's a pie chart that shows the complexion of models being used by your customer base today, what did it look like a few months ago? What does it look like today? What do you think it'll look like in a year?

Yeah, I will caveat this with saying that right now enterprises haven't gone too opinionated yet into the routing procedures. Okay?

This is something that will happen over the next 6 to 12 months. But right now, they're just going from no router to router. That's kind of the first change. Then it's going to be like the exact nature of the routing.

At the beginning of the year, it was less than 1% of tokens went to open models. In the first quarter, it became a single-digit percent. It has now crossed into being a double-digit percent of tokens. Um, now percent of tokens is not always the same as percent of cost, because the open tokens are cheaper. Um, but it's pretty crazy to see the growth there.

What's your forecast?

[sighs] My sense is that we will asymptote towards vast majority being open, just because it provides you more optionality and it's cheaper. Um, but that doesn't mean they're going to be like — that's a token share, not necessarily a leverage share. Because maybe there are 1% of tokens that are incredibly incredibly valuable and are like very key decision-making, and then the rest are more like implementation tokens or lower stakes if you will.

I don't think there's going to be a world in which it's ever going to be 100%.

Y —

I think the frontier of intelligence will inherently always be valuable for every business, just because the stakes are going to get higher and the intricacy with which you think is going to be more important, but we'll be better at offloading certain tasks.

And this is like — you can loosely think of this: already with the way orgs are structured, where you know, in general, engineering leaders are more tenured engineers who in theory have more wisdom and each kind of minute of their brain power is higher leverage, in theory. Um, and even, you know, you can also imagine consider a human engineer and try mapping over the course of their day like how much brain power they're using — and like, you know, it's probably going to be really low for a lot of it, but then there're going to be some moments where they're going pretty high, like they're deeply concentrating and thinking about some, you know, systems design problem or whatever.

All of those low-leverage moments we want to automate away, and like, we want those very high-leverage moments — sometimes, you know, we're referring to them as like the "eureka moments" or the moments where they're doing something that's very high leverage. What if those aren't just moments, but what if those are like hours at a time, because you don't have to deal with all the other stuff?

And I think that's kind of the way to think about intelligence allocation. If you're an engineer and you were writing docs — that is such a low-leverage use of your time. Like you've become an expert in your craft and you used to spend hours writing docs. Like I remember it was actually valuable. Like I remember Stripe had so much alpha for just having incredible docs. But imagine all the other stuff those incredible engineers could do if it wasn't writing documentation. Like we should live in a world where everyone can have docs as good as Stripe, and that is strictly beneficial for everyone. And then the question is: okay, what do those really smart engineers do with their time once they don't have to do that?

商业模式：从 Usage-Based 到 Outcome-Based

Maybe this a good time to talk about business model, given that, you know, especially with the rise of open-weight models, the cost differential — um, I imagine that means very different things for your cost structure but very similar value delivered to customers. How do you think about business model and pricing?

Yeah, this is more what our customers want and need as opposed to what we want and need. So for example, I think right now usage-based is clearly the way to go. We want to be aligned with what they are doing and what we are doing. I think seat-based doesn't make sense at least for what we are doing.

My sense is that eventually we will change to outcome-based. Now, I don't think the enterprise is ready for that, and we've learned our lesson from those first two years. We are not going to impose things. [laughter]

Right.

Um, but my suspicion is that, you know, in the 2030s things will probably look more like outcome-based.

Yeah.

What does outcome-based mean for your market? What would be the definition of an outcome?

So maybe here's a way to put — so right now we are usage-based. Like the more tokens you use, you know, the more you pay, the more we get. Um, now since we are model-independent, we kind of with our router are kind of pointing a token cannon at either OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, GCP, you know, any one of these people.

Uh, to a certain degree this is like a really dumbed-down version of a marketplace, where right now there is a buy side — the buy side is an engineer who wants a task done — and then you have the model providers who are saying, either in benchmarks right now, "We perform at this cost and this performance," and then we determine who we go to for that given task.

Yeah.

There's a world in which tokens — they might bid in a certain way of saying, "Here is our cost for this task. We will get this task done at this cost no matter what," but they're pricing it such that they hope that they can make a margin there. If they price it wrong, they're at a negative margin. If they price it right and win the bid, then they get the positive margin.

And the way you determine if the task was successful is by some validation loops, because no one is using these tools anymore where it's just like "write me code," "great, thank you." It's generally, "write me code, and here's how I know it was done well."

And similarly, if you are a model lab and you are given "here's a task, here's the validation criteria," you'll be able to say roughly how much you think you would be willing to pay to get those tokens, and you know, you want to have some margin on that. And then in that world, that's a way that you kind of dynamically shift from usage-based to outcome-based.

Um, I think that there's so many questions with this, and this is very much forward-looking. Um, but I think there's a lot of questions about how do you subdivide tasks? You know, divvying that up I think is something that's not obvious.

Yeah.

But as these tools get better, doing things like that actually becomes way easier.

Yeah. That's fascinating.

Yeah.

Yeah. If you can scope a task and then create a competitive marketplace, that'd be a fascinating version of the future.

Yes. And as a user, it then creates an incentive to be very thorough in your validation criteria.

Yeah.

Because, you know, there are stories of like, you know, you ask an agent to fix my code and it deletes your code. It's like, you know, the solution is just get rid of it all.

Like that Silicon Valley episode.

Yeah. But like, so you need to make sure your tests are very thorough, because technically it could hit all of your —

Vaulton will go rogue.

Yeah. Exactly. [laughter] Exactly. Yeah. Yeah. Reference.

软件工厂：每家公司其实都有一个（只是很低效）

Um, maybe zooming out a little bit. You named the company Factory. Actually you named it Droid before Factory.

That's right.

But you named it Factory before this concept took off, and now it feels like everybody wants to build a software factory.

Where do you think we are today in terms of the building of software factories, and how close are we to the ultimate vision of a software factory?

Yeah, everyone has a software factory whether they know it or not. It's just a very inefficient one. So it's kind of like — it feels like, you know, pre-industrialization where, you know, people were manually sewing things together or woodworking or whatever it might be, and these things are very inefficient.

Like right now, if you go to an organization that has more than 10,000 people, and you were to ask about the process by which they decide and release a feature, there is like hundreds or maybe thousands of people in that process, and most likely they couldn't even draw it for you. Like there's very low likelihood that they would know what that process looks like. Um, that is not because they think that is the right way of doing things. That is just kind of the nature of building large software as it is kind of today.

But with these systems, so much tribal knowledge can be codified. So much of this stuff that typically would require, "Oh, we need to ask this guru who's been here for 30 years who has the wisdom. Oh, we then need this approval and that approval. Oh, and I forgot there was some doc that said we always have to do this checklist." Um, and it relies so much on human behavior and redundancy. So much of that can be automated and refocused on what actually moves the needle for our business.

And I think this move towards software factories is a move towards: how do we figure out what are the actual inputs that determine what features we need to build? And that might be inputs from the customers, inputs from the market, inputs from product leaders at the company. And let's be very clear these are the signals, the inputs that we are taking in here. Okay great, we have those signals. Then what is the process by which we build this?

Um, and really mapping out the assembly lines of how you are building software is really important, because then you get to close the loop and say: did this actually deliver outcome for our business?

公司即 AGI：反向传播 vs 直觉

Talking before about the tokenomics — if you're that CIO and you're faced with that question of "where do you put every incremental token?", really the question two years from now is going to become: where do you put every incremental dollar? And so you're going to have to be asked: do you put that incremental dollar towards headcount or towards tokens? And if tokens, to where in the org?

And these are things that you can only really know when you have these kind of feedback loops that give you examples of like, "Hey by the way, we made those decisions based on this data. And it did not matter at all. We added these new features and no one cared. It didn't create more retention. It didn't create more usage or whatever metrics that business is looking to optimize."

And the only way to do this is: like, you need kind of more rigor and more process. It almost feels like 10 years from now we're going to look back at this previous era of software and it's going to feel like businesses in like ancient times where they didn't do accounting.

It's going to be like — it's going to be like marketing in the day of Mad Men, right? Where it's like all creative and you have no idea what's actually working.

It makes no — like it's like, "Oh yeah, let's ship that feature. Oh, I think it went well. Yeah, we had — I got some metrics on that. Yeah."

It's like, no —

If you guys read the blog post that Jack Dorsey put out about how every company is like an AGI —

Yeah.

There's also this degree to which if your company is an AGI, you want to optimize the weights.

Yeah.

You want to figure out what nodes are doing what things, which are load-bearing, which are not, which need more tokens, where do you need more nodes? And in order to do that, you don't train a model by vibes. I mean, okay, actually you kind of do — but [laughter] you don't — I guess more importantly, you don't do back-prop in a model by vibes. Like you are running those actual calculations and you are seeing when we change this node what happens. Now you might be making bets on how to change the model by vibes, but you are — it's pretty mathematical in what you are doing.

Meanwhile at companies, you know, people are determining token budgets just by shooting from the hip. People are laying people off by shooting from the hip and just being like, "Oh yeah, like 20,000." There is no way there is science to laying off 20,000 people. That is just like, "Here is a chunk and let's just see what happens."

Instead, I think in these organizations, the way they can do things is much more mathematical of like: this part of the business matters a lot and does better if we give it more tokens. It doesn't actually matter if we give it more humans, so let's give them more tokens. There might be other parts of the business where actually giving them more tokens doesn't matter, but more people matter, because if we build more relationships with our customers and deeper relationships with our customers, that matters.

But these are things that we're going to need like quantitative insight on, and you need a software factory to do that. Otherwise, you're just like shooting from the hip and just guessing, which won't work as well.

Token 与 Headcount 的极限比例

In the limit, how much do you think people will spend on tokens versus on engineering headcount?

It'll depend on the business. I think every business will have a balance and it just depends on — like an easy example is: generally salespeople, they probably don't need that many tokens if they're good salespeople. Because generally the — where they provide the most alpha is when they're in the seat face-to-face with their customers talking about the customer's problems, understanding, you know, how they build software in our case and how we can make that, you know, more efficient, more productive. They can use tokens a little bit of like, "Oh whatever, generate them some, you know, AI debrief, take some notes, votes, like help them with the follow-up," but that's so minimal, the number of tokens it basically doesn't matter.

Like if you add more tokens to the sales team, it probably won't change their output. If you add more humans to the sales team, it probably will. Meanwhile, engineering teams are pretty different, where engineering teams generally — it seems like you want people to own an outcome end-to-end, but then if you give them more tokens, they can produce a lot more.

And so it seems like there — and then there's a lot of kind of places in between, of like operations, finance, marketing. These are places where they're neither here nor there, where I think they're somewhere in between and it kind of depends on your business. But I think every business is going to have to ask: what is our core competency?

核心能力回归：披萨店不需要工程师

Something that we see a lot in the market — or we used to see, and now they finally kind of hit reality — what we used to see is, "Oh, like we're going to build our own software development agents." And we're like, "Okay, like you're a like a consumer uh logistics company, are you sure you want to do that?" Like, "Yeah yeah, we have to do this." And it's like, "Okay."

And then six months later it's like, "Wait, actually this is not a core competency for our business. We don't want to hire, you know, AI engineers to be doing this. Our core competency is, you know, consumer logistics. That's what we want to focus on."

And I think this is an opportunity for every business to double down on their core competency and what matters for them, and then procure externally whatever it is that doesn't matter for them. Like a trivial example of this is — I don't know — in the days of the early internet, you probably had to be a programmer to build a website. And like websites generally help if you're a pizza shop, cuz you want to have people come to your pizza shop, they want to be able to — or like whatever. At that time would you say it was a core competency of a pizza shop to have engineers? Like certainly not. That is kind of a byproduct of a brief moment in time. But then there were companies out there that helped you build a website, you don't need to be technical. And this is why we live in a world where like most pizza shops don't have an engineering department, which I think is probably a good thing.

Um, and I think similarly a lot of businesses have dealt with the reality of: if you want to do XYZ other thing, you have to bring in people of this type of role. But I think that's been like something you had to do, not because it's a core competency of the business. And allowing businesses to focus and double down on the things that they are best at, I think is going to be good for the consumers of their business.

And so I think we're just going to see a lot of ruthless refocusing on what actually matters. Um, which is going to be cool to see.

企业如何转型：全员黑客松 + 允许失败

On that — so you know, every company kind of has to go through this process of reinvention. You know, 10 or 20 years ago people talked about digital transformation. And I don't know if anybody's given it a buzz word now, but "AI transformation" something of that sort. Couple years ago you ran into a bunch of organizations that just weren't ready to deal with autonomous agents. Things you've seen your customers start to change — and so the question is, when you look at your customers as they kind of go up this maturity curve and sort of reinvent themselves for the future, um, any good tricks or techniques that you've seen them use to repot themselves a bit?

Yeah, I mean, I think um, surprisingly, like the companies that have been doing companywide hackathons really end up doing well. It seems relatively trivial, but just setting aside a day where everyone in the workforce is just like, "Build with AI." It really sets the tone and sets the pace.

So just give me a look —

I tried to force him to build stuff [laughter] with coding agents. It didn't go so well.

We'll work on it. We'll do after this.

You know, we gave it a great effort.

But that's it. Like, it literally just setting aside the time to do it. And like even if it fails miserably, like it's fine. And also like the orgs that are okay with failing.

Like it feels like there are some who are like, "We need to do it exactly right. But we need to make the right decision from day one." No, like you're going to make mistakes. Everyone is going to —

And the orgs who are kind of leaning into it and embracing it to a certain degree, I think, are succeeding. Like one of our largest customers is EY. EY is not necessarily known to be at the absolute frontier of AI. But I think for them, they were just like, "Look, this matters. There have been other transformations that we relate to. We're not going to be late to this. Like we're just going to go in. We might mess up." But like obviously respecting like SEC, the things that you're not allowed to mess up and put those aside —

But like —

Let's go and get our engineers to mess around and build this stuff and see where it breaks and understand what they like and what they don't like. Um, I think that really matters a lot in the ones that we're seeing succeed. And also the ones who are pretty bold in reinventing the processes that they've put in place, and just saying, "Hey, there's no sacred cows. Let's put this aside, try something out. If it doesn't work, we'll put that sacred cow right back."

Um, and I think that's been kind of a determining factor there. Um, and when it comes from within — if it comes from the board, probably not going to go well.

Yeah.

If it comes from within like the tech team or the ICs or the leadership, that's when we see it go better.

12 个月预测：从同步到 90% 异步 Token

Do you have any predictions for the most important changes that are going to happen in your space over the next call it 12 months?

A lot of AI consumption is going up like crazy, and everyone's super super excited because the revenue is going wild. Like a lot of this is synchronous usage. In other words, if everyone woke up sick tomorrow, like a lot of Claude Code usage would be zero, because it's all just, "Hey Claude Code" or "Hey Codex" or "Hey Droid," right?

I think in 12 to 24 months like 90% of tokens will be asynchronous tokens. So these are going to be, you know, Droids on their own autonomously being like, "Hey, here's some signal that I found from a customer. Let's go fix it or let's go create a first-pass solution to this."

And I think that is going to be where the real agent-native stuff begins, because right now we're still kind of in copilot mode. Like if you're going to an agent and say, "Hey, go do this for me," it is more agentic because it's not going to come back and ask you a ton, but it's still like you are kicking it off.

Like if you guys have ever been to Tesla's factories, which is one of the sources of inspiration for the name — it's just robotic arms everywhere going and doing stuff. Like it's not like there are people there going and, you know, attaching the widget to the thing. Um, and this idea of a "dark factory" where the lights are off and things are just happening — that is where software development is going.

That's kind of where the name came from is like — you know, Elon was always talking about "the factory is the machine that builds the machine."

Yeah.

And that's been something that we took to heart. Um, and I guess also that combined with his whole thing about how you're destined to become the opposite of your name.

Um, and in our case, you know, Factory becomes artisanal. It's kind of a good flip there.

乐观愿景：短期阵痛，长期解放

So what's your most optimistic version of the future both for Factory and for the world at large?

So I think short-term there's going to be a lot of turbulence, because I think a lot of companies have misallocated resources pretty poorly. There's been a lot of bloat. Um, and I think the correction that's going to happen there is going to be really painful for a lot of people. And I think that's something that I think every AI CEO should really bear much more responsibility than they currently are for. Um, and also figuring out ways to address and kind of ameliorate in some way, because this is something that is going to be very painful for a lot of people.

Now, I also have optimism that we can actually address that faster than we think. We just need to start now in terms of addressing that.

Now the longer term — and why I think this is a good thing, and why I don't believe at all like, you know, the BS that people are saying of, "Oh, engineers are going away" — generally there is a huge number of problems in the world, a large subset of those problems can be solved with software, a small subset of those problems are currently being solved with software.

And so in the short term this means that, okay, for a given problem that was over-allocated engineering resources, okay, we need to reallocate those. "Reallocate those" is a kind of cold way of saying some people are going to lose their jobs.

But I think the thing that's going to happen in the longer term is: we need engineers. Engineers are some of the best systems thinkers and the best problem solvers. And there are so many problems that can be solved with software that are not being solved with software. And so that means that we are going to take those engineers and have them go and solve problems that previously were not being solved. That is such a net good for the world, because again there are so many of these problems that we are not solving, and also there's so many problems that we are maybe solving but with really shitty software. And like this is going to enable people to solve it with incredible software.

And you know, the vision for Factory is that we are kind of the factory that allows them to go and build this incredible software to solve these different problems. And these problems range from things that are trivial to, you know, like government software typically is not very good, whether it's like DMV or IRS. Web — like all that stuff is generally a pretty poor experience. Um, we don't need to live like that. We can live in a world where all software is really fantastic.

Um, but also things like, you know, pharmaceutical research. Like so much that goes into solving diseases is not just like a biology problem. A lot of it requires the best software engineers in the world. And previously those problems haven't allocated the right dollars to attract the best engineers. But now because of what's happening, I think we will be much more closely allocated to like: these are the biggest problems, let's get the best minds and the best problem-solvers to solve that.

Um, I think it's kind of our job as an industry to do that relocation, reallocation as quickly as possible, so it's not 10 years but maybe like 6 months or a year.

收尾

Wonderful. Matan, I think the clarity and consistency of your vision over time has just always been very inspiring. And then just seeing how much you've grown as a leader and how much Factory has grown as a company, even since the last time we did this training data episode. It's truly all inspiring. So, thank you for joining us again to share what you're up to.

I appreciate it a lot. Thank you.

Thank you.

[music]

[music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、"付钱送客"是最反直觉的护城河建造术
Matan 最令人震惊的决定不是那些看似大胆的技术选择，而是主动把已经到手的 $2M 收入退回给客户。这在传统商业逻辑里近乎自杀——但它揭示了一个被大多数创业者忽视的**"信任的负熵原理"**：
在企业软件销售中，信任是一种熵增系统。一旦客户开始怀疑你的产品，衰减速度远快于建立速度。他实际上做的是**用现金购买未来的谈话权**——花 $2M 买下了"12 个月后我可以再次敲门"的期权。这种反向嫁妆式的操作，比任何 NPS 调查、任何 CS 团队都更能刻画一家公司的品格。
更深层的跨领域连接是：这个动作在物理学上等价于**"退火"（annealing）**——为了让系统跳出局部最优，你必须先主动提高能量、破坏眼前的稳定态。绝大多数创业公司卡在 $2M–$10M 之间死掉，恰恰是因为他们不敢做这种"负梯度动作"。
## 二、Harness 的悖论：多模型让系统更强，而不是更弱
这是整场对话里最反直觉、也最少被注意到的技术洞察。所有人的第一直觉都是"模型和执行框架协同设计（co-design）"会带来最佳性能——就像苹果的软硬件一体化

item.title: [Bits + Bips] The Stablecoin Rails War: Who Actually Wins?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、稳定币战争的真正战场：不是技术，而是"自我颠覆的意愿"

表面上这集在讨论 Stripe 收购 PayPal、Circle 被挑战、USDG 借 Robinhood 上位——听起来是产品与分发之争。但真正被反复触碰的隐藏结构是：PayPal 不是败给了技术，而是败给了自己的合规律师和董事会。Austin 说了一句极其耐人寻味的话——"PayPal chose to fail"。这不是竞争失败，这是主动选择的失败。

这里有一个反直觉的观察：在稳定币这个赛道，拥有最多用户的公司反而最难成功。因为用户越多、监管暴露越大、律师越保守、"母舰保护逻辑"越强。PYUSD 的失败不是产品失败，是组织免疫系统排斥新器官的故事。这也解释了为什么真正跑出来的往往是 Robinhood 这种"体量足够大能给分发、但小到还敢冒险"的中段玩家。

跨领域连接：这和生物学里的"体型-代谢-创新窗口"规律惊人一致。大象不能跳跃，不是因为它没肌肉，而是因为它的骨骼-质量比不允许。PayPal 的组织质量太大，反而失去了做稳定币最需要的那种"跳跃动作"。

二、开源中国模型 = AI 版的"稳定币时刻"，但方向反了

这集把 Kimi K2、DeepSeek 和稳定币讨论放在一集里绝非偶然——它们其实是同一个结构性事件的两面：基础设施的去溢价化。

一个让人意外的对照：美国前沿实验室现在的处境，正是 2022 年 Circle 眼睁睁看着 USDT 抢占市场的翻版——你更合规、更"负责任"、有更多护栏，结果对手直接把产品免费开源出来。David Sachs 引用的那个例子简直是黑色幽默：Hugging Face 想用美国模型分析真实的网络攻击载荷，被 guardrails 拒绝，只好切到中国 GLM——过度合规反而成了国家安全漏洞。

这里藏着一条更深的规律：任何试图通过"道德溢价"来收租的行业，最终都会被开源+新兴市场组合拳击穿。稳定币是这样，AI 是这样，未来量子计算大概率也是这样。Chris 顺口提到的"apps on quantum stacks"其实不是随口一说，而是同一个模式的第三次演出预告。

跨领域连接：这个模式在制药行业的仿制药冲击、汽车业丰田对底特律的降维打击、乃至印刷术打破教会的知识垄断中都出现过。每一次都是"高护栏方"低估了"低成本+高分发"的组合。

三、被所有人忽略的暗线：这一集其实是一部"内部人如何被自己组织出卖"的合集

如果你把这一集所有故事排成一列，会发现一个惊人的共同结构：

  • Riot 数据中心事件：被竞争币种资助的 Greenpeace 通过环保活动家操纵地方舆论
  • PayPal 的失败：内部想做事的人被合规和董事会挡住
  • Anthropic/OpenAI 的困境：自我施加的 guardrails 反而让中国模型接管了实用场景
  • Trump 加密项目的伦理麻烦：家族的 10 亿美元曝光成了 Clarity Act 通过的最大障碍
  • 国会议员交易个股 vs. 加密项目：Austin 的神来一笔——"如果国会议员不能做加密项目，为什么可以炒个股？"

这不是五个独立故事，而是同一种"内耗动力学"的五种表达：真正的敌人从来不是外部竞争者，而是组织内部那个"为了保护现状而牺牲未来"的机制。

一个出人意料的洞见：在快速变化的行业里，"合规成熟度"和"战略死亡率"呈正相关。这不是说合规不好，而是说当整个行业的底层技术在重写规则时，把力气花在优化旧规则上就是慢性自杀。PayPal 花了几年把 PYUSD 做成"区块链版 PayPal 余额"，而 Robinhood 直接把它做成"发钱给你用的收益产品"——一个把稳定币当成负债管理，一个把它当成用户获取工具。

跨领域连接：这和罗马晚期军团为什么打不过蛮族是同一个道理——不是罗马变弱了，而是它把太多资源花在维持既有秩序（护墙、边防、税制），最终连打仗的钱都没了。今天的 PayPal、Anthropic 的 guardrails 团队、以及那些花几百万请律师而不是给开发者付费的银行 stablecoin 联盟，都在演出这场戏的现代版。

But I don't know — I feel like there may be a comeback on the horizon. I remain hopeful because it's the right thing for the country. And a lot of these politicians will — you know, things get weird towards the end. We all know that. And I hope in the end, like even Senator Warner, who's a Democrat, had some generally positive things to say recently. So ethics is where it's at.

And will ethics ever be good enough for the Democrats vis-à-vis the president? No, they're going to continue to want to push it. But I'm very hopeful that we get something that's palatable. Because do you really want to be an individual who's heading into a very, very, very tight midterm race and you're on the run and you vote against something that sets fair shake and the crypto folks off?

If you're Schumer right now, you've got one thing on your mind. That's how do I get a majority? How do I respect control? And it all comes down to that electoral calculus. That's why if we get something to the floor, we get a vote on the books. That's where that electoral calculus comes into play. That's what I want to see. That's our best shot for succeeding. There were a couple of paths where we would have had a couple of shots on goal. I think we're down to one. I want to see it come to the floor.

Austin: So I'll say I agree on the one-shot-on-goal framing. We're going to get one good chance at this. And that's really all we're going to get given the timing. That's certainly true. I think you're right that ethics is where the rubber meets the road. I want to be clear and say the following: I think the BRCA — there's a place to get to yes from the Democrats on a bill that is actually good. I think as they've gotten more up to speed on it, they've realized some of the lines they were being fed were probably not totally accurate. If you look closely at things like Tornado Cash and the DOJ and FinCEN literally disagreeing with each other, we do need clarity on how these things work — pun not intended.

I think that's solvable. I think on the yield compromise, if I'm being honest, the big banks have alienated so many people now they've just moved on. That's over.

Ram: They haven't moved on. They want clarity. They want clarity badly.

Austin: Well, now they want clarity because they've realized if they don't get it, they're stuck with Genius, which is even more permissive than what they were —

Ram: It's more than that though, Austin. They want clarity because of federal preemption. They do not operate well in state-regulated things.

Austin: See Illinois slapping a transfer tax that doesn't work on crypto, right?

Ram: They want federal preemption. They're going to press the throttle down. We get this bill, you're going to see banks come in. We get this bill, you're going to see Basel start looking better. And then once we have bank liquidity, it's a brand new world for crypto.

Austin: And to the electoral math, I actually think one of the things that could be helping the bill that people have not thought about is how badly the Democrats seem to be doing picking functional candidates in Maine and Michigan. By which I mean, if the Republicans are looking at it and being like, "we like the territory, we're going to play offense not defense," they may force a vote for that exact reason.

I think the key to getting it through is going to be: can we get an ethics provision that is stiff enough that the administration probably doesn't like it, that the Democrats will vote for, but is not so stiff that somebody is going to throw their body in front of it to stop it? There is some sort of pivot point there. And to me, Chris, you tell me if you disagree — I think that efficient balance is probably forcing the Trump family out of their crypto endeavors, but without punishing them for things they did before the ethics guardrails were in place.

Chris: I haven't seen the text. I know blind trust will have something to do with it. Yep. You hate to have individuals specifically targeted for any political reason whatsoever. It needs to apply to both sides. I hope they compromise. And then if we have something good on the ethics side, well, let's adopt it for every other market because we have equal problems there.

Austin: I was going to say that may be the other playback from the Democrats that I do think would be helpful — is if congresspeople can't run individual crypto projects, why are they trading individual stocks?

Chris: All right. Yes, sir.

收尾

Austin: So on that note, we will know in a couple of weeks whether Clarity is going to move or not. But for this week, today, we are out of time. So thank you as always for joining us for Bits and Bips.

One last reminder before you go — Bits and Bips has its own channels now. The old feed won't carry these episodes anymore. Subscribe so you don't miss a single one. Now, thank you for joining us. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding.

Until then, everyone — thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

## 一、稳定币战争的真正战场：不是技术，而是"自我颠覆的意愿"
表面上这集在讨论 Stripe 收购 PayPal、Circle 被挑战、USDG 借 Robinhood 上位——听起来是产品与分发之争。但真正被反复触碰的隐藏结构是：**PayPal 不是败给了技术，而是败给了自己的合规律师和董事会**。Austin 说了一句极其耐人寻味的话——"PayPal chose to fail"。这不是竞争失败，这是**主动选择的失败**。
这里有一个反直觉的观察：**在稳定币这个赛道，拥有最多用户的公司反而最难成功**。因为用户越多、监管暴露越大、律师越保守、"母舰保护逻辑"越强。PYUSD 的失败不是产品失败，是**组织免疫系统排斥新器官**的故事。这也解释了为什么真正跑出来的往往是 Robinhood 这种"体量足够大能给分发、但小到还敢冒险"的中段玩家。
跨领域连接：这和生物学里的**"体型-代谢-创新窗口"**规律惊人一致。大象不能跳跃，不是因为它没肌肉，而是因为它的骨骼-质量比不允许。PayPal 的组织质量太大，反而失去了做稳定币最需要的那种"跳跃动作"。

item.title: [a16z] American Dynamism Presents
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、三个"下潜"：硅谷正在从平面撤回 Z 轴

三段发言看似跨越海洋、矿业、核能三个毫不相关的领域，但如果把它们叠在同一张坐标系上，你会看到一个惊人的方向性一致——它们全部在往"Z 轴"走：Ulysses 向下潜入海底，Moriana 向下钻入地壳，微反应堆则把人类反向（深空）投射。过去二十年硅谷把力气花在 X-Y 平面上的"信息流铺展"（社交、SaaS、消费应用），而 American Dynamism 这批公司在做的其实是同一件事的镜像：放弃平面，重新征服深度。这不是"硬科技回归"这么简单——这是硅谷第一次公开承认，抽象层已经吃到了天花板。

二、隐藏的产业三角：这三家公司其实是一个闭环

大多数人把它看作 a16z "投了三个不同赛道"，但它们其实构成一个自洽的工业环路，出人意料地相互喂养：

  • 微反应堆需要铀和稀土 → Moriana 挖
  • 深海多金属结核矿床需要 24/7 水下自动化作业 → Ulysses 潜
  • 自主水下机器人集群需要长时供电与离岸能源 → 微反应堆供

换句话说，你以为这是"分散配置"，其实是一盘垂直整合的棋——一个不依赖现有石化-电网-港口体系的平行工业基础层。这个视角一旦打开，你会发现这不是三家公司，而是一个尚未命名的"新工业操作系统"的三个原生模块。

三、语言的秘密：他们全部跳过了"产品"，直接讲"文明"

一个几乎没人注意的细节：这三位创始人没有一个人提到客户、市场、收入或产品功能。Turner 说的是"整个行业"；微反应堆创始人直接跳到"人类作为文明离开出生的恒星"。这是一种典型的目的论式路演（teleological pitching）——不卖功能，卖必然性。

跨领域联想：这种语言结构与其说像科技创业路演，不如说更像 19 世纪的铁路大亨宣言，甚至像宗教劝进书。它标志着一次语义转向：核能不再是"清洁电力"，而是"星际移民技术"；矿业不再是"大宗商品"，而是"文明基础设施"；水下机器人不再是"作业工具"，而是"海洋神经系统"。当一个行业开始用这种终末论口吻说话，通常意味着资本正在为它准备一个远超当下市场规模的估值框架。

一个反直觉的收尾观察

有趣的是，"American Dynamism"这个词本身就在暗示：美国正在把创新的语法从"颠覆（disruption）"换成"动能（dynamism）"。前者是破坏性的、面向存量的；后者是牛顿式的、面向真空的。这不只是词汇变化——它意味着这波公司默认前方是空的（海底、地壳、太空），不需要打败谁，只需要率先抵达。这是一种极其罕见的、类似"新大陆心态"的投资叙事，上一次出现是 1990 年代的互联网。

📝 转录文本

Ulysses — Underwater Robotics

We started Ulysses 3 years ago in the effort to build underwater robots to solve a very specific problem.

The broader vision of what we're doing is that you have a network of surface and undersea vehicles, and they're operating 24/7 to solve these critical tasks all around the ocean.

Moriana Minerals — Modernizing the Minerals Industry

There's this minerals industry that no one has yet really taken today's modern technologies and applied it holistically to the industry. And so we see a bunch of opportunity to go and attack it.

My name is Turner Caldwell. I'm the CEO of Moriana Minerals.

Nuclear Micro Reactors — Leaving Our Star

Nuclear micro reactors that are mass produced, that are reliable in the most wild scenario, enables humans to leave the star that we were born at — the sun — and go to other ones.

And it's imperative that we do it as a civilization.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The Institutions Holding Off WWIII – Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：和平的建筑师，是被战争碾碎的一代

Paine 在这里悄悄埋了一个心理学的炸弹——UN、IMF、NATO、WTO、EU 这些今天被视为"精英俱乐部"的国际机构，其实是一群创伤最深的人在集体 PTSD 里搭出来的避难所。他们一战被送去越壕沟，大萧条中养家，二战又把自己的孩子送上前线。三次死亡循环之后，他们得出的结论不是"要更强的军队"，而是"要更多的律师和外交官"。

这里藏着一个让人后背发凉的推论：当一代人没有经历过体系性的崩溃，他们就会开始厌倦维持体系的成本。 今天欧美对多边机构的疲惫、对"规则"的嘲讽，本质上不是政治问题，而是代际记忆的自然衰减。Putin 之所以敢动手，某种程度上是因为记得战壕的人全死光了。

跨领域连接：陆权 vs 海权 = Web2 平台 vs Web1 割据

Paine 说陆权玩的是"负和游戏"——你抢邻居的地，抢的过程中把地打烂了。这套逻辑在数字时代有个精确的镜像：封闭生态 vs 开放协议。

  • 陆权 = 苹果生态 / 微信小程序 / 抖音闭环：控制你能触达的每一寸"领土"，通过内部通信线（interior lines）榨取租金。
  • 海权 = TCP/IP / 集装箱 / SWIFT：不控制节点，只控制协议。任何人接入都能受益，网络效应产生正和增长。

更妙的是，Paine 提到"maritime powers 通过 exterior lines 触达全球"——这几乎是平台经济学的地缘政治版本。海洋国家不是征服海洋，而是把海洋做成了低摩擦的交易层（transaction layer）。今天美国跟中国的真正竞争，不在于谁的芯片更快，而在于谁的"海"更多人愿意航行——美元、SWIFT、英语、普通法、云计算，都是这片"海"的组成部分。

出人意料的暗线：乌克兰战争其实是 Mackinder 的"复仇"

结尾处 Paine 一句话轻轻带过——冷战的热战都发生在"Mackinder 内边缘新月带"（Intermarginal Crescent）——海权与陆权的摩擦生热带。但如果你打开地图看：乌克兰正好躺在这条新月带的最中央。

这里有个让人不安的洞见：Putin 打的不是乌克兰，他打的是"新月带的物理属性"。 只要地球还是这个形状，只要黑海还在那儿，只要顿巴斯的黑土还能通粮食走管道，这场战争的地理逻辑就会一次次地重演——不管沙皇、苏联还是俄联邦在克里姆林宫。

更深的一层反转：Paine 暗示，冷战期间"全球增长率上不去"不是因为技术不够，而是因为陆海两派都在新月带"按秤盘"——一方按下去，另一方按下去，秤永远不平，但秤上的东西一直在被消耗。这解释了一个经济学长期困惑的现象：为什么 1945-1990 年的技术革命（半导体、抗生素、喷气机）没能带来匹配的经济起飞？答案可能不是"技术不够好"，而是"新月带的血在偷偷抽走复利"。

一个衍生的、几乎无人讨论的推论：今天 AI 革命的经济回报，很可能同样会被下一轮陆海冲突的"新月带征税"稀释掉。 台海就是新的顿巴斯。

📝 转录文本

The End of Cold War I: A Miracle of Our Lifetimes

Uh, if you look at the end of the last Cold War, too — sadly we're into the second one — but look at how world trade just takes off. It was a miracle of your lifetimes. It lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty.

Uh, the problem for the likes of Putin is that this wealth-producing trade was not happening at his house, but the houses of those vested in the trading order, not in extortion. But with the second Cold War, we're into more inefficient things again.

Interior vs. Exterior Lines: The Third Distinguishing Characteristic

All right, this brings me to the third distinguishing characteristic of continental and maritime powers. And it has to do with the transportation revolution.

So, continental powers historically have leveraged interior lines of communication that allow them to garrison their empire, deploy their armies against neighbors, and then to form a contiguous alliance system. And that worked well when uh, power was a function of land. Well, that's not true anymore.

The maritime powers uh, are using these exterior lines of communication, the ones by sea, to give them access not just to the people right next to them, but to the entire globe — which opens the possibility for them to form a global alliance system. And from this reliance on interior versus uh, exterior lines of communication, it gives you the possibility of what sort of alliance systems that you can have.

The Industrial Revolution Puts Continental Empires on Notice

All right, the industrial revolution put uh, continental empires on notice. Not simply because land transport is so much uh, more expensive than sea transport, but but but because it opened the possibility of a positive-sum world order.

The land empire MO of beating up all your neighbors — well, it's negative-sum. What do I mean by that? Is you're fighting over territory, you're damaging the goods while you're fighting. So, whatever someone lost in pristine territory now looks like this. And it's negative sum. You're destroying wealth at a very rapid clip.

Whereas, the maritime world is: "No, boys. Don't do it that way. You want to have trading partners. You want to have it win-win. So, everybody makes money. So, we have compounded growth." And this maritime order is focusing on freedom of navigation, free trade, international laws and institutions that facilitate trade in order to minimize transaction costs so we can maximize the money.

Alliances as the Ultimate Insurance Policy

And the insurance system for all of this is alliance system. So, most countries aren't maritime by geography. But if they all gang up together and they coordinate diverse instruments of national power when they're dealing with these rogue continental states that want to upend the trading system, they can turn out in force to protect the rules that protect them all.

And here's the ultimate insurance policy that was created by the greatest generation — which were the conscripts of World War I. The people who were told to go up and over trenches and to see how that would go. And the ones who survived came back and tried to raise their families during the Great Depression. And then by the time they were of the age to be strategic leaders, they're off sending their own kids to fight World War II.

And they concluded — and this is, this generation is in Europe and the United States both — they concluded that the solution to Great Depressions and World Wars was institution building on a global scale. And they built institutions that have lasted to the present and held the peace, until in the industrialized world until Vladimir Putin decided to word cuz magic.

But they create the UN, the IMF, NATO, the predecessor institutions of the World Trade Organization, and also of the the European Union. And their idea is: we must hash out our differences with diplomats and lawyers, cuz when you send the soldiers in, whatever gains you think you're going to get are going to be inferior to what you would have done with the diplomats. It's — it's too ruinous fighting each other.

The Cold War's Hot Edge: Mackinder's Intermarginal Crescent

All right. So, if you look at where the fighting that did go on in the Cold War — cuz it was cold in the industrialized world, but it was really hot elsewhere. A lot of it's on this Mackinder's Intermarginal Crescent, which is where the maritime and continental worlds hit.

So, if there's civil wars going on in there, uh the one side of the Cold War wants to put its finger on the scale, and the other one wants to put its finger on the scale, and there we go. And that is all wealth-destroying, and helps explain why growth rates and things weren't as uh — or globally had problems — cuz you're destroying wealth. All right.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here, and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [YC Root Access] The First Dedicated YC GPU Cluster - With Together AI
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏的角色反转：YC 正在变成"算力工会"

这场对话表面在讲 GPU 集群，真正发生的却是 YC 商业模式的一次静默突变。Jared 自己点破了那个关键词——"founders union"（创始人工会）。这不是修辞。传统 VC 卖的是"钱 + 建议 + 网络"，而 YC 现在开始卖 集体议价权：用 8000+ 组合公司的规模去谈一个单个 seed 阶段公司永远拿不到的算力合约。

这背后的对标不是任何一家 VC，而是——医疗行业里的 GPO（Group Purchasing Organization）。医院联合起来集中采购药品和器械，因为单个医院议价能力太弱。YC 在做的事情结构上一模一样，只不过采购的是 H100 而不是心脏支架。一旦这个类比成立，你会预感到：下一步 YC 大概率会把这套"集采模式"扩展到能源合约、数据标注、甚至合成生物学的湿实验室时间。VC 正在悄悄变成一个 共享基础设施运营商。

二、最反直觉的观察：AI 公司正在"反向变成制药公司"

Vipul 顺口提到自己 2018 年做的是 pharma 公司，Jared 顺势说"现在连保险、医疗都成了软件公司"。但对话里没人点破的是——方向是双向的。

软件行业过去 20 年最大的骄傲是"零边际成本"：写一次代码卖一亿次。但你仔细听 Vipul 说的那句话："compute is going to be the biggest expense in some ways for development and product。" 这句话在传统 SaaS 语境里是荒谬的——研发成本怎么可能是最大开支？可如果把它翻译成 pharma 语言，就完全自然了：训练一个模型 ≈ 一次三期临床试验；FLOPS ≈ 试剂消耗；GPU cluster ≈ pilot plant。

于是我们看到一个惊人的对称： - 传统行业（保险、医疗）在软件化，从资本密集走向零边际成本 - AI 原生公司在制药化，从零边际成本重新走向资本密集

"软件吃世界"这句话在 2026 年正在被改写为"世界重新吃软件"。而 YC 的这次动作，本质上是承认了这个转向——它开始像 Big Pharma 的 CDMO（合同开发生产组织）一样为 portfolio 提供共享"生产设备"。

三、被忽略的定价曲线：Jevons 悖论在 AI 里正在爆发

Vipul 说了一句技术味道很浓的话，但含义远超技术："as models get better, the value of tokens is increasing, which has an impact on the value of flops."

这句话的经济学翻译是：算力不但没有因摩尔定律而变便宜，反而因为下游价值提升而变得越来越贵。这是 19 世纪煤炭经济学里的 Jevons 悖论——效率提升不减少消耗，反而放大消耗，因为每一单位的算力现在能变现更多。

跨领域连接：这跟纽约地租的逻辑完全一样。曼哈顿的写字楼没有变得更"好用"，是华尔街的产出让每一平方英尺的租金水涨船高。GPU 集群正在成为 AI 产业的"曼哈顿地产"——供给曲线几乎垂直，需求曲线在无限上移。

于是隐藏的商业洞见浮出水面：Together AI + YC 这个合作最有价值的部分不是"便宜的 GPU"，而是"把 24 个月的地租承诺切成几周的短租"。他们在算力市场里发明了 WeWork 模式——只不过 WeWork 输在了办公空间需求缩水，而算力需求还在指数级扩张，所以这次"WeWork for GPUs"可能真的会成。

四、一个可能被低估的信号

留意 Jared 提到的一个具体数字："公司为下两年算力所需的预付款 超过了它们当前的现金余额。" 这不是一句轻描淡写的话——这意味着一大批 AI 原生 startup 在传统资本结构下 数学上不可能存在。YC 这次实际上是在用组合基金的信用给单个 startup 做算力层的债务证券化。

如果这个模式跑通，下一步逻辑上必然出现——GPU-backed securities（算力资产支持证券）。就像 2000 年代的按揭证券化一样，会有人把"未来 GPU 使用权"打包成金融产品在二级市场交易。你今天在这条 YC 播客里看到的，可能是一个全新资产类别的胚胎。

📝 转录文本

Intro

[music] Hey everyone, I'm here with Vipul, CEO and co-founder of Together AI, and we've got some exciting news. YC and Together are partnering to bring online the first dedicated YC GPU cluster. This gives our portfolio of AI-native startups easier access to the compute they need to build and scale.

Vipul, thanks for being here.

So great to be here.

What Together AI Does

Vipul, why don't you start by telling us a bit about Together AI. What exactly do you guys do?

Yeah. So, you know, we started the company almost exactly four years ago and, as you know, my co-founders are professors and academics, and we were quite convinced at the time that generative AI was going to be a very foundational technology. And I think we also had a sense that, because of the capital structure required, we may see large concentration, and we really wanted to create a platform for innovation — for, you know, the sort of participatory side of Together.

So what we've built at Together AI is really a cloud service that's designed for the whole life cycle of generative AI, which is everything from building models to post-training open models to serving them at scale.

Who Uses Together

Nice. And could you tell us a little bit about how companies actually work with you? You know, YC — we acquired the first GPU cluster for YC itself to share to our companies. Tell us a little bit about the types of companies that have worked with Together in the past.

Yeah, you know, our focus is really on AI-native startups, and we have over 8,000 customers today. And this ranges from, you know, small research groups who are sort of still figuring out what they want to do and experimenting — and this is just such an empirical field that we enable them with access to compute or access to inference services — all the way to some of the biggest names like Cursor and Cognition and 11 Labs. And these companies are training models, and we're serving their models at scale for them.

Yeah. One of the really incredible things from my perspective over the last year has been all the different types of what we would call AI-native startups that have been built, right? You have companies that are training their own models from scratch, where they're now able to use this GPU cluster to get access to compute, right? Especially in this environment.

You have AI-native services companies that are often building on top of models and increasingly building on top of open-source models hosted at places like Together. And then you have kind of everything in between, from data providers to application-layer companies. So there's this whole landscape of companies in the YC portfolio, and they all have kind of very heterogeneous compute needs. And so I think for us, having a partner where there's different ways to work with you guys has been a big win for a lot of companies.

Yeah. And I think that flexibility is particularly important because you're trying to be efficient with your capital, and being able to deploy it behind the workloads you want — and you want really rapid sort of iteration. I think we have sort of really helped create a platform that allows companies to be able to do all these things efficiently.

Building an AI-Native Company Today

Building a company in today's AI-native world is quite different, I imagine, from the days you started your company.

Uh, what are you seeing? What do you think are the main challenges that YC startups are experiencing?

Yeah, I think there's a bunch of different ones all at once. It's a very exciting time at YC. I think one of the really cool things is way more things look like software companies now than ever before. Like when I ran my company, we were a pharma company — this was back in 2018. At the time, saying that you were a software-first pharma company was sort of an absurd concept.

Now I think it is actually very common to think of industries in which things you don't necessarily think of as software companies — whether it's insurance or healthcare or pharma or whatever else — are software companies for the first time. Which expands just the pie of things that people might work on in Y Combinator.

At the same time, it means there's whole new challenges. Right, there's whole new industries in which people are facing bottlenecks that they didn't face before. So on compute — right, one of the things that's very different, you know, eight years ago when I was running my company, we could just like go to AWS and get a thousand, you know, instances with GPUs, and yeah, they were like maybe expensive or whatever, but it wasn't that hard to get them. Like, you could get them, and you can get them on spot instances, and we don't have to do long reservations and whatnot.

I think now what we see is, as people's compute needs go up, actually just having access to capacity is a really big problem — let alone great pricing. And I think, you know, for us, with this partnership, being able to secure capacity, secure it at a really great price, have great support also available, and make it so startups don't have to commit to two years — they only have to commit to a few weeks, right? Makes it so that for startups that have these heterogeneous computes, you can kind of solve for that.

And so it kind of solves for this bottleneck that can help them access all of these weird new markets that are now for the first time software problems.

Compute as a Fund-Level Differentiator

And do you see this becoming a differentiator from the perspective of the fund? It is becoming harder and harder, and I feel as models are getting better, right, the value of tokens that are being produced is increasing, which sort of has an impact on the value of flops and the cost of compute. And you may have this curve of, you know, ever-expanding cost of compute. So finding ways of enabling companies seems important.

Absolutely. Especially because, you know, YC has become probably the biggest seed funder of research-style companies. You know, probably the very first real machine learning seed investment was literally OpenAI.

Uh, OpenAI was built as YC Research.

Um, when Sam was president here. And then since then we've funded all sorts of companies developing their own models in a bunch of different verticals. There's companies like Deepgram making voice AI models. There's companies that are then distributing those and building their own companies, like Vapi for example, or Retell — voice AI companies. There's a new one called Miso Labs — just launched a few weeks ago — that has an incredible new emotive voice model.

In other domains, like in language, you have companies building new edge device models or different variants of model architectures that aren't the ones that are currently already being scaled up. And then you have this whole long chain of other modalities in which people are doing research, whether it's in biology or in healthcare or kind of you name it.

And so I think what's really exciting right now — and actually I didn't even say anything about hard tech, where there's actually tons of interesting robotics companies that we're funding these days. And with a lot of these, um, they are research bets. They are not companies where we expect them to commercialize in significant ways immediately. They're ones where they have to solve a hard technical problem, and access to compute ends up being a big bottleneck for a lot of them.

And so yeah, we very much see securing access to compute as a really important thing — to attract the best founders to do, and then also to enable them to succeed both during the program and afterwards. Like what's great is companies can get on this cluster, or you know, our future ones, basically during the batch, and then continue to grow with whatever their compute provider is for a very long time.

Yeah, yeah. And we are definitely seeing that. It's been pretty exciting to track the journey of some of these companies that we've onboarded.

Why Together for the Partnership

What was it about Together that led you to do this partnership with us?

[YC's next batch is now taking applications. Got a startup in you? Apply at ycombinator.com/apply. It's never too early, and filling out the app will level up your idea. Okay, [music] back to the video.]

There was a few things. Um, one is we really prioritize speed. I think being able to work with a partner who is excited to get a cluster up really fast, and then also build it in a way that works with startups with lots of different needs.

You know, we have some companies who are just looking for a single node and they just want access now, but they're in the scaling mode where you could totally see them becoming a lot bigger. There's others who are buying 256 GPUs on day one and looking to scale to several thousand very soon. And being able to offer a product that actually supports all of those use cases was a big ask.

And then the second was having a great engineering and research team that could help actually enable the best practices in these companies. You know, a lot of the founders — they have really great engineering backgrounds. They have trained models in other places where there's been managed compute available to them. They haven't necessarily had to manage their own compute cluster. And so having a partner that can help with just showing the ropes, so that, um, yeah, of course there's a lot that's managed by Together directly, there's some parts that the founder themselves need to figure out, but they can make it so it's not a zero-to-one right away, right? And there's a lot of best practices to encode. I think that was a big part of it.

And then I will say, like, just lastly personally, I've actually followed a lot of the research from Together for many years. Like I'm friends with Ce and I've, you know, seen some of the work that they've put out in research papers in the past.

Research and Product

And so actually maybe something I'd be curious if you want to share a little bit more about — like how do you guys think about all of your research efforts, you know, work like FlashAttention for example, and all the other work you guys do, and how that fits into your product offering. Like how do you balance those two things and how do companies benefit from that?

When we founded Together, we felt that there was going to be quite a bit of research and effort that's going to go into making models better — you know, reducing loss and building better and better models. And there was this entire space of production AI, which — it's a science and it was understudied, and it's really kind of, you know, linear algebra executing in these novel accelerators. It's a new form of computer science, and we felt it was going to be very important, because this is a very, very scaled endeavor, and [snorts] you are deploying large amounts of capital. The cost of training and the cost of producing tokens is very high, and you want to make it really efficient.

So a lot of our research has focused on AI systems — from, you know, approaches to doing attention, and that continues to be a really sort of rich field, as now, you know, attention is going after longer and longer context — to, you know, architectures. We also did work on the Mamba architecture, which is now making its way into, you know, long-context attention like in the Nemotron.

I was going to say that the latest Nemotron models also seem to use it, right?

Yeah. And compilers. And so this is a very interesting and productive area of research for us, and for the companies that work with us, because we can accelerate their workloads, make them generally achieve the best unit economics possible on these workloads. And that's really — it's very useful to early startups, but then also the scaled ones who care a lot about the economics of their applications.

Preparing for the Compute Shortage

Yeah. I was going to ask you on that latter point — like, you know, when you think about a lot of the research companies you've worked with, you've seen a lot of them scale on Together platform. What should early-stage companies who are starting to use the Together cluster or a different compute provider think about now to prepare for what's coming, both in terms of the compute shortage and how to sort of set themselves up for success as their company starts to work and get product-market fit?

Yeah, you know, there's so much infrastructure now, right, relative to even a couple of years ago. From really frontier-class open models that are accessible, there's so much machinery and [clears throat] tooling for, you know, training models, post-training them. There's rich sources of data sets. So I think you can be incredibly efficient in terms of kind of using this machinery and deploying it, and, you know, we do see many of the YC startups we're working with are very proficient with the current set of tools that exist.

I think the compute planning is definitely something that — it's complex, right? When you are a seed-stage company, you have a certain amount of capital and your sort of perspective of what you're going to do with it is very different from, you know, once you get to a next level of scale. And so I think part of what we are trying to do is build products and price and package them in ways that allow companies to be able to scale up to the next stage. And I think some of the collaborations that we are doing are going to be sort of essential in, you know, helping companies underwrite. And I think this is where companies are very different from software companies — because you really have to think about this is going to be the biggest expense in some ways for development and product.

Yeah, yeah. I mean, I think a big challenge we see — and I think we saw it before, having what really motivated setting up this cluster, was a lot of companies… just to put into numbers, you know, the upfront they would need to pay in order to secure the capacity for their next two years of compute was greater than their current cash balance. And so you just could not do that unless you go and raise and basically put all of your money into a compute partner.

And so a big thing we look to solve with this is, you know, use some of YC's scale so that we can secure access to that compute, so an individual startup doesn't have to make a 24-month bet. They can make a few-month bet instead, which is much more doable with access to capital dollars in the way they currently flow. And so they can kind of continuously scale and not have to lock up all their cash basically, and make it so, you know, they raise at more effective terms for themselves.

Feedback From the Portfolio

Yeah, yeah, absolutely. What is the kind of feedback that you're hearing from these companies?

Oh, it's been great. I mean, I think — well, what's very cool is, you know, there's lots of different companies who have different needs. You know, some with training clusters versus inference clusters. I think they've really loved working with your guys' support team to build the right kind of workflows to work really well and understand the kind of realistic underlying compute setups to actually have really good performance and availability.

And then we've made it so that they can sort of book in advance, and now companies can plan out their compute several months in advance, which has been very helpful for them, where some of them might know that they need to do a big training run three months from now, and they can choose to buy a relatively small amount of compute for a while and then a much larger amount. And that flexibility is great for them.

And, you know, across the portfolio of companies, there's still enough to service all the demand at all times. So the cluster is at 100% utilization, but for any individual company who doesn't have, you know, a fixed utilization, it's really helpful to have this sort of lever they can pull and plan out in advance.

Looking Forward

Yeah, yeah. I'm really looking forward to expanding this. I think it's working. It's been a very creative way of solving this problem, and I think it's working really well. And I think this is going to become essential to startups who are thinking about creating AI products.

Yeah, I think you're going to be hearing from me quite a lot about how we can make this thing even bigger. I think in general, you know, at YC, we think of ourselves as sort of a founders union. You know, I think a lot of how we — what we push to do is, regardless of how someone's building technology, whether it's a research company or an application company or whatever else, is to give the shared resources to allow the founder to have a lot of the leverage that a much bigger company might have — whether that's in terms of raising capital and having things like Demo Day to support that, or a GPU cluster in the way that a bigger company might have, or access to certain advisors or whatever else. And, um, yeah, I'm excited to bring compute as one of the levers we can pull to kind of enable that for people.

I'm really excited for where this is going to go.

Awesome.

Cool. Thanks so much for coming. This is going to be awesome, and excited to keep working with you guys.

Thanks for having me.

[music] >> [music]

item.description:
## 一、隐藏的角色反转：YC 正在变成"算力工会"
这场对话表面在讲 GPU 集群，真正发生的却是 **YC 商业模式的一次静默突变**。Jared 自己点破了那个关键词——"founders union"（创始人工会）。这不是修辞。传统 VC 卖的是"钱 + 建议 + 网络"，而 YC 现在开始卖 **集体议价权**：用 8000+ 组合公司的规模去谈一个单个 seed 阶段公司永远拿不到的算力合约。
这背后的对标不是任何一家 VC，而是——**医疗行业里的 GPO（Group Purchasing Organization）**。医院联合起来集中采购药品和器械，因为单个医院议价能力太弱。YC 在做的事情结构上一模一样，只不过采购的是 H100 而不是心脏支架。一旦这个类比成立，你会预感到：**下一步 YC 大概率会把这套"集采模式"扩展到能源合约、数据标注、甚至合成生物学的湿实验室时间**。VC 正在悄悄变成一个 **共享基础设施运营商**。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"现金流反转"：芯片与云厂的角色互换

视频里最容易被一带而过、但其实最锋利的一张图，是那条紫线（半导体未来12月现金流冲到4500亿美元）与黄线（超大规模云厂现金流从3000亿跌向近零）的十字交叉。

这不是普通的板块轮动，而是产业链话语权的一次结构性倒置。过去十年，云厂是"甲方"，芯片厂被采购、被压价；现在的图景变成——云厂正在把自己所有的自由现金流"倒进"芯片厂的口袋里。用生态学的比喻，这不是共生，是寄主与寄生虫的暂时性反转：芯片是宿主，云厂是被抽干的宿主。

出人意料的推论：市场担心"大科技会不会砍资本开支"，其实问反了方向。真正应该焦虑的是——当云厂现金流真的归零，谁来接盘下一轮资本开支？ 现在托底的是"未来AI收入"这张远期支票。这张支票的兑付节点，恰好就是主播提到的"Google Agentic Commerce落地"。所以谷歌财报的关键根本不在capex数字，而在C端AI变现的第一声硬币落地声。

二、Russell 2000的"身份漂移"：一个指数正在悄悄背叛自己

主播提到罗素2000因为里面的AI权重股（如Bloom Energy）大跌而拖累整个指数，这句话背后藏着一个指数认同危机：

罗素2000被投资界作为"小盘股、市场风险偏好、经济健康度"的代理指标使用了三十年。但现在它已经不再代表小盘股情绪——它代表的是"AI基础设施的能源边角料"。

这有点像语言学里的"语义漂移"——"gay"这个词一百年前意思是"欢快的"，现在几乎没人这样用了。指数也在经历同样的过程：同样的名字，实际所指已经变了。

跨领域连接：这与生物学的"生态位替代（Niche Displacement）"惊人相似——一个物种占据某个生态位的名号还在，但里面已经被入侵物种偷偷替换掉了。如果你还在用罗素2000做"小盘/宏观风险"的判断，你实际上是在读一份被篡改过的地图。 真正代表美国小微企业情绪的指标，可能反而藏在等权标普里那条"横着走的线"里——那条线才是真正"没有AI叙事加持的美国经济体温计"。

三、英特尔的"隐形悖论"：越基本面向好，市场越不给面子

主播用了很克制的一句话："我只能看到英特尔的基本面在变得越来越好，无非就是价格贵和便宜。"

这句话里藏着一个反直觉的现象：在AI叙事主导的市场里，基本面改善反而不是最强的股价催化剂。为什么？因为当整个市场的定价机器被"故事完整性"（narrative coherence）驱动时，一个有多条平行叙事线、每条都不算最锋利的公司（英特尔同时讲代工/CPU/封装/美国制造/新CEO），反而不如只讲一根线但讲到极致的公司（英伟达=AI训练算力）值钱。

这在心理学里叫"分类流畅性偏差（Categorical Fluency Bias）"——人类大脑对"一句话能讲清"的东西估值更高。英特尔的悲剧不在于业务不好，而在于它"太丰富所以难以被一句话总结"。

由此推出一个反直觉的操作洞察：主播反复强调的"大科技持仓可以稍高一些更安全"，其实和他对英特尔的判断构成了同一枚硬币的两面——当叙事拥挤时，避险不是去买"没故事"的公司，而是去买"故事最粗的那根"。这与传统"高PE=风险"的教科书直觉正好相反。真正的杠杆压缩（台湾杠杆ETF已跌去22年那种幅度）不发生在故事最弱的地方，反而发生在故事线最集中的芯片板块——这才是市场当前最深的一层不对称。

📝 转录文本

开场与市场概览

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场奉选小陶。

今天期内容首先我们回顾一下7月份到现在为止市场的这个走势，包括截止到上周五看一下市场的参与度，看一下CNN的恐慌贪婪指数，主要就是给市场把个脉；然后我们看一下FactSet数据对于第二季度财报的一些指引；最后我对于本周将要发布财报的一些公司稍微去做一个展望和聊一下，包括特斯拉、包括英特尔，好吗？

那我就废话不多说，直接开始今天内容。在开始之前，大家记得留言点赞加转发。我在上周四还是上周三的时候接受了168X 他们这个频道的一个采访，那个采访差不多一个多小时吧，大家感兴趣的话可以登录我的一个X，关注我的X账号，然后在X账号上面可以去看一下那段采访的一篇总结。其实是一个比较好的方式了解一下我对于下半年市场的这个看法，包括现在当下的一个仓位，好吗？

一、7月份至今各类资产走势（QTD）

看一下QTD，就是从7月份到现在为止资产价格的走势：

  • 美元小幅下跌
  • 美债收益率：两年期几乎是没有动的，也就是市场对于加息和降息这个预期整个7月份是没有动的；但是长端这一块上涨的幅度比较大，十年期上涨了8个基点，TLT下跌了2.2%
  • 美股：三大指数都出现了下跌。道指其实几乎没有下跌，跌0.3%；标普下跌的幅度也比较小 2.6%（注：应为约0.6%）；但纳指下跌的幅度最大 2.6%
  • 芯片板块从7月份到现在为止下跌了将近19%，那么YTD从最高的110%吧，现在下降到了73.3%
  • VIX：出现了14%这个上涨，主要是来自于上一周了，过去一周时间里面VIX是上涨了25%。那VIX的一个上涨也和一部分原油的一个上涨有关
  • 原油：7月份上涨了19%
  • 比特币：7月份也走的不错，上涨了9.3%
  • IGV（软件板块）：上涨了2.4%
  • 罗素2000：出现了下跌，下跌的幅度不小

主要是因为罗素2000里边的一些权重股是和AI相关的，比如说Bloom Energy也在里面，那Bloom Energy下跌的幅度比较大，所以罗素2000也下跌的幅度比较大。所以现在罗素2000其实已经和中小盘股或者整个市场风险偏好有一点脱钩了，因为里边那些权重股是和AI相关的，就有点类似于标普500是一样的一个道理。

那么所以我们看到其实YTD到现在为止，罗素2000上涨19.4%还是走的非常的好，遥遥跑赢了三大指数，为什么？那跑赢和芯片板块是一样，就是因为罗素2000里面的权重股是和AI相关或者是AI的一个获益股。

7月份到现在为止，大科技股们看一下上涨9.3%，出现了比较好的这个反弹。相比之下，标普的等权指数几乎是在横盘。

二、市场参与度与恐慌贪婪指数

截止到上周五，市场的参与度我们来看一下：

  • 纳指：现在是处在一个中性稍微偏悲观的一个位置，20均线和50均线 41%和45%
  • 罗素2000：55%和63%，处在中性偏乐观的位置
  • 标普500：58和63，处在一个中性偏乐观的位置

整个市场现在处在一个中性偏乐观的位置。主要这一波的一个回调是来自于芯片。

在上周日和大家分享CNN的恐慌贪婪指数里面的这张图，上周日我记得当时CNN的恐慌贪婪指数正好是在一个中性的位置。那随着过去一周的一个下跌，我们看到CNN的恐慌贪婪指数来到了悲观的位置，现在是在37左右。

在上周我和大家更新的时候，我特别挑了这张图出来——CNN恐慌贪婪指数里面市场的一个避风港需求。那避风港需求它主要衡量的是股市和债市之间的一个回报差。当这一个回报差在比较高的位置，就是代表过去20天里边股市跑赢了债市。当时我说如果画这条线的话，接下去我们可以期待的是股市和债市之间的一个相对回报差可能债市这边要走的好一点。

那其实在过去一周里面，我们看到债市基本上是没有动的，那股市出现了下跌，所以这条线出现了回调。那回调完之后，这两者之间的回报差接近于零了，也就是说其实已经处在一个比较中性的位置了。

三、芯片板块的杠杆去化

前面讲到了芯片板块的这个回调，来看一下台湾这边的margin loan，台湾这边的杠杆，这边是日交易的一个杠杆，可以看到在过去一段时间里边这个杠杆下跌的幅度非常的大。

那其实X上、在社交媒体上已经有人在讨论韩国那边的杠杆现在处在什么那个位置，我看完之后基本上还是处在一个相对比较高的位置。和最高幅度相比可能下降了20%左右，但是绝对值来说还是在一个相对高的一个位置。

然后我看到美国这边和芯片板块相关加杠杆的ETF在过去一段时间下跌的幅度堪比22年的这一波下跌。所以整个芯片板块我认为比较艰难的这个时刻可能在我们身后，但你说市场马上就要再回去，我觉得不大现实。通常来说，在一波去完杠杆之后，你再要回到这个新高的话，这中间有很多事情要发生。起码这个故事线，就以前的这个故事已经结束了，结束完之后你需要一个新的故事线，可以把价格带到更高。

那现在我们在第二季度这个财报，马上本周将会有一家大科技、两家大科技发布财报。其中一家谷歌，谷歌的这个财报，特别是资本开支，对于整个芯片板块的情绪面会起到非常大的这个影响。有任何资本开支增速放缓的这个信号，对于芯片板块都不是一个利好。

四、现金流预测：芯片 vs 超大规模云厂

然后我们来看一下这张图，这张图很有意思，是未来12个月现金流这边的预测。

图里紫色这条线是Semiconductor芯片板块的一个现金流，你可以看到在过去这一段时间上涨的幅度速度非常的快，而且这边是衡量的体量已经达到了4500亿美金，$450 billion。

黄色这条线Hyperscaler，所有的这些大云厂商，他们的现金流从3000亿美金现在下降到几乎为0。

从这个角度出发，可能市场不是那么的偏好Hyperscaler后偏好这些芯片板块也合理吧，因为芯片板块短期特别是你看未来12个月，它现金流的这个增速非常的确定，其幅度也非常的高。然后主要的这个现金流是来自于大科技这边的花费。

但是反过来也是一样，也是现在市场担心的：就是大科技有没有可能放缓资本开支这个增速？就我觉得主动权是掌握在大科技这边，这也是我手里现在拿的大科技，我完全不担心市场出现回调。那有任何资本开支放缓的这些增速就来自于这些大科技的话，我认为对于大科技的股价应该都是一个利好。所以我觉得还是应该有一个相对比较平衡的这个仓位。那在当下的话，我认为持有大科技或者大科技的仓位过高一些，我认为会更加的合理和安全。

五、Mag 7 与标普493 的盈利增速对比（FactSet数据）

讲到Mag 7，我们从FactSet数据去出发，看一下第二季度Mag 7的增速：

  • EPS同比增速：31.1%，非常的高
  • 剩下标普493：22.8%
  • 整个标普500 Q2市场预期的增速：24.7%

那这一个季度EPS增速主要来自于哪里呢？其主要来自于5家公司：

  1. 美光：上年的同期才1.9亿，然后今年来到了25.1亿
  2. 两家能源相关公司：因为能源价格的一个上涨，所以两家和能源价格相关的公司EPS的增速幅度也非常的高
  3. 博通：上年是1.69，今年预期是3.2
  4. 英伟达：上年是1.05，今年是2.08，就是英伟达和上年去都对比的话，EPS同比增速1倍

如果我把两家芯片公司（美光和英伟达）去掉的话，那整个标普500 EPS增速从24.7就直接会降到16.8。

在第一季度，我们看到就是过去的这个季度，我们看到Mag 7同比增速63.2%，493是7.9，这个差距非常的大。

第二季度我说现在市场预期31.1，其他公司是22.8，那我认为这个数字最后可能会停在40%左右。因为基本上大多数的Mag 7他们最后出来的结果、财报出来的这个结果都会比市场的预期要高。那么当然了，493也会比市场预期要高，但是493高的这个幅度可能不会有Mag 7会更高。

然后第三季度我们看一下这中间的这个差距会越来越小：第三季度Mag 7是在31.8，493是25.5。那么从第二季度再次有了一个台阶的一个上升。到第四季度，Mag 7还会开始出现增速上的一个放缓，22.8%，标普493仍然保持在25.3%。

那如果大家担心说Mag 7这个同比增速和标普493之间可能会缩小，是不是应该去投资标普493？其实这个问题在上年年底、上年第三季度第四季的时候市场就已经讨论过。原本市场预期在2025年（口误为2026）又会出现EPS增速反转的这种情况，但是我们在2025年完全没有看到，相反，第一季度这一个同比增速的一个差距在越来越大。

那么而其实如果今天不是有Mag 7的话，我们单去看标普493 EPS的同比增速18%、23%、26%，其实已经非常非常的高了。那只是在这个前提下Mag 7它的一个增速会更好。所以我觉得拆开看可以看，可以拿Mag 7和标普493去做对比，但是我们单看标普493——因为标普493也算衡量整个标普500的一个健康程度嘛，或者营收的一个盈利的这个增速——所以单看标普493的话，这个盈利增速其实也相当的高。

整个2025年现在市场预期EPS同比增速24.5%。在年初的时候市场预期是15%，也就是和年初做对比，现在已经比年初要高了10%。那随着第二季度财报出来之后，相信这一个差距会越来越大。

六、估值水平

最后是估值。下面处理蓝色这条线Forward PE，那FactSet上面的一个数据，截止到上周五是在20.5倍左右吧。那5年的这个平均是在20倍，也就是现在略微高于5年的这个平均，高的幅度多少，1%~2%左右。10年的平均在19倍。所以现在基本上标普500这个估值是处在一个中心的位置。

七、本周财报预告

最后我们来看一下本周将要发布的财报。发财报之前，本周其实没有一些宏观数据。然后在下下周就会有下一次这个美联储会议——一晃，我记得凯文·沃茨（Kevin Warsh）第一次美联储会议好像就在上一周呃，不知不觉马上要来到他下一次的一个第二次的美联储会议了。

所以本周下半周开始吧，美联储的成员就会进入一个禁默期了。那因为上一周公布的CPI数据、PPI数据基本上已经确定7月份是不会加息（口误，应为降息），即使现在市场还有15%的这个概率在那边，但7月份是不会降息，9月份现在降息这个概率仍然是在67%、65%左右。所以本周没有非常重要的一些宏观数据，那主要就是财报了，接下去财报季度将会越来越精彩。

周二盘前：MSCI

下一周我们将会看到周二的盘前会有MSCI。

周三盘前：Moody's

包括在周三盘前的一个Moody's。这两家公司主要是通过这两家公司可以看到，可能要几个月之前马世钟在讨论像SPGI（S&P Global）这一类的公司，他们会不会受到AI的这个影响。那我个人的看法是，掌握这些独有的数据，他们在评级这一块的一些业务，包括核心业务本身不但（应为"并不"）会受到AI的这个影响。而我前面特地去看了一下SPGI的这个走势，在过去这段时间其实走的还是不错的。虽然还没有把前段时间可能要大半年之前的那一波下跌的跌幅还没有完全擦掉，但是过去这段时间做的还是不错的。所以MSCI包括Moody's如果财报如果不错的话，可以把SPGI一类的标的都会往上带。

周三盘前：GEV

然后是周三的盘前GEV，那这家公司从订单、从很多个角度去看，GEV的财报不会有任何的一些风险。那对于他们来说，更多的还是产能的这个提升。

周三盘后：特斯拉 + 谷歌

周三的盘后就非常的精彩了，几乎是整个市场的一个焦点。那在周三的盘后——我记得我在App上应该有个直播的，是不是公开的直播我要确认一下，我记得应该是一个公开的一个直播——周三的盘后会有特斯拉的财报，然后还有Alphabet。

特斯拉：其实我有一段时间没有去跟了。最近我有看到有些Robotaxi开始上线了，可能现在在多少 40多辆还是100多辆，那么从上线的这个速度来说可能让一些人比较失望。那我个人仍然认为今年是累计特斯拉仓位的时候。我现在还没有开始累计，但如果有机会的话我可能会加仓特斯拉。现在还没有看到，我个人认为特斯拉的一个爆发点是在他们下一代芯片要推出的时候，或市场可能会提前去走嘛，或者提前去布局。

谷歌（Alphabet）：那谷歌应该是整个周三盘后市场最关注的一家公司的一个财报吧，没有之一了。为什么？因为谷歌的资本开支这个体量基本上和亚马逊是持平的。在上一个季度的财报里面，管理层有聊到他们已经给了2027年的一个资本开支，当时他们用的一个词我记得非常的清楚叫"substantially higher"。这个词的一个解释就起码在2027年的增速也能够达到40%至50%。但他们26年的增速是非常的高了，但我不知道市场能不能够满意。

那我个人猜测在这一次财报会里面，在资本开支这一块，谷歌可能不会透露从数量上去看，可能不会透露任何会放缓的一些信号，从体量上去看。但是我不知道从言语上来说他们会不会给自己稍微淡化一些，或者我说到这个痛稍微把它压低一些。为什么？是因为大科技现在疯狂的巨大资本开支，其实会反射他们、反射就是整个成本上升。

然后另外一点就是谷歌这边的一个margin，云服务这边的一个margin。谷歌的云服务的margin整个这一个季度吧，起码大科技这些云服务，我期待他们的一个margin会比上一个季度要更好。从Anthropic向另外两家公司去购买算力，包括购买算力的这个成本就可以看到，这个supply的这个价格就可以看到现在整个市场里边算力仍然是短缺。

另外一点，谷歌的财报里面其实我希望听到他们Agentic Commerce，那么在AI Agent这一块的一些落地，在C端这一块有没有一些落地。所以我基本上周三盘后会非常关注谷歌的这个财报。那谷歌的财报对于市场的这个影响，我认为也是非常非常的大。

周三盘后：ServiceNow / IBM / TI

然后接下来这两家公司ServiceNow，那主要是软件这一块。ServiceNow我个人对于他们的业务本身没有那么的担心。然后IBM，最后是TI（德州仪器）。那后面两家公司在市场里面现在讨论度也是相对会高一些。

周四盘前：诺基亚

最后是周四。周四的盘前会有诺基亚。诺基亚这家公司我会和大家跟一下，然后在周四那期视频里面我和大家稍微聊一下诺基亚这一次一个财报。财报本身我并没有太多那些指引和展望。

周四盘后：英特尔

周四的盘后会有英特尔。那过去这一段时间嘛，两三周，英特尔下跌的幅度会比较的大，现在价格在多少 92、93。英特尔财报里面的一些重点：

  1. 良率：第一点最重要的就是良率
  2. CPU的出货：然后第二点。在上一个季度财报里面，他们把压库存的这些CPU全部给卖掉了，这一个季度其实没有多余的CPU可以去卖了。从增速这个角度去看，不会比第一季度要好，这是在上一个季度财报里面就已经做出过的这个展望
  3. 封装业务：看一下他们封装这块会不会有些额外的客户

其实在所有AI的一些相关的标的里面，我个人认为英特尔其实是比较稳，而且不单是从一个从各个角度：从CPU也好，和AI相关也好，从代工也好，从美国这边的一个制造业的这个角度去出发也好，包括从陈立武的执行力也好，包括他们的良率也好——我只能看到英特尔的基本面在变得越来越好，无非就是它的一个价格短期之内贵和便宜的问题。好么？

所以周四的盘后和大家聊两家公司：诺基亚和英特尔。那我自己持有的公司特斯拉、英特尔。

八、活动预告与结语

最后今天的活动来自于Investing.com，主要是他们量化的一个选股策略。下面有3个以前成功的例子，分别是英伟达、SMCI、AppLovin，这三个成功的例子回报的相当的好。

7月份，Investing.com正在举行一个大促销，高达60%的这个折扣。Pro一档加币是9.49美金的话在8块钱不到；Pro Plus加币24.49美金的话应该是$17.8左右。

那这个平台本身我建议大家即使不订阅的话也可以去参考、也可以去用，因为这里边有很多的一些数据、财报数据、包括财报会议、包括一些纪要在上面都有。所以这个平台本身就已经是一个非常好的一个投资工具了。大家如果感兴趣的话，包括如果用我的这个链接的话，在这个基础上可以再便宜15%。所以我会把链接放在置顶的留言里面，大家感兴趣的话可以自己去订阅。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

## 一、被忽视的"现金流反转"：芯片与云厂的角色互换
视频里最容易被一带而过、但其实最锋利的一张图，是那条**紫线（半导体未来12月现金流冲到4500亿美元）与黄线（超大规模云厂现金流从3000亿跌向近零）的十字交叉**。
这不是普通的板块轮动，而是**产业链话语权的一次结构性倒置**。过去十年，云厂是"甲方"，芯片厂被采购、被压价；现在的图景变成——云厂正在把自己所有的自由现金流"倒进"芯片厂的口袋里。用生态学的比喻，这不是共生，是**寄主与寄生虫的暂时性反转**：芯片是宿主，云厂是被抽干的宿主。
**出人意料的推论**：市场担心"大科技会不会砍资本开支"，其实问反了方向。真正应该焦虑的是——**当云厂现金流真的归零，谁来接盘下一轮资本开支？** 现在托底的是"未来AI收入"这张远期支票。这张支票的兑付节点，恰好就是主播提到的"Google Agentic Commerce落地"。所以谷歌财报的关键根本不在capex数字，而在**C端AI变现的第一声硬币落地声**。
## 二、Russell 2000的"身份漂移"：一个指数正在悄悄背叛自己
主播提到罗素2000因为里面的
