item.title: [a16z] Amjad Masad on Building Replit in Public
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的护城河，是他"默默无闻的那些年"

大多数人把 Amjad 的走红理解为"他抓住了 AI 浪潮"。但仔细听这段对话，他自己给的答案完全反直觉——他能今天扛住舆论压力，是因为过去很多年他不够红。

他把这称作 "linear growth of personal profile"（个人影响力的线性增长），但更精准的类比是他自己提到的举重"progressive overload"：你只能在能承受的重量上练技术，突然被压 200 公斤的人不是变强，是被砸碎。他把 HackerNews 上的实习生公关翻车、早期各种失言，都当成"低海拔试错"。

这里有个让人不安的推论：现在一夜爆红的 AI 创始人们，其实是被剥夺了这段"廉价犯错期"的一代人。他们没有"linear obscurity"这份储蓄，却被要求以顶级 CEO 的姿态输出。这解释了为什么很多新锐 CEO 的 Twitter 越来越像 PR 文稿——他们不是不真诚，他们是没经历过便宜的失败。

二、"被取消是一种选择"——这句话真正的对手，其实是你的边缘系统

Amjad 用了一个很轻的语气说这句话，但他自己随后把最深的洞察埋进去了：在祖先的村庄里，被驱逐等于死亡。你的大脑并不知道 Twitter 和部落是两回事。

于是"不回应、不撤退、继续发帖"看起来是策略问题，其实是跟三万年前的神经回路对着干。这里有个跨领域连接特别有意思：这套逻辑跟斯多葛派、以及现代的暴露疗法（Exposure Therapy）完全同构——它们都是在教你的边缘系统重新校准"什么算真正的威胁"。所以他去纽约学 improv，本质上不是在学演讲，是在给杏仁核做脱敏训练。

真正让人意外的是他给 Anthropic 的建议："sit back and let it play out"（往后靠，让它自己演完）。当一个人能把国家级公关危机当成一部剧看，他其实已经完成了神经层面的迁徙——从"部落成员"进化成了"观众"。这才是"unkillable"的底层机制。

三、"Going Direct" 是伪装成广播的一种极端的倾听

这可能是全场最容易被误解的观察。所有人都以为"公开建设"（Build in Public）的关键是多发，但 Amjad 明确说："Posting is not time-consuming. The thing that's time-consuming is understanding the meta."（发帖不费时间，费时间的是理解元叙事）。

换句话说，Satya Nadella 的那篇 20-30M 浏览的长文之所以爆炸，不是因为写得好，而是因为他准确地捕捉到了整个行业当天正在争论的那个问题，然后把微软的世界观穿在这件外套里递出去。

这里有个非常美的跨领域类比：这跟冲浪一模一样。新手以为冲浪是"划得快"，但老手知道冲浪的 90% 是坐在板上读浪——读风、读潮、读周期。你不制造浪，你只是让自己出现在正确的浪即将破碎的位置。

于是"CEO 影响力"的真正稀缺资源不是文笔、不是勇气、不是账号——是对当下集体情绪场的诊断力。这也解释了一个让人意外的推论：Dario Amodei 不玩社媒，反而是最纯粹的"Going Direct"——他直接对准了这个时代关于"AI 安全"的元叙事，让产品和信念本身成为帖子。

四、附赠一个反直觉的战术观察：Jason Lemkin 事件是一场柔道

Replit Agent 删了他的数据库，他公开发难。Amjad 明明知道技术上一键可恢复、明明可以甩锅"用户错误"——但他没有。他公开认错，然后两天内推出 dev/prod 隔离功能。

这看起来是"谦逊"，其实是极其锋利的攻击性动作。柔道的核心不是抵消对方力量，而是顺着对方的动能把他甩到你想让他去的位置。Jason 用力越猛，Amjad "认错"的杠杆就越长——最终把最响亮的一位公开批评者，变成了每天用 Replit + 10 个 agent 跑数百万美元 SaaS 业务的头号案例客户。

这里的规律可以抽象出来：在高关注度公关战里，"防御"是最贵的操作，"认错并进化"是最便宜的操作——因为它把对方的能量拿来推进你自己的产品路线图。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

Amjad: Being canceled is a choice. You can choose to get canceled and retreat from the public eye, but I think if you're still out there — at some point, honestly, the haters kind of give up.

Some people ask, "Hey, how should I think about X versus other platforms?" You have to understand the meta, because the way to go viral is to dress up your argument, your worldview, in the current conversation.

Twitter's influence is amazing, but it tends to be elite, kind of inside-group influence. I think Instagram, Facebook — still YouTube — is where you get to the early majority.

Interviewer: Does every CEO need to become an influencer now?

Amjad: Look, I think there's so many paths to success. I don't think there's one. Replit would have probably died if I wasn't telling a story that is larger than the company itself. Dario is an example where he's not playing the social media game — the product sort of speaks for itself. So I think it comes down to the…

Interviewer: Thank you for joining us.

Amjad: Of course.

Why Going Direct Kept Replit Alive

Interviewer: So Replit is a 10-year-old company. For the last two years, it's gone absolutely vertical, but there was a period of time well before that where the company was in the zeitgeist — partially because of your go-direct efforts. I mean, you're one of the best CEOs on X. You're also now getting big on Instagram and other platforms. What has the business impact been of your efforts going direct? And does every CEO need to become an influencer now — or how have you sort of conceived this?

Amjad: Yeah, I think Replit would have probably died if I wasn't telling a story that is larger than the company itself. The company wasn't successful commercially, but we've been very successful at fundraising, recruiting — and I think if you build a company that's successful right out of the gate commercially, you might not need to do all of that. But if you're trying to meme a dream into reality, I think you have to play that game.

So yeah — I think otherwise we would have not existed, because we had to do that for so many years before. It turns out everything I said was true, but at the time it wasn't real. It was a dream.

Getting Good at Communicating: Improv, Storytelling, Exposure Therapy

Interviewer: And you at one point decided to go big on this. You weren't always big on Twitter. A lot of people here — a lot of CEOs — maybe it doesn't come supernaturally to them, and they have to make a decision of, "How do I get good? Am I going to do this, and if so, how do I get good at it?" What was your journey to saying, "Hey, I'm really going to invest in this and I'm going to get good at this"?

Amjad: Well, I think the journey starts even outside of Twitter — like, how do you get good at communicating? How do you get good at public speaking? I always wanted to be able to be an influencer, for lack of better words.

I remember I was in New York when I first came to the States, and I had terrible stage fright. Like, I'd be sitting here and my heart rate would be like 150, I'd be sweating. And I thought, how do I deal with this? How do I get better at this? So I went and took improv classes in New York, and then took a storytelling class.

I'm a big fan of exposure therapy — anything you're afraid of, just go do more of it until you're desensitized. And the best way to get desensitized is to just make a fool of yourself every day doing improv. I ended up doing shows and got pretty good at it.

And then I think the benefit that I had is Replit didn't blow up right out of the gate. It was this very linear growth to my personal profile. So I could make mistakes with very little attention on me.

I made a lot of PR mistakes. Still, if you go to Hacker News and sort by the top, we had this PR crisis on Hacker News where I had an issue with some ex-intern at Replit — I just totally botched that communication. But still, that wasn't large enough. I was still within the Hacker News community, which — they still hate me, which is fine, they'll hate you anyways. That's like the rite of passage: Hacker News loves you, then they hate you, then you become successful.

So you kind of make mistakes, and they're not at the public stage just yet. The stakes get higher as I'm able — it's sort of a progressive overload, like in powerlifting. You're carrying more weight. It never gets easier, but you're able to do more and more over time.

I feel for the founders that are just now — their company's blowing up and they're in the public eye. You can see founders of big, now-trillion-dollar companies really fucking up on a massive stage. But getting the reps in has been super helpful.

Build in Public — and the Rise of Authenticity

Interviewer: And so, is that your advice? People want to just get exposure therapy, one tweet a day? What's the best way to get started?

Amjad: A few things. One is the concept of build in public. It wasn't coined when I started doing that, but the idea is — as a CEO, you're going to do a good amount of writing and communicating to your employees, to your investors. You can just do it publicly.

I've always been a believer that there aren't really a lot of secrets that you need to keep inside a company. So a lot of your otherwise-private writing, you can put it public — and that way you carry people in the journey with you, and you're getting the reps in.

Whenever there's a piece of communication or a story I want to tell and there's a choice between public and private, I might bias toward public. I often write something publicly and then paste it on Slack and just say, "This is what I wrote." That's been helpful.

The other thing is authenticity. Being yourself is kind of a big radical thing that maybe started happening with Elon 10 years ago. CEOs were supposed to be this very polished thing — they had to be filtered through this prism of PR, and journalists were kind of the way to get to the public.

Elon was the first kind of building a public platform. And I think Zuck to some extent as well — seeing Zuck, at some point when journalists kind of turned on him, he started going direct. You start following the stories, and Zuck changed the entire narrative around him by just being himself and actually talking directly to people.

The story of Trump is also very illustrative. Trump was successful despite the negative bias in the press, and it was mostly Twitter initially — people forget that. Trump had amazing bangers. What was my favorite one? "I've never seen a thin person drink Diet Coke." Which is true.

Or Kanye — Kanye's banger is like, "I hate waking up in the plane and I see a bottle of water in front of me. Now I gotta take care of this." "I don't have a manager. I can't be managed." Right? I can't be managed.

You see these people come up and people start associating with them — and obviously they're very authentic. There's this shift in people's minds where they crave authenticity.

Interviewer: Hunter Biden.

Amjad: Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer: You can do anything, but if you're a good poster, you can get away with it.

Amjad: He can post his way to the presidency, for sure.

Cancellation Is a Choice

Interviewer: It's funny you mentioned the intern thing, because I remember that, but I also remember forgetting it. A lot of people say, "Oh, what if I say the wrong thing? What if I get my company into some sort of controversy or scandal?" Is it just that attention spans are so short that it's just the next situation? What do you say about that?

Amjad: Well, you need to — I think PR crisis can be deadly if you retreat afterwards. If you're not in the news… The thing about Trump, Elon, etc., is that there is a next thing. And by the way, the next thing could be worse. But just the fact that you're still in there, you're still in the game — people will be like, "Oh, this guy's unkillable, uncancellable."

Being canceled is a choice. You can choose to get canceled and retreat from the public eye, but if you're still out there, at some point honestly the haters kind of give up. They're like, "All right, I guess we can't do anything to this guy. Let's go to the next guy."

Interviewer: There's this great book, So You've Been Publicly Shamed, and it chronicles the stories of a number of people who've gotten canceled over the past 15 years. And that's basically the takeaway — the people who are truly canceled are the ones who shut up. They're the ones who retreat. But the ones who just keep going — it's forgettable. There's so many people, you know, Brian Johnson has wholly revived their image or presented a whole new image, and people just forget the thing they were almost canceled for.

The Mental Game and Principles as Armor

Amjad: I will say, the mental aspect of it is pretty difficult.

Interviewer: I was going to ask that next.

Amjad: This story has been told a trillion times, but in the ancestor village, if you become an outcast, that's pretty deadly — you can literally die, you can't find food. So our limbic system, when you get a massive reaction online, kind of puts you in fight-or-flight. It can really affect you. You can't sleep, some people can't eat. It can be really damaging.

But exposure therapy helps a lot. The first one's really hard, the second one is like, "Ah, it'll blow over."

Also, having good principles. Acting on principles is important. No matter what people think of what's happening at Anthropic, it's absolutely true in my mind that they believe everything they're doing — they believe in safety, they believe in their mission. And I think that gives them incredible strength to keep going. Oftentimes principles and self-interest coincide, and that's a good thing. You can ascribe what they're doing to some kind of cynical marketing ploy, but the strength that they have is based on their principles, and that really keeps them going.

Advice for Anthropic (and the Government Fight)

Interviewer: Earlier you were alluding that the stakes are really high with these. What advice might you have for Anthropic or OpenAI in terms of some of the communication challenges or opportunity?

Amjad: It's obviously way above my grade. I've never battled with a United States government. Not yet. One-day goals.

Look, I honestly think it's kind of a win-win for them. If you game out what's going to happen — with Anthropic, Fable comes back, it's going to be a huge flood towards Fable. It's kind of like, "This thing was banned by the government."

Actually — Steve Jobs once did this ad. They had a Mac, I don't know, the big towers, the Mac Pro I think it's called, that had tremendous compute power that was subject to export control. So they had this ad where it's military tanks going and surrounding the Mac, and the Mac in the middle — showing that this thing is so powerful the US government doesn't want you to have it, so you should go buy it.

It's a tremendous marketing opportunity for them. Their reputation is already pretty big. Even if they can't get Fable back on the market, they still win the PR game of "we're a company that's principled and doing the right thing." So my advice would be: don't stress out too much, and honestly, just sit back and let it play out.

Don't Feed the Trolls

Interviewer: You're describing the mental game — a lot of things we'll hear from CEOs is, "Oh, I don't want to have to tweet, and then I'm in meetings, now I have to think about the responses, and I have to respond back, and now I'm in sort of…"

Amjad: You don't have to respond back. That's the thing.

Interviewer: Right.

Amjad: You don't have to respond back at all. That's another thing you have to learn — to not feed the trolls. That reply, like, "Oh, I gotta get back" — it's like the New Yorker comic: "Babe, come to bed." "No, someone's wrong on the internet."

It's very tempting, but actually the baller thing to do is like, "Oh yeah, the plebs can fight in my comments. I don't need to worry about it." So I think it's a trap to think that anything you put out, you need to immediately defend.

Obviously, if something is getting a lot of airplay and people are misunderstanding you, you should correct it — and again, you should do it in a principled way. You should do it because, "Hey, this is what I actually believe. Here's what you got wrong." But don't be overly defensive about it. Don't appear that this is something you're getting emotional about — because anytime you show weakness publicly, it actually feeds the trolls and feeds the haters, because they feel like they can get to you.

When to Respond: The Jason Lemkin Story

Interviewer: What advice would you give for when companies are being dragged by someone on Twitter or in the press — when to respond versus when not to engage?

Amjad: That's an art thing. I think it comes down to business impact — will it actually have impact on my business?

For example, last year in July we had this story with the founder of SaaStr, Jason Lemkin, where Jason had just started vibe coding — had never vibe coded or coded anything before. As he's working with Replit Agent, Replit Agent sort of misunderstood him or something, and then deleted the database.

At the time we didn't have production/development separation. So the production database — now we actually separate them by default, the replication can't even write to the production database, it can only read — and we have backups, we have snapshots, you can go back to a certain day or time. So the mistake that Replit Agent did was one click away from being fixed. But from his perspective, he didn't know that. And Replit Agent started freaking out — models at the time used to get really anxious, especially Claude.

He tweeted the screenshot where Replit Agent was going kind of nuts. And it started gaining traction, gaining traction, gaining traction. In my mind, I know we already fixed this issue, but the story has become so massive and obviously it's going to have business impact, it's going to be in the press.

I could go out and fight it — say we did nothing wrong, we had backups, it's a user error, whatever. But I think the right thing to do was to own up to it. The fact that we didn't have development/production separation is a bad thing. And two days later, we rolled out that fix.

My response got a lot of positive interaction and got a lot of airplay because I started with, "Hey, we messed up, and this is what we could have done better."

But sometimes you can give attention to things that you don't want to give attention to, especially once your profile grows — especially if you apologize. I would say: just focus on the business impact.

Interviewer: Yeah.

Amjad: By the way, Jason is a huge fan now. He runs his entire SaaStr business — multi-million dollar business — with him, another employee, and like 10 agents based on Replit Agent.

Interviewer: That's awesome.

Does Every CEO Need to Do This?

Interviewer: You mentioned earlier that you sort of developed a desire for this. For CEOs who are so locked in, they're just not that interested in doing this — would you recommend they cultivate the desire to do it, or would you recommend someone else on the team can do it? Does it have to be the CEO, or how would you think about this?

Amjad: Look, I think there's so many paths to success. I don't think there's one.

There are a lot of companies where it's not the CEO that's out there. Like Grok — with a Q — Sunny is the person on Twitter, but the CEO is kind of not on there. They've done a great job. Obviously the company's great, the IP is great, but they also meme'd their way into success. Part of the story that's not being told is they actually had a lot of trouble fundraising in Silicon Valley — they had to go to Saudi and all of that. So that's an example where the CEO is not out there.

You look at Dario as an example, where he's not playing the social media game. The product sort of speaks for itself, and he's writing these big essays.

So I think it comes down to the predisposition of the CEO. Do you actually enjoy it? Do you think you can be good at it? Forcing people to do it — they can come out and be totally cringe and actually be negative on the brand. Obviously they can learn over time and do it, but it really depends on the situation.

Interviewer: Have you gotten any leverage or way to lower the activation energy? Any help doing it? Is it possible for others too, or is it just all you, whenever you think of something?

Amjad: I have the benefit of this long period of incubation. If your company is already high-profile, you don't want to practice in public. So maybe getting some coaching earlier on.

Platform Strategy: X vs Instagram vs YouTube

Interviewer: Some people ask, "Hey, how should I think about X versus other platforms?" Maybe their customers aren't on X, etc. How do you think about that?

Amjad: X is very good for Silicon Valley, for tech, for the in-group messaging — maybe one hop outside of Silicon Valley, which is the early adopter, if you're targeting early adopters. I would also cluster Hacker News within that.

But once you want to go to late adopters or the early majority — if you think about this bell curve of adoption — Twitter actually becomes not very impactful there. It can still be very important. Just this morning, journalists reached out to me to talk to me about a tweet I made about some of the stuff that's happening with Anthropic. So Twitter can still be a place where stories start.

And that's another thing — back to the conversation of why this is important — the landscape shifted so much that journalists report on Twitter. So it kind of starts on Twitter. Twitter's influence is amazing, but it tends to be elite, inside-group influence.

I think Instagram, Facebook, still YouTube — is where you get to the early majority. I was late to YouTube, to Instagram. I just started focusing on it maybe in February or something like that. And we're getting an insane amount of views and the followership… you start to build this clips machine of just your interviews. The podcast is interesting because it's the medium that can be turned into every other format.

I feel like I should have maybe done Instagram like a year or two ago. So I was a little late on that. I thought it was going to be harder. Turns out — you can just do this clipping and grow not just your account, you can grow a lot of different accounts that way.

But I would start with Twitter, because that's where the news starts to happen. This is where you can have outsized influence.

Interviewer: Are you bullish on the platform? Do you think that in the next 3 to 5 years, it will stay the same?

Amjad: I think it is actually kind of risky, because the algorithm changes so much. You might do something that angers the powers that be, and without anyone knowing, things might change for you in terms of your reach on X. So there's less transparency than Twitter 1.0. So it is a little risky.

But I think the platform has so much staying power. It's really hard to replace. You can change the name, you can destroy the brand, and the platform will still be very valuable. It's one of those things where I think there's no way you can avoid it.

Who Inspires Him: Balaji, Satya, and the Meta

Interviewer: Who are some CEOs or leaders that inspire you in terms of how they go direct — that you've learned from looking at what they do?

Amjad: Obviously, we were all in the school of Balaji. Balaji and Lulu — we had this group in the pandemic. What was it called? Going Direct. Yeah, Going Direct. We talked about strategies and critiqued some of our approaches or other people's approaches. That was very useful.

Balaji was kind of early to this stuff. Where I might disagree with Balaji is — I don't think you should be antagonistic to reporters. There's no reason to. You can actually be friends with them and they can be positive towards you. You can help them out. They're just humans at the end of the day, and they respond to incentives. We've done pretty well in maintaining our relationships with reporters. Obviously Sharon Oz recently joined us and that upleveled our game with reporters and more of that type of media. So studying that is very important. There's enough content out there to get started.

Who else? Palmer, Alex Karp, Elon — obviously I mentioned Elon. I think Satya is doing such a great job.

Interviewer: What about what he's doing?

Amjad: It's much less tweet-length things, but he's able to put out very well-reasoned arguments that play into the zeitgeist in a very smart way and advance their point of view. Like the essay he put out over the weekend — it got 20-30 million views. Very few essays get that much attention. But it comes at a time where everyone is thinking about token costs, everyone's thinking about — and this is the important thing about going direct.

You can go direct and get zero views. It's really easy to not pay attention to you. You have to understand the meta. And I think that's the thing that's more time-consuming than posting. Posting is not time-consuming. The thing that's time-consuming is understanding what the larger debate is — because the way to go viral is to couch, or dress up, your argument, your worldview, in the current conversation.

I thought that what Satya did with his essays is very much at the heart of the discussion today, and then he advanced the point of view of Microsoft.

Interviewer: Yeah. I think it's a good place to wrap. Please give it up for John.

Amjad: Thank you, man. Thanks.

[music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、真正的护城河，是他"默默无闻的那些年"
大多数人把 Amjad 的走红理解为"他抓住了 AI 浪潮"。但仔细听这段对话，他自己给的答案完全反直觉——**他能今天扛住舆论压力，是因为过去很多年他不够红**。
他把这称作 "linear growth of personal profile"（个人影响力的线性增长），但更精准的类比是他自己提到的举重"progressive overload"：**你只能在能承受的重量上练技术，突然被压 200 公斤的人不是变强，是被砸碎**。他把 HackerNews 上的实习生公关翻车、早期各种失言，都当成"低海拔试错"。
这里有个让人不安的推论：现在一夜爆红的 AI 创始人们，其实是被剥夺了这段"廉价犯错期"的一代人。他们没有"linear obscurity"这份储蓄，却被要求以顶级 CEO 的姿态输出。这解释了为什么很多新锐 CEO 的 Twitter 越来越像 PR 文稿——**他们不是不真诚，他们是没经历过便宜的失败**。
## 二、"被取消是一种选择"——这句话真正的对手，其实是你的边缘系统
Amjad 用了一个很轻的语气

item.title: [Business of Sport] McCullum Gone, The FA Need to Stand Up to FIFA, & The Rise of Jannik Sinner
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、麦卡伦下课背后的"责任逃逸"结构学

大多数评论都在讨论麦卡伦的战绩，但真正值得注意的是访谈中两个人的语言结构对比：麦卡伦用"四年周期"来定义自己的失败，而 Richard Gould 用"过去六到九个月的几个结果"来描述同一件事。时间尺度的选择本身就是一种权力表达——运动员被训练在长周期里承担责任，而管理者习惯于把时间窗口切得越短越好，因为窗口越短，可归因的责任就越小。这不是英格兰板球独有的病，而是所有"运动员出身 vs. 行政出身"的组织里反复出现的裂缝。

一个出人意料的观察：麦卡伦之所以能坦然承认失败，恰恰是因为他曾经是顶级球员。视频里那句"能爬到运动巅峰的人往往对自己诚实，否则爬不上去"是全场最深的一句话。也就是说，Gould 的推卸并非人格缺陷，而是他所处的选拔机制从未奖励过诚实——行政官僚是被"避免出错"筛选出来的，而运动员是被"直面失败"筛选出来的。两种物种，无法通婚。

二、FA 与 FIFA：把"投票权数学"错当成"影响力物理"

节目里最反常识的一段，是 Stubbings 指出：如果你根本拿不到男足世界杯、女足世界杯又无人竞争，那么"讨好 Infantino"的成本收益公式就崩了。这其实揭示了体育治理里一个被长期忽略的悖论——一票一权制度让小国的选票溢价，反而给了大国"道德套利"的空间：越是没什么可失去的传统强国，越是唯一可能改革体系的人。这个逻辑几乎完美对应企业治理里的"沉默的大股东困境"，也让人想起冷战后期北欧小国在联合国的道德操作空间——当经济依赖度低到某个阈值，道德本身就变成一种可交易的资本。

跨领域连接：Infantino 突然把世界杯扩军到 64 队，与 Netflix 每逢续约季就推出"新剧宣发攻势"是同构的——当你的位置依赖于连任票，你的产品线扩张就不再服从市场逻辑，而服从选票逻辑。世界杯不是在变大，是在变成竞选传单。

三、辛纳、意大利网球俱乐部与 LTA 三亿英镑的"错误路径"

Stubbings 抛出的数据非常刺眼：过去 20 年，四个大满贯东道国男子冠军只出了一个——安迪·穆雷，而穆雷根本不是 LTA 培养的。LTA 花了约 3 亿英镑的精英项目预算，产出接近零。而意大利没有大满贯，却拥有 4500 个网球俱乐部（英国 2000 个），产出四名 TOP 20 男子选手。

这里藏着一个在体育之外同样成立的结论："公园球场"（公共可达性）和"俱乐部教练"（结构化师徒制）是两种完全不同的资本形态，前者是流量资本，后者是知识资本。LTA 把大部分钱砸在场地和公园里，看起来像"普及"，但真正培养冠军的是分布式的、有小型作坊感的俱乐部生态。这几乎是"图书馆 vs. 学徒制"、"MOOC vs. 博士导师"的翻版——普及型基础设施不会自动产出精英，因为精英是通过高密度的一对一反馈生长出来的。

更让人拍案的是节目里那个隐藏的诊断：LTA 培养出来的两个当家球星——Draper 和 Raducanu——都被伤病拖垮了。这不是偶然。当一个体系无法通过大量比赛和俱乐部竞争筛选出"抗损耗身体"，而是通过财政注入把少数天赋塞进温室，那么这些温室植物在真实赛季里必然骨折。这与硅谷"早熟独角兽"的失败模式惊人相似——过度资本化的早期成长会跳过必要的抗压训练。

四、一个被所有人忽略的跨领域连接

节目最后聊到马术障碍赛（Show Jumping）时，出现了三个联赛互相冲突、观众彻底混乱的局面。Stubbings 用了"叙事清晰度（narrative clarity）"这个词——Bernie Ecclestone 之所以让 F1 成为全球生意，不是因为车更快，而是因为他杀死了竞争性叙事。

把这条线拉回前三段：ECB 缺乏叙事清晰度（谁负责？）、FIFA 缺乏叙事清晰度（世界杯到底是什么？）、LTA 缺乏叙事清晰度（3 亿英镑到底在买什么？）、Show Jumping 缺乏叙事清晰度（哪个联赛才算真的？）。整期节目其实在讲同一件事的四个变体：当一个组织无法说清"我是谁、我在做什么、谁该为此负责"时，再多的钱都会以最昂贵的方式蒸发。这才是这一集真正的隐藏主题。

📝 转录文本

开场：花园装束与忙碌的体育周末

Stubbings： Good afternoon, Charlie. Back in the Belfry shirt on open week. It's my um it's it's become my gardening shirt. Has it?

Um well, apologies to any of the PR and marketing people out there from the Belelfrey. Um but it was a slightly cooler. It was slightly — Thank you. It was a slightly cooler day today. So, I thought it was time to go and dig up some weeds cuz the last couple of weeks it's been like, oh, I can't really face sort of digging up weeds in in sort of 35° heat. So, I thought I'd put my gardening clothes went out to do some weeding before I knew where I was. I was like, I'm going to miss my train. So, I had to jump onto the train in my gardening clothes. That's what you find me in today, Charlie. My gardening clothes.

Charlie： Very luxury gardening clothes, I must admit. I'm sure the Belfry will be delighted on that. It's a — It's a lovely golf shirt. Anyway,

Stubbings： thank you very much.

Charlie： Um uh — Oh, Charlie, what an exciting weekend it was. There was so much sport on, wasn't there?

Stubbings： I know. It was almost hard to know which way to turn. Um at times um and uh

一、麦卡伦被解职：一份坦诚的告别，一次失败的问责

Charlie： I mean obviously everyone's favorite topic to associate us with has had another development this week, hasn't it? I mean, every time something with this happens, Charlie, my phone does buzz and it gives me a kind of element of of pride and fear at the same time. But Brenda McCullum has finally been relieved of his duties as head coach of the test match England cricket team whilst remaining as head coach of their one-day teams, both their one day and T20. Brendan McCullum, head coach of the England cricket team for just over four years. We've been through before what his performance record was like. Average um pretty much won and lost a similar number of games. And when I say average, that's not average for England. England should be in the top three sides in the in the world. When he took over, I think we were seventh and when he left, we were seventh. Um, so effectively, he has only achieved an average level of performance despite a few moments of glory. It's basically not very good.

Stubbings： More recent history, seven out of nine tests lost. Yeah. His last his last nine tests lost seven of them. So

Charlie： yeah. Um and and really if you if you go back what McCullum had effectively done is within a test environment that had got a bit stale and a bit like tight and a bit sort of miserable he'd come in like with a bit of breath of fresh air and gone hey don't worry everybody enjoy yourselves and to a bunch of established test stars like broad and root and these types of guys that was a moment of relief and needed to happen at that particular moment in time but once that had been achieved and once the burden had been lifted off those players then it was revealed that the emperor had no clothes he's not actually really a coach he's a vibes man and once he no longer had a whole bunch of world-class players to deal with he was unable to coach players through to becoming world-class players and the whole thing ended up becoming a terrific mess so it is what it is I thought did you listen to the interview that he gave um post losing that that role.

麦卡伦访谈：一场令人意外的高水准告别

Stubbings： I did I thought it was one of the best things that he'd done in position actually.

Charlie： I thought it was great. I thought it was great. I thought that it's easy to forget that McCullum himself was a highlevel test player and generally speaking people who make it towards the very top of an elite sport are quite honest with themselves when they need to be otherwise they don't tend to make it there. And it was a very levelheaded

Stubbings： honest accountable description of what had happened.

Charlie： Um now what McCullum said was fundamentally we didn't win the big series. That's what I was brought in to do. The big series being the home and away series against India and Australia being the other two big test plane nations with big budgets and all this type of stuff. If you don't win those big moments and those big matches and those big series, then ultimately as the coach, that's on you. He then went on to apologize for not having done so to English cricket fans. And when he was invited various at various moments to sort of somehow claim he'd been hard done by, he refused. He said, "No, I'm afraid when you don't make when you don't win the big moments, when you don't win the big series, ultimately as as a as a test coach of England, you you're going to get, as he put it, the finger the finger on the shoulder."

Stubbings： Yeah. Um, so I thought that was very well done him. Right.

责任的错位：早就该发生的决定

Charlie： I agree. Um, and just on on that before you move on to the next part of it, I while we have been hugely critical, this show started just at the end of the ashes. We've talked a lot about this and from day one we were very affirmative in our position that we believed that he should not have continued in his position post then.

Stubbings： Yeah.

Charlie： That ultimately, you know, was a decision that was made above him. So anything that's happened since then really it's kind of been always like you should — he shouldn't even be in this position, right? This is now the accountability almost is shifting. He's going to behave in the same way and you can't — it's very difficult to ask him to behave in any other because he does have a set of beliefs and he'll have to shift what he believes to then fit something someone else does. So that was the point we made back in February. That was the point we made. We said it's totally unreasonable to expect him to change and then to maintain any credibility by so doing. He can't. He fundamentally has to say the same and by saying the same the same mistakes will be made and the same mistakes being made is the reason why he shouldn't be staying in the same position. Correct. Who was it who made the decision to leave him in post?

Richard Gould 与"艰难决定"的反讽

Stubbings： Well, Richard G — the chief executive of the ECB — who if you remember when he made the announcement that McCullum key and Stokes actually he made the Trump — he basically said

Charlie： oh god I hated this announcement. Please please please oh Charlie you're going to repeat it.

Stubbings： No I won't cuz I don't have it in front. Basically, he said something like, "The easy decision is to get rid of them, and we're not going to make the easy decision.

Charlie： I — I'm — I'm — I'm the big guy here taking making the big calls. I'm the tough guy. I'm the guy who's making the difficult decision, which is not to fire people, but to keep people because that is the right thing for the long term." Yeah. Right. That's what Richard Gould said in whether it was March March time, right?

Stubbings： Yeah.

Charlie： Um at which point Brenda McCullen was embarking on a three-month holiday. um which did rather make G's statement rather strange. Um so let's whine forward four months and say first of all how did that go? Answer terribly. We lost a home test series for the first time since 2012 and not to Australia or India but to a mid-ranking test team who had almost all of their best players out injured. So it went terribly terribly terribly terribly. And as you say quite rightly, Charlie, that's not on McCullum. That's on Gould. McCullum though showed accountability for it. Dig gold.

Stubbings： He did not.

一个五岁女儿的启示：接受自己犯错的能力

Charlie： He actually — I was actually quite worried watching this and I

Stubbings： I was cring — I was

Charlie： Yeah. Um, I tell you what I was worried is I — I sort of started to sort of feel like a shrink cuz I remember when my daughter was four and when she would do something wrong, she found it really really difficult to accept that she'd done it and found it really really difficult to apologize. So quite a lot of coaching went on to say it's okay to say sorry. It's okay to get something wrong and accept you've got something wrong. It doesn't make you a terrible person. It's what enables everybody else to move on. This is the coaching that's been going on with my five and six-year-old daughter over the last two years. I might just be putting my hand up here to help the ECB of Richard Gould because I think Richard Gould needs the same help that my 5-year-old daughter needed. Richard Gould seems to me to be pathologically incapable of taking responsibility for anything at all. He was even asked very straightforwardly, looking back in retrospect with the benefit of hindsight, do you now think, given that you've just fired McCullum in July, do you now think that letting him carry on in March might have been the wrong thing to do? No. Absolutely it was the right thing to do.

Stubbings： But but sorry, can we just say, well, you know, the first thing about that is — and you know, we kind of got around to this and then this and then no, it wasn't. the the the time it took him to get to any answer and then he never really gave a good one. It came across as just incompetent and — and I was — I think I said to you on the phone he said I almost — there's a — I'm almost uncomfortable having conversation post that interview because I felt it was someone that was just completely out of their depth. Do you get the same sense watching Richard Gould in that position that I get when I'm watching Nani Madu playing playing in the World Cup for England, which is here is a — here is a guy who, bless him, should not be anywhere near this level of of of of the game right?

两种截然不同的问责姿态

Charlie： But there was there was something a bit worse than that. There was something a bit worse than that. And I'll tell you what it was, which is that McCullum was offered offramps by his interviewer. Come on, Brendan. You know, you must be feeling a bit sore about all this. No, honestly, I've had it coming to me. Come on, Brendan. You must think that actually you've done quite well. No, actually, we've — we messed up the big series. The way that Gould said it was, well, you know, I think basically everything's been absolutely brilliant, but you know, at the end of the day, there have been a few bad results over the last 6 to 9 months was his phrase. Now, notice the difference between these two things. McCullum looks back over four years and says, "Over four years, we haven't won the big series." which is the truth, the honest truth, right? Because if they had beaten India and Australia at home or India away, then the Ashes series might be put in context with that broader level of achievement. But beating up on Zimbabwe and Ireland does not warrant then losing all the big series, right? And McCullum accepted that and fronted it up and even when he was given the opportunity not to do so, he insisted on saying it. Gould's dishonest proarication which is oh it's just a — it's just about a few results in the last few months that's all it is it's not — there was nothing — nothing to see here there's nothing major going on here it's just a couple of results have gone against us I mean really — you answered your own question — this is the one we get asked and you know in the other line of business we often get asked okay what where are athletes most um most impressive in business or where have you seen them to be most valuable in investment let's just say right everyone expects oh they're great leaders or they bring — no no what they're amazing at doing is they seek out crit criticism.

Stubbings： They — they look for feedback to understand how they can harness something to get better. Accountability for an athlete generally is a very easy thing to do because they've been forced into situations where they have to be accountable if they ever want to get better. Now, you know, for all of this, we can look at Brendan McCullum as a — as a coach, but you know, he was an exceptional player in multiple formats of the game. Therefore, to get to the level that he did as a player, he had to be able to understand how to improve. And to do that would be to absorb criticism. Yeah,

Charlie： the executive

Stubbings： is the opposite. And watching those two interviews, I just straight away it was just complete deflection and lack of ability to, as you say, own something that was so clearly wrong at the — and didn't take a genius. You know, we were sitting here going that cycle has ended. This needs to end. We — we haven't even touched on it, but you know, the fact that Rob Key is staying in position here. this needs to be a completely different — the lack of accountability and the lack of responsibility feeds through very heavily into the players um as in the players see the senior — the bosses ultimately — the suits as they might call them trying to dodge responsibility the message that sends the players first of all it means they have contempt for the suits right because hang on a second we're going out there and if I hook one and it gets caught I get absolute pelters but this guy over here makes a big decision as far as I can — All he has to do is just sit on a bench give me a cozy interview. Then he goes back up to the boardroom for a glass of pimps. Really? Like is am I meant to respect that? So that's the first thing and that's why it's absolutely critical when you are an executive that you are very much out and center in front of it owning the entire thing because the entire thing is down to you. The whole thing literally the whole thing.

"Where is Rob Key?"——真正的问责在哪里

Charlie： Now if Gould himself wants to take a slightly broader view of his own role as chief executive of the ECB, I'm also in, you know, looking at the development of cricket for young ones. I'm also looking at the the women's game. I'm also having to look at the accounts of the ECB. I'm also having to speak with sponsors. I'm going to delegate responsibility for the England men's team to my managing director of men's cricket, Rob Key. He could do that, right? he could say it's my job to decide whether Rob Key stays in his position, but as long as he is in his position, he's the one who takes responsibility. So, it's quite interesting seeing something um the — the two voices on English cricket that I respect the most and Nasa Hussein and Mike Afton being level-headed people mostly certainly Afton's occasionally Hussein who speak truth but they're not angry about it. It's not like they've got a chip on their shoulder. They just say it as they see it and they were just saying where's Rob Key? He's been integral to the decision to get rid of McCullum as he was integral to the decision to appoint McCullum.

Stubbings： He's integral to all the decisions that have been made around this. Where was he when Ben Stokes retired? Where was the interview around that? Where was he when McCllum — when McCullum was fired? Where was the interviews around that? Where was the context that he was putting around it? And where was he putting his hand up saying, "Do you know what? This is on me. This is all on me. Don't blame Brendan. Don't blame the players. Brendan's lost his job and that's very, very sad. I'm afraid my judgment was it had to happen. But I had to take my share of the blame as well cuz I select him in the first place." And then when the opportunity came to rotate him back in February, I went — I went again. And in retrospect, that was the wrong thing to do. I made a mistake. And in the — in the words of various cricket commentators and pundits, where's Rob Key? This is endemic that in an organization where all the top people are avoiding and dodging responsibility and accountability, it is absolutely inevitable as night follows day that the shambles continues down through the organization.

麦卡伦仍执教白球队：一个说不通的安排

Charlie： Michael Vornast um and he's a bit late to the party on some of this because he was a big supporter of Bazull for an awful long time and was a big supporter of Stokes and all the drinking and all this stuff stuff. He was fine with all of that. But — but I will say that he pointed up a key problem in the decision to keep McCullum as the white ball coach. Even though he's lost his job as the test coach, which is you're now having for the new guy coming in to be test coach is not only taking over a dressing room that's been molded by McCullum, he's taking over a dressing room that McCullum still has 50% control over. Right now, how's that meant to work? And I think I can't remember the exact exact phrase that Vaughn used, but it was something along the lines of, you know, watch out, this could get worse from here. You know, this — this shambles may not yet be at an end. And that's what it feels like because there's no clarity. There's no clean break. That the most we're getting from the ECB is, yeah, look, you know, we lost a couple of games. Uh, sorry. Um, so we thought we'd fire somebody. Um, I hope nothing to see here because actually what we really want to talk about is women's cricket until we lost that as well. And then we don't want to talk about that either.

Stubbings： If you're going to change this, this isn't moving a couple of people around really. This is top to bottom

Charlie： here

Stubbings： problem. So, so needs to go. So, who's accountable for that?

Charlie： Well, exactly. That's that's

Stubbings： who is it?

Charlie： Well, Richard Thompson.

顶层的问题：董事会与深层结构

Stubbings： Richard Thompson, the chairman. Right. So as at each level people are revealed not to be able to do their job eventually it becomes clear that the real problem

Charlie： well yeah but

Stubbings： is at the very top

Charlie： and then then we need to look at the board

Stubbings： and uh

## 一、麦卡伦下课背后的"责任逃逸"结构学
大多数评论都在讨论麦卡伦的战绩，但真正值得注意的是访谈中两个人的语言结构对比：麦卡伦用"四年周期"来定义自己的失败，而 Richard Gould 用"过去六到九个月的几个结果"来描述同一件事。**时间尺度的选择本身就是一种权力表达**——运动员被训练在长周期里承担责任，而管理者习惯于把时间窗口切得越短越好，因为窗口越短，可归因的责任就越小。这不是英格兰板球独有的病，而是所有"运动员出身 vs. 行政出身"的组织里反复出现的裂缝。
一个出人意料的观察：**麦卡伦之所以能坦然承认失败，恰恰是因为他曾经是顶级球员**。视频里那句"能爬到运动巅峰的人往往对自己诚实，否则爬不上去"是全场最深的一句话。也就是说，Gould 的推卸并非人格缺陷，而是**他所处的选拔机制从未奖励过诚实**——行政官僚是被"避免出错"筛选出来的，而运动员是被"直面失败"筛选出来的。两种物种，无法通婚。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、把「割肉美光」放进整段独白里，你会发现一个被忽略的元交易模式

投资TALK君今天最真诚的一段，不是关于芯片周期，而是他反复回到同一个动作："我把ISRG清了，我把AMD换了Intel，我把Oracle换Microsoft的仓要考虑，我把美光加了但知道错了不加了"。

如果把这些换仓动作抽出来做时间序列，你会发现一个惊人的、他自己都没明说的规律：他不是在"买卖股票"，而是在不断替自己的"认知敞口"做再平衡。基本面变差→清仓ISRG（不是止损，是"取消订阅"这家公司）；对Oracle判断更清晰→用Microsoft换Oracle（不是加仓，是"迁移信念"）。

这个模式的反常识之处在于——大多数散户把仓位当作对股票的承诺，而他把仓位当作对自己判断的租约。租约到期（判断变了）就退租，不管有没有亏损。这解释了为什么他能反复强调"割肉不重要，认知才重要"——因为在他的操作系统里，割肉根本不是损失事件，而是信息更新事件。

二、他讲「因子失效」时暴露了一个跨领域的深层规律：任何被命名的东西都会失效

他随口提到的那家量化基金研究——"当越来越多人使用某个因子，因子本身就失去了预测力，退化为纯粹的风险衡量工具"——这句话如果你只把它当量化知识听，你就错过了它最锋利的地方。

这是Goodhart定律在金融市场的完整形态："当一个指标成为目标，它就不再是好的指标。" 但更惊人的跨领域连接是——这条规律在语言学里叫"符号的能指化"，在传播学里叫"meme的稀释"，在人类学里叫"仪式的空洞化"。

举一个你绝对没想到的连接：为什么"AI Agent"这个词最近突然让所有人反感？因为它正在经历和"动量因子"一模一样的死亡过程——从一个有预测力的概念（能识别真正的技术突破），退化为一个人人都能贴的标签（失去了区分能力）。Coding会被商品化，"AI Agent"这个词本身也会被商品化。TALK君今天反复讲coding会commoditize，但他没意识到自己讲的这套框架同样适用于所有热词，包括他自己正在使用的所有KOL话术。

三、最出人意料的观察：他今天讲得最好的是Uber，但他把Uber放在了错的框架里

他讲Uber用AI提升operating leverage，讲Working Pod，讲Forward Deployment Engineer——这些他都零散讲了，但他自己都没意识到这三件事拼在一起是什么。

它们是同一个东西的三个面：AI落地不是"技术问题"，是"组织形态问题"。 Uber的Working Pod、软件公司的FDE、Anthropic的Sonnet被Codex追赶——这三件事共同指向一个被市场严重误读的真相：AI这一轮真正的护城河不在模型，也不在算力，而在"AI-native的组织结构"。

这里有一个极其反常识的推论：如果这个假设成立，那么未来最值钱的不是模型公司，也不是Hyperscaler，而是那些能把AI"嵌入进别人组织"的中间层公司——Palantir的FDE模式、Accenture的咨询壳、甚至Uber自己内部孵化的"AI转型方法论"，都可能成为下一轮的稀缺资产。

跨领域连接：这和19世纪末电气化的历史惊人一致——真正赚钱的不是发电机制造商（西门子、通用电气最终利润率有限），而是教工厂如何用电重新设计流水线的咨询公司和电气工程师群体（Frederick Taylor的科学管理运动的经济基础就是这个）。TALK君今天嘴里的"FDE"，本质上就是AI时代的Frederick Taylor。

所以今天这场直播里最被低估的一句话不是"美光是不是周期股"，而是他一句带过的"Uber可能是第一家真正看到operating leverage的公司"——这句话如果是真的，那它对整个二级市场估值框架的冲击，比任何一次芯片下跌都要深远。因为它意味着"AI增效"从叙事变成了财报里可量化的margin expansion，而这才是市场真正能定价的东西。

item.description:
## 一、把「割肉美光」放进整段独白里，你会发现一个被忽略的**元交易模式**
投资TALK君今天最真诚的一段，不是关于芯片周期，而是他反复回到同一个动作：**"我把ISRG清了，我把AMD换了Intel，我把Oracle换Microsoft的仓要考虑，我把美光加了但知道错了不加了"**。
如果把这些换仓动作抽出来做时间序列，你会发现一个**惊人的、他自己都没明说的规律**：他不是在"买卖股票"，而是在**不断替自己的"认知敞口"做再平衡**。基本面变差→清仓ISRG（不是止损，是"取消订阅"这家公司）；对Oracle判断更清晰→用Microsoft换Oracle（不是加仓，是"迁移信念"）。
这个模式的反常识之处在于——**大多数散户把仓位当作对股票的承诺，而他把仓位当作对自己判断的租约**。租约到期（判断变了）就退租，不管有没有亏损。这解释了为什么他能反复强调"割肉不重要，认知才重要"——因为在他的操作系统里，割肉根本不是损失事件，而是**信息更新事件**。
## 二、他讲「因子失效」时暴露了一个跨领域的深层规律：**任何被命名的东西都会失效**
他随口提到的那家量化基金

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Putin's Playbook – Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、地缘政治的"负外部性引擎"：为什么强者身边总是废墟

表面上看，Paine 描述的是俄罗斯的"顺序吞并"战略——一次消化一个邻居，制造缓冲区，等待时机。但真正令人震撼的洞察藏在她随口提及的一句话里："环顾俄罗斯和中国，它们被地球上一些最功能失调的地方所包围。是运气不好，还是它们本身就是共谋？"

这里揭示了一个反直觉的系统性真相：大陆型霸权不是"恰好"生活在废墟中，废墟是它生产出来的副产品。这就像生态学里的"顶级掠食者悖论"——为了维持自身的生态位，它必须持续制造周边的"生态贫瘠"。健康的邻居是威胁，只有失败国家才是安全的缓冲。

这带来一个跨领域的意外类比：这与平台经济中的"焦土策略"几乎同构——某些超级平台通过持续压低生态位内其他玩家的生存能力（而非直接消灭）来维持不可替代性。俄罗斯对乌克兰做的事、腾讯早年对独立开发者做的事、Meta 对新兴社交产品做的事——在结构上是同一种"生态位维稳"逻辑。

二、陀思妥耶夫斯基的"东方主义"：文学作为帝国潜意识的泄露

Paine 引用陀思妥耶夫斯基那段"在欧洲我们是奴才，在亚洲我们是主人"的日记，是整段演讲最耐人寻味的一击。

这里有一个大多数俄罗斯文学爱好者从未察觉的黑暗结构：《罪与罚》、《卡拉马佐夫兄弟》里那种对救赎、屈辱、被拯救的痴迷，其实是一种"帝国自卑—帝国补偿"的精神机制。当一个文明在西方面前感到二等，它就必须在东方创造出属于自己的"更低等的他者"来维持心理平衡。

跨领域连接来了：这与心理学中的"踢猫效应"（displaced aggression）在民族尺度上的呈现完全一致。陀思妥耶夫斯基不是在写游记，他是在为整个俄罗斯民族的心理位移提供哲学许可证。而更令人不安的是——Klyuchevsky 那句"俄罗斯是一个正在殖民自身的国家"，说明这种位移最终会转向内部：当外部扩张受阻，同样的暴力逻辑会向国内的社会阶层实施。布尔什维克对整个贵族阶级的清洗，本质上是对外扩张受挫后的"殖民能量"的内收。

三、一个惊人的观察：连续型帝国没有"止损函数"

Paine 提出了一个几乎无人注意的关键机制缺陷——"没有辞职委员会"（no council on when to quit）。这句轻描淡写的话是整个演讲的隐藏核弹。

海洋型帝国（英国、荷兰、美国）有天然的止损机制：股东、议会、财政周期、商船公司的资产负债表。赔钱的殖民地会被"卖掉"。但大陆型帝国的扩张成本是隐藏的、递延的、由沉默的农民承担的，因此它从未收到"停止扩张"的价格信号，直到系统性崩溃。

这里有一个让人后背发凉的跨领域映射：这与现代 AI 系统中的"奖励黑客"（reward hacking）在数学上同构。一个没有对齐机制的智能体，会不断优化其单一指标（领土/参数量/用户数），直到系统因为忽略了未被计价的外部成本而突然崩溃。普京不是一个失败的战略家，他是一个"对齐失败"的智能体——他的效用函数里没有"何时停止"这一项。

而更深的洞察是：中国和俄罗斯历史上反复的王朝崩溃循环，可能不是"腐败"或"外敌"造成的，而是这个缺失的止损函数在起作用。它们不是被打败的，它们是被自己缺失的反馈回路噎死的。这也解释了为什么 Paine 说 "there are no enduring alliances in this world"——因为任何理性的邻居最终都会意识到：与一个没有停止函数的实体结盟，等于把自己的存活概率外包给对方的内部崩溃时刻。

📝 转录文本

大陆型安全范式的游戏规则

In this world, there are certain rules for playing this game.

Rule number one: no two-front wars. I've shown you all the neighbors. If they gang up on you, it will be game over — in a very bad way — for you.

Secondly: no great power neighbors. Why? Because today's friend can be tomorrow's foe. And that spells trouble.

So, what do you do? You take on your neighbors sequentially, like one at a time. You set them up to fail, you destabilize the rising, you adjust the failing, and you set up buffer zones in between, and you await the opportune moment to pounce and absorb.

This is Vladimir Putin's game.

"豺狼国家"策略

Better yet, you get the neighbors to do the work for you. How? You sow their mutual resentments, you get them to fight each other, you deluge them with fake news — so that Russia can play the role of the jackal state: once the neighbors have sufficiently weakened themselves and weakened each other, Russia can move on in and steal a kill made by others.

这一范式的内在缺陷

This theory of security has certain problems.

One, you're surrounding yourself by failing states. You can look at Russia and China, and they're surrounded by some of the most dysfunctional places on the planet, and you can go, "Gee whiz, are they unlucky? Are they complicit?"

And moreover, there are no enduring alliances in this world, because the neighbors figure it out. The hegemonic power is just a long-term problem.

And there's also no council on when to quit. Like, how much territory do you take before you choke on it? And it turns out that there's been a tendency over the course of China's and Russia's long histories to overextend. And this helps account for the implosions of various empires and dynasties.

但请勿低估其历史有效性

Now, before you dismiss this security paradigm, understand: it was very effective. Certainly prior to the Industrial Revolution, no one cared in this world about collateral damage or killing a bunch of innocent people. This paradigm is all about killing people, breaking things, to take territory.

And you've seen it operating in real time in your own lives — in Syria, Ukraine, and other places. This is why those ancient ruins, the ones that still remain, are ruinous — because this sort of warfare is ruinous.

三段俄国精英的自白

All right. Here is one of the preeminent historians of the late Tsarist period, Vasily Klyuchevsky, who's describing his country. He said:

"The history of Russia is a history of a country in process of colonizing itself. Her area of colonization grows in tandem with her national territory — at times shrinking, at times expanding — age-old movement. Therefore, the periods in our history are the stages which our people have gone through in the occupation and development of the land acquired by them."

There is absolutely no mention of the people who actually live on this land. It's like irrelevant from his point of view. But this is the way Russians have long looked at things: that if you have small neighbors, someone big may take them over. And even worse, if the weak become strong in their own right, it's dangerous. So you want to keep moving outwards and expanding.

And here, a generation earlier, you have Fyodor Dostoevsky — the novelist, the author of Crime and Punishment and other light reads. Here he is confiding in his diary:

"In Europe we are hangers-on and slaves, whereas we shall go to Asia as masters. In Europe we are Asiatics, whereas in Asia we too are Europeans. Our civilizing mission in Asia will bribe our spirit and drive us thither."

So this idea of empire is very deeply rooted in Russian thinking.

And here is Count Sergei Witte. He's probably the most distinguished public servant in the late Tsarist period. He was a finance minister. And he's looking at the world in 1903 and he goes:

"Look, the problem for Russia is to obtain as large a share as possible of the outlived oriental states."

And he's thinking of the Ottoman Empire, but particularly of China. And he goes:

"Look, Russia historically, geographically has the undisputed right to the lion's share of the expected prey. And this elemental movement of Russia began a long time ago with Ivan the Terrible, aptly named. And the absorption by Russia of a considerable portion of the Chinese Empire is only a question of time — unless the Chinese get their act together."

So here you have a statesman at the highest levels of the Russian government who is looking at Russian national security — it's all about territorial expansion.

普京，以及大陆型战略的终极风险

Well, Putin also looks at the world this way, apparently.

The problem for the likes of Putin is: if a continental power botches strategy, its known world can vanish forever. And this is what happened to Imperial China, Imperial Russia, and many venerable civilizations.

I love this photograph of an aristocrat's whimsical palace that's long gone — as a result of one of the most horrific genocides of the 20th century, when the communists made good their promise to get rid of entire social classes. And I mean, get rid of — like, gone forever. With the Bolshevik Revolution and the ensuing Russian Civil War, followed by collectivization, and then the Great Purges that finished the job.

This is the continental world. It is a world without insurance policies.

Okay, now for the maritime world.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

## 一、地缘政治的"负外部性引擎"：为什么强者身边总是废墟
表面上看，Paine 描述的是俄罗斯的"顺序吞并"战略——一次消化一个邻居，制造缓冲区，等待时机。但真正令人震撼的洞察藏在她随口提及的一句话里：**"环顾俄罗斯和中国，它们被地球上一些最功能失调的地方所包围。是运气不好，还是它们本身就是共谋？"**
这里揭示了一个反直觉的系统性真相：**大陆型霸权不是"恰好"生活在废墟中，废墟是它生产出来的副产品**。这就像生态学里的"顶级掠食者悖论"——为了维持自身的生态位，它必须持续制造周边的"生态贫瘠"。健康的邻居是威胁，只有失败国家才是安全的缓冲。
这带来一个跨领域的意外类比：这与**平台经济中的"焦土策略"**几乎同构——某些超级平台通过持续压低生态位内其他玩家的生存能力（而非直接消灭）来维持不可替代性。俄罗斯对乌克兰做的事、腾讯早年对独立开发者做的事、Meta 对新兴社交产品做的事——**在结构上是同一种"生态位维稳"逻辑**。
## 二、陀思妥耶夫斯基的"东方主义"：文学作为帝国潜意识的泄露
Paine 引用陀思妥耶夫斯基那段"在欧洲我们是奴才，在亚洲我们是主人"的日
